chunk_findings.detail: Changing these hooks to `pass_filenames: true` makes ruff receive explicit file paths instead of `.`. Ruff does not apply its `exclude`/`extend-exclude` patterns to explicitly passed paths unless `--force-exclude` is supplied. The new entries (`uv run ruff check` and `uv run ruff format --check`) omit that flag. Thus, if the repository’s ruff configuration excludes a tracked Python path (e.g. `[tool.ruff] exclude = ["ddflow/_vendor"]`) and a branch modifies a file under that path, pre-commit will pass it explicitly to ruff and ruff will lint/format-check it, potentially failing the push even though the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` invocation would have skipped the excluded file.
chunk_findings.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml:ruff-check

chunk_findings.detail: The new scoping drops the environment’s `SKIP` whenever the command already carries its own leading `SKIP=` assignment. The removed implementation explicitly merged the inherited `SKIP` with the command’s own skip (`SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}..."`), because a shell command-prefix assignment overrides the inherited environment. Now, given environment `SKIP=slow-tests` and `command="SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files"` with a valid `since`, `scope_to_diff` returns `SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref <since> --to-ref HEAD`. When run through the shell, `SKIP` is exactly `lint`, so the `slow-tests` hook is not skipped even though the selected-tests plan set it; the old behavior would have skipped both `slow-tests` and `lint`. This can cause CI to run hooks that were meant to be skipped (or fail because a skipped hook now runs).
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff`

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test’s pre-commit hook will not run in the pre-push stage, so the second test fails (and the first passes vacuously). In `pre-commit`, a hook’s `stages` defaults to `[commit]` unless specified, while `CI.run`’s default command is the pre-push command `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push`. In `test_the_branchs_own_bad_python_still_fails_the_push`, the branch diff contains `mine.py` with `BAD = 2`, but the hook `changed-python-clean` is not selected for the `pre-push` stage, so pre-commit exits successfully without executing the script; `res.status` is `"passed"`, causing the assertion expecting `"failed"` to fail. If `pre-commit` is not installed, the whole file skips, so the intended regression gate may also be silently skipped.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_diff_scope.py:31

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert " --to-ref HEAD" in cmd` is an unanchored substring check, so it also matches `--to-ref HEAD~1` (or `--to-ref HEAD^`). If `scope_to_diff` returned `SKIP=frozen-workflow-files pre-commit run --from-ref base --to-ref HEAD~1`, the test would pass even though the CI diff excludes the pushed `HEAD` commit and could miss errors in the tip. The test should require the target ref to be exactly `HEAD`, not merely start with that text.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_the_commands_own_skip_applies_to_the_diff_scoped_run_too

chunk_findings.detail: The new leading-`SKIP=` parser assumes the assignment value is a single non-whitespace token optionally wrapped in one quote layer. A valid shell command such as `SKIP='lint, slow' pre-commit run --all-files` with a valid `since` matches only `SKIP='lint,` because `\S+` stops at the space; `lead.end()` then leaves `slow'` in `run`. The returned command becomes `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint," slow' pre-commit run --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`, which the shell parses as an unmatched quoted word (`slow'`) instead of invoking `pre-commit`, so the CI command is corrupted rather than preserving the original quoted `SKIP`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_LEADING_SKIP

chunk_findings.detail: The double-quote branch of `_leading_skip` does not implement shell escaping: inside a double-quoted `SKIP` value it treats a backslash as an ordinary character and the following `"` as a closing quote. For the valid shell command `SKIP="lint\"slow" pre-commit run --all-files` with an inherited environment `SKIP=slow-tests`, the parser closes the quote at `\"`, then treats the real closing quote as opening a new quote and returns `None` because it ends inside a quote. `scope_to_diff` then emits the original assignment unchanged except for the `--all-files` rewrite, e.g. `SKIP="lint\"slow" pre-commit run --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`. The shell sets `SKIP` to `lint"slow`, shadowing `slow-tests`, so the inherited skip is not merged and the skipped hook/test runs. The same escaping bug can also split a valid command inside a quoted value (`SKIP="\" --all-files" ...`) and rewrite the `--all-files` that belongs to the `SKIP` value, producing a malformed command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test only checks prefixes for the `lint, slow` and empty-`SKIP` cases, and only checks the scoped suffix for the `$(echo pwn)` case; it never asserts that `--all-files` has been removed for any of the new inputs. Thus a `scope_to_diff` implementation that returned, for example, `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'lint, slow' pre-commit run --all-files` or `SKIP="" pre-commit run --all-files` would satisfy the assertions even though the command would still lint the whole tree, which is the behavior the change is supposed to prevent. It should assert `--all-files` absence and the exact `--from-ref <since> --to-ref HEAD` suffix for all three quoted/empty-`SKIP` cases.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_quoted_skip_values_stay_literal_and_an_empty_one_stays_an_override

chunk_findings.detail: The new double-quote scanner still does not implement shell backslash escapes. Inside `"..."` it appends a backslash as an ordinary character and then processes the following character as if it were unescaped. For the valid command text `SKIP="a\\b" pre-commit run --all-files` (two backslash characters between the quotes), the shell would resolve the assignment value to `a\b`, but `_leading_skip` returns `a\\b` with `active=False`, so the surrounding `scope_to_diff` path rebuilds a single-quoted literal containing two backslashes and the CI run receives a different SKIP value. The same branch also treats `SKIP="lint\$slow" ...` as active even though `\$` is a literal `$`, causing the inherited SKIP not to be merged. This contradicts the docstring’s “value the shell would resolve it to” and the earlier requirement to merge a parseable leading SKIP with the environment’s SKIP.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new double-quote escape handling and the unquoted backslash handling do not account for backslash-newline line continuation. In shell, an unquoted `\<newline>` removes both characters, and inside double quotes a backslash also retains special meaning before a newline (not only before `$`, backtick, `"` and `\`). Given a multi-line CI command such as `SKIP=a\` + newline + `b pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell parses the assignment value as `ab` and the command as `pre-commit ...`, but `_leading_skip` appends the newline as part of the value and returns `a\nb`; `scope_to_diff` then rebuilds a single-quoted value containing a newline, changing the command. The same corruption occurs inside double quotes, e.g. `SKIP="a\` + newline + `b" ...`, where the expected value is `ab` but the parser keeps both the backslash and the newline.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The added double-backslash assertion only checks a prefix ending at `pre-commit run `. A returned command such as `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'a\b' pre-commit run --all-files` satisfies the `startswith` assertion even though `--all-files` was not replaced by `--from-ref/--to-ref`. The test would therefore pass while the CI run still lints the whole tree, which is the failure mode the diff-scoping change is meant to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:240

chunk_findings.detail: `_scope_the_run` uses `run.rpartition(" --all-files")` but does not guard against the marker being absent. If `run` contains no literal ` --all-files`, `rpartition` returns `head == ""` and `tail == run`, so the function returns ` --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD` concatenated in front of the original run. For example, given `scope_to_diff("pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push", tree, "base")` (or a `SKIP=...` variant with the same run), the result is something like ` --from-ref base --to-ref HEADpre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push` (or `SKIP="..." --from-ref base --to-ref HEAD pre-commit run ...`), which is not the original command and is not a valid shell command. The previous `run.replace(..., 1)` behavior left a command without `--all-files` unchanged; this change makes that path malformed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: Choosing the **last** literal ` --all-files` can replace the wrong occurrence and leave an actual `--all-files` flag in the run. For input `command="SKIP=lint && pre-commit run --all-files # see --all-files"`, `_scope_the_run` finds the ` --all-files` in the trailing comment, not the flag passed to `pre-commit`, and returns a command equivalent to `SKIP="lint" && pre-commit run --all-files # see --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`. The CI command still runs `pre-commit run --all-files`, so the whole tree is linted despite the diff-scoping change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: Outside quotes the escape handling treats `\<char>` as an escape pair for every following character, but in shell a backslash outside quotes is literal unless followed by `$`, `` ` ``, `"`, `\`, or newline. Given shell command text `SKIP=a\bc pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell assignment value is `a\bc`, but `_leading_skip` drops the backslash and produces the parsed value `abc`; the rebuilt command then skips `abc` instead of `a\bc`, changing the skip list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new backslash-newline case checks only the rebuilt prefix and that `--all-files` is absent; unlike the adjacent `a\b` case, it does not check that the diff range was appended. Given the test input `SKIP="foo\<newline>bar" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, a `scope_to_diff` implementation that correctly parses the continuation but returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'foobar' pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push` (or `... --from-ref HEAD --to-ref HEAD`) satisfies all assertions for that case. CI would then not scope the run to the branch diff, potentially linting nothing, while the regression test still passes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:244

chunk_findings.detail: When `_leading_skip` declines a double-quoted `SKIP` assignment containing shell expansion, `scope_to_diff` passes the whole command (including that verbatim assignment) to `_scope_the_run`. Given `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --all-files)" pre-commit run --all-files` with a valid `since`, `run.find("pre-commit run")` matches the text inside the double-quoted assignment, and the first ` --all-files` after that match is also inside that assignment. The function returns `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD)" pre-commit run --all-files`. The operator’s assignment is no longer verbatim, and the real `pre-commit run` still receives `--all-files`, so the CI run still lints the whole tree. This is a regression from the previous last-occurrence behavior, which would have selected the real trailing flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The “first ` --all-files` after `pre-commit run`” heuristic is not quote-aware, so a quoted file argument before the real flag can capture the replacement. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files' --all-files` with a valid `since`, `at=0` and the first literal ` --all-files` in `run[at:]` is the one inside the quoted `--files` argument. The returned command is `pre-commit run --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD' --all-files`, leaving the actual `--all-files` flag on the run (so the whole tree is still checked) and inserting the diff range into a file argument. The added test only covers the opposite order, where the real flag appears before the quoted argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new “only the default phrase” logic still uses plain substring replacement: `if DEFAULT_COMMAND in run: run.replace(DEFAULT_COMMAND, ..., 1)`. That replaces the first textual occurrence of the default phrase anywhere in the command, not necessarily the actual `pre-commit run` invocation. For example, with a valid `since=abc`, input `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files 'pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files' --all-files` contains `DEFAULT_COMMAND` only inside the quoted `--files` argument. The function returns `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files 'pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref abc --to-ref HEAD' --all-files`, so the real pre-commit run still receives `--all-files` and still lints the whole merged tree (and the quoted file argument is corrupted). The added test uses only a partial quoted marker (`' --all-files'`), so it does not cover a quoted argument containing the full default phrase.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The scanner does not keep the whole shell word when a `SKIP` value contains command substitution. It marks `$`/backtick as “active” but still ends the word at the first whitespace or operator after that marker. Given `SKIP=$(echo pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files) pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, after `SKIP=` it sees `$`, then the next character `(` is in the operator set and breaks the word; `_leading_skip` returns `(None, "SKIP=$", "(echo pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files) pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files")`. The shell assignment word is the entire `SKIP=$(...)` expansion, and the untouched remainder begins only after the matching `)`. A caller that uses `verbatim` as the immune assignment and searches `rest` for the default run phrase can therefore rewrite the text inside the command substitution (or emit a truncated assignment) while leaving the real run’s `--all-files` flag in place.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: Inside a double-quoted `SKIP` value the scanner treats every inner `"` as closing the outer quote, so it does not track quoting inside a command substitution. For `SKIP="$(echo "foo bar")" pre-commit run --all-files`, the outer quote is opened, the inner quote before `foo` is seen as closing it, and the following space inside the inner quoted string triggers the word-end break. `_leading_skip` returns a `verbatim` value ending at `SKIP="$(echo "foo` and a `rest` beginning with ` bar")" pre-commit run --all-files`, even though the shell word is the whole assignment. Thus a quoted command-substitution argument containing spaces or shell operators is not kept verbatim-immune; scoping code that trusts the returned `rest` can treat text inside the substitution as the command remainder and corrupt the command or miss scoping the actual run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The quoted-run case only asserts `cmd.endswith(f" --to-ref HEAD")`, not the full `--from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD` range. For example, if `scope_to_diff` returned `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files)" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref HEAD --to-ref HEAD`, the test still passes: the prefix assertion is true, the `--all-files` count is still one, and the command ends with `--to-ref HEAD`. That would scope the CI run to an empty diff (`HEAD..HEAD`) or omit the required start ref entirely, defeating the regression test’s purpose.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_a_skip_value_with_shell_expansions_runs_as_written

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_sub_end` spanner counts parentheses inside `$( ... )` without tracking quoting inside the substitution, so it can misparse a valid shell word. For `SKIP=$(echo '(') pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files` with a valid `since`, `_sub_end` starts at `$(`, then sees the `(` inside the single-quoted `'('` and increments depth to 2; the real closing `)` only brings depth back to 1, so `_sub_end` returns `-1`. `_leading_skip` then falls back to the old word break at the following `(`, splitting the assignment after `SKIP=$` and putting `(echo '(') pre-commit...` into the rest. `scope_to_diff` therefore reconstructs a malformed command / fails to replace the real `--all-files` flag. The same quote-blindness also causes premature termination for inputs like `SKIP=$(echo ')') ...`, where the quoted `)` closes the outer substitution in `_sub_end`'s counting. The added regression probe (`SKIP="$(echo "foo bar")" ...`) has balanced unquoted parentheses and does not exercise this case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_sub_end

chunk_findings.detail: The new quote-aware scan only honours backslash escapes while `inner` is empty: the `elif c == "\\"` branch is part of the outer `if inner:` / `elif` chain, so when a double-quoted span is active a backslash is ignored. In shell, inside double quotes a backslash before `"` escapes the closing double quote. For the valid command `SKIP=$(echo "a\")b") pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, `_sub_end` starts at `$(`, opens `inner="` at the first quote, ignores the backslash, then treats the escaped `"` as closing the quote. The following literal `)` inside the quoted word is therefore seen while `inner` is empty, so it decrements depth and returns an end index at that inner `)` instead of the substitution's real closing `)` after `b"`. The caller then believes the command substitution ended early and parses the remaining `b") pre-commit ...` as the rest of the command, so the diff-scoping/rebuild can corrupt or miss the actual `pre-commit run` invocation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_sub_end

chunk_findings.detail: The machine/load facts are still captured when `build` runs, which is after `RC.check` has executed the repro command (the new `check` argument is passed into `build`). The earlier fix only supplies a pre-run event-log snapshot and pre-run item/lease state (`st`); it does not make `F.machine(repo)` read the load at filing time or during the repro runs. For example, with `repro_runs=10` and `repro_test_timeout_s=30`, a repro command that burns CPU for several minutes can finish, the system can idle, and the bundle will record a low load average even though the intent requires recording the reproduction conditions (load, xdist) at the moment of the repro. This is the machine-load portion of previous finding #2 that remains unfixed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:out["machine"] = F.machine(repo)

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-run event-log snapshot is taken outside the guard: `events = log.read_all() if hasattr(log, "read_all") else log` runs before the `try` block. If reading the event log raises (for example, `log.read_all()` gets an `OSError` from a locked or corrupted log while `bug found --repro-cmd ...` is executing), the exception escapes `attach` and the bug is not recorded. That violates the function's own invariant that filing must never fail for want of evidence; every other evidence step (`RC.check`, `build`, `store`) is guarded and degrades to `{"repro": {"unavailable": ...}}`, so this is a concrete failure introduced by moving the snapshot before the repro run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` treats every non-`None` shell exit code as a completed repro run, so a failure of the outer redirection to the tail file is counted as a repro failure even though the repro command never ran. The random tail-file names only prevent a poisoned run from pre-creating the *next* file; they do not prevent the tails directory itself from being deleted, full, read-only, or removed by a tmp cleaner. For example, with `repro_runs=2` and `repro_tail_bytes > 0`, the repro command `rm -rf "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}"/ddflow-repro-*` deletes the throwaway tails directory during the first run and exits 0. The second run is still launched as `( ... ) > /tmp/ddflow-repro-*/<random> 2>&1`; the shell cannot create the tail file, exits non-zero without executing the repro command, `_one_run` returns that exit code, and `_run_at` records `failures: 1` and `reproduced: "yes"`. The same wrong verdict occurs for a harmless repro command like `true` if the tails filesystem is full or the tails directory is removed between `mkdtemp` and the run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion makes the bundle test pass whenever the shell line for `uv run pytest tests/test_x.py` exits non-zero, without proving that pytest actually ran at the recorded sha. On a host where `uv` is missing, not on `PATH`, or cannot start the project, the shell exits 127/usage-error before pytest is invoked; `_one_run` still records that as a completed repro run and `check` sets `reproduced="yes"` because the earlier fix only randomized tail-file names and did not distinguish shell/exec failures from a real test failure. In that environment the test passes while no repro command was run in the scratch checkout, and `bug found --repro-cmd "uv run pytest ..."` would record the bug as reproduced/confirmed instead of unavailable/unconfirmed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_bundle.py:85

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to pin that the repro tail file is “outside the checkout” and “never dirties the reproduced tree,” but it only asserts that the recorded shell line starts with `(` and contains `" > "` and `" 2>&1"`. It never inspects the redirect target. If `_one_run` builds a line such as `( repro_cmd ) > <scratch_checkout>/.ddflow-repro/1.out 2>&1`, the assertions still pass even though the tail file is created inside the scratch checkout. A repro command that inspects the working tree (for example, `git status --porcelain`, a test that fails on unexpected files, or a subsequent run that sees the leftover tail file) would then behave differently, yet this test would not catch the regression.

chunk_findings.detail: Changing `ruff-check` and `ruff-format` to `pass_filenames: true` makes Ruff receive explicit file paths. Ruff, by default, checks explicitly supplied paths even if they match `exclude`/`extend-exclude` or `.gitignore`; the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` respected the project’s Ruff exclusion configuration. With this change, if the repository has any intentionally excluded Python file (for example generated `*_pb2.py`, vendored code, or migrations containing an unused import), a diff-scoped run or `pre-commit run --all-files` that passes that path to `uv run ruff check` will now report the error and fail the push/CI, whereas it was skipped before. The same applies to `ruff format --check` at `.pre-commit-config.yaml:44`. Add `--force-exclude` to both entries (or otherwise filter excluded paths) to preserve the previous semantics.
chunk_findings.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml:38

chunk_findings.detail: `scope_to_diff` validates `since` with `W.rev(tree, since)` but then interpolates the original `since` directly into the shell command string: `command.replace(" --all-files", f" --from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD", 1)`. If `since` is a ref name containing shell metacharacters (for example a Git ref such as `foo$(touch /tmp/pwn)` or `foo;touch /tmp/pwn`, which can be valid ref names), `W.rev` can resolve it, so the function returns a command like `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref foo$(touch /tmp/pwn) --to-ref HEAD`. When the CI runner executes that command through a shell (as the surrounding command forms, including `SKIP=` prefixes and the previous `rc=0; ...; exit $rc` pattern, require), the shell expands/executes the injected content on the CI machine. The safe value is the commit hash returned by `W.rev`, or the ref must be quoted with `shlex.quote` before interpolation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail:
The test’s lint hook swallows non-“BAD found” grep failures. `SCRIPT` is `#!/bin/sh
if grep -q BAD "$@"; then exit 1; fi
exit 0
`, so it only exits 1 when `grep` exits 0 (marker found). If `grep` exits 2 because a passed file is missing/unreadable, or exits 127 because `grep` is not available, or misparses a filename beginning with `-` as an option, the `if` condition is false and the script falls through to `exit 0`. For example, `scripts/lint.sh deleted.py` returns 0 even though it could not check the file; a diff-scoped pre-commit run that passes a deleted or oddly named file could therefore see the hook “pass” when it did not actually lint the input.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_diff_scope.py:SCRIPT

chunk_findings.detail: The new SKIP-merging path rebuilds the leading assignment by inserting the raw captured `SKIP` value inside double quotes, so shell quoting in the original value is not preserved. Given `command = "SKIP='lint' pre-commit run --all-files"` and a resolvable `since`, `_LEADING_SKIP` captures `'lint'` and the function returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint'" pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`. When this is run through the shell, `SKIP` becomes the literal `'lint'` (or `inherited,'lint'` if `SKIP` was set), not `lint`; pre-commit therefore does not skip the `lint` hook, whereas the previous command preserved `SKIP='lint'` and did skip it. This can cause a hook the command intended to skip to run, potentially failing CI, whenever a leading `SKIP=` assignment uses single quotes or otherwise depends on shell quoting.

chunk_findings.detail: The new quote-stripping step only checks that the captured `SKIP` token starts and ends with the same quote character; it does not check that those quotes form a single balanced layer around the whole value. For the valid shell command `SKIP='lint','format' pre-commit run --all-files`, the captured raw token is `'lint','format'`. The code strips the first and last single quotes, producing `lint','format`, and rebuilds the command as `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}lint','format" pre-commit run ...`. When executed by a shell, pre-commit receives a `SKIP` value such as `lint','format` (or `inherited,lint','format`), which splits into hook IDs `lint'` and `'format`, not `lint` and `format`, so the intended hooks are not skipped.

chunk_findings.detail: After stripping a quote layer, the value is re-embedded inside double quotes, so characters that were literal inside single quotes become shell-active. Given `SKIP='$(touch /tmp/pwn)' pre-commit run --all-files`, the function returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}$(touch /tmp/pwn)" pre-commit run ...`. Executing that with a shell performs command substitution and creates `/tmp/pwn`, whereas the original single-quoted assignment would set `SKIP` to the literal string `$(touch /tmp/pwn)`. The same applies to other shell metacharacters such as backticks or `$HOME`, changing the command's semantics and potentially executing arbitrary code from a CI command/config value.

chunk_findings.detail: `_leading_skip` only treats quote characters as grouping, so it does not recognize an unquoted command substitution as part of the leading shell word. For the valid POSIX command `SKIP=$(echo lint) pre-commit run --all-files`, the loop breaks at the space between `echo` and `lint`, returning `own="$(echo"` and `run=" lint) pre-commit run --all-files"`. `scope_to_diff` then emits `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'$(echo' lint) pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`; when executed, the stray unquoted `)` is a shell syntax error (and, more generally, the assignment word has been cut in the wrong place). The parser should either handle command substitutions or return `None` for a word it cannot parse instead of producing a malformed command.

chunk_findings.detail: The parser treats only whitespace as terminating the leading `SKIP=` word, not shell operators. Given the shell command `SKIP=lint;pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell parses the assignment value as `lint` and the remainder as `;pre-commit run --all-files`, but `_leading_skip` consumes the `;` and the following `pre-commit` until the next space, returning own `lint;pre-commit` and rest ` run --all-files`. `scope_to_diff` then rebuilds something like `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint;pre-commit' run --all-files`, so the actual `pre-commit` command is swallowed into the SKIP value and the command tries to run `run`. Even `SKIP=lint; pre-commit run --all-files` keeps the `;` in the literal SKIP and skips the intended merge.

chunk_findings.detail: The double-quoted branch does not implement shell backslash escapes. For a valid command whose characters after `SKIP=` are double quote, backslash, backslash, double quote (`SKIP="\\"` in shell source), the shell resolves the assignment value to one backslash, but the code appends both backslashes and returns own `\\`; `scope_to_diff` then re-emits the wrong literal. The same branch also treats an escaped closing double quote as closing the quote, so an unbalanced shell word such as double quote, `a`, backslash, double quote, space is accepted as own `a\` instead of returning `None` as the docstring requires.

chunk_findings.detail: When `_leading_skip` returns `None`, the original leading assignment is left in the command and the existing diff-scoping step replaces the first ` --all-files` in the whole string. chunk_findings.detail: The parser still ends the leading `SKIP=` word only on whitespace; it does not stop at shell operators. chunk_findings.detail: The visible parser still marks unquoted `$` as shell-active, so a command such as `SKIP=$(echo --all-files) pre-commit run --all-files` is declined by `_leading_skip` (or at least cannot be safely re-quoted). `scope_to_diff` then performs its global replacement of the first ` --all-files` in the whole command string, which is the argument to `echo`, producing `SKIP=$(echo --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD) pre-commit run --all-files`. chunk_findings.detail: `_scope_the_run` replaces the textual *last* occurrence of `" --all-files"`, not the pre-commit run’s own flag. Given a valid command such as `run = "pre-commit run --all-files --files ' --all-files'"`, `run.rpartition(" --all-files")` selects the occurrence inside the quoted file argument and returns `pre-commit run --all-files --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD'`. The actual `--all-files` option is left in place, so the command still runs over all files (defeating the diff-scoping fix), and the file argument is corrupted. The same failure occurs with a trailing comment, e.g. `pre-commit run --all-files # --all-files`, where the flag is unchanged and only the comment is rewritten.

chunk_findings.detail: The new anchor is still purely textual: it finds the first literal `pre-commit run` and replaces the first literal ` --all-files` after it, without parsing shell tokens or quotes. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files'` (or the same command behind a parseable `SKIP=lint;` prefix), there is no `--all-files` option for `pre-commit`; the only occurrence is a quoted file argument, yet the function rewrites it to `pre-commit run --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD'`, so a run without the flag is not left untouched. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files' --all-files`, the first textual occurrence is again the quoted file argument, so that argument is rewritten and the real `--all-files` remains, leaving the run unscoped. The same textual search also regresses the unparseable leading-assignment path: for `SKIP=$(echo pre-commit run --all-files) pre-commit run --all-files`, `_leading_skip` declines on the unquoted `$` and the whole command is scoped, but the first `pre-commit run` is inside the command substitution, so the substitution is corrupted and the actual `pre-commit run --all-files` is left unchanged. chunk_findings.detail: The new scoping test is a plain substring match, so it rewrites `DEFAULT_COMMAND` wherever it appears in the shell string, not only when it is the `pre-commit run` option. The same failure occurs for a declined leading assignment such as `SKIP=$(echo <DEFAULT_COMMAND>) <DEFAULT_COMMAND>`: the first match is inside the command substitution, so the substitution is changed while the real `pre-commit run` still receives `--all-files`. chunk_findings.detail: The parser only declines shell expansions for `$`/backtick, but shell assignment values also undergo tilde expansion. For a command such as `SKIP=foo:[REDACTED:path] pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell would resolve `[REDACTED:path]` after the unquoted colon to the home directory, so `SKIP` becomes `foo:/home/<user>/bar`; `_leading_skip` instead returns the unresolved literal `foo:[REDACTED:path]`, and the caller’s rebuild single-quotes that value, leaving a literal tilde. This violates the function’s stated contract of returning “the value the shell would resolve it to” and changes the value passed to `pre-commit`.

chunk_findings.detail: `scope_to_diff` rewrites a parsed leading `SKIP=` assignment whenever the original command contains the substring ` --all-files`, even when `_scope_the_run` decides not to scope the run. For example, with an inherited `SKIP=ruff` and `command = "SKIP=lint; echo ' --all-files'"`, `_leading_skip` returns `own="lint"`, `_scope_the_run` returns the run unchanged because there is no default run phrase, but the function still returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint'; echo ' --all-files'"`. When executed, the shell sets `SKIP` to `ruff,lint` for subsequent commands, whereas the original command set it to `lint`. If no diff range is actually added, the command should remain as written; the `_scope_the_run` fix does not answer this because the leading assignment is rewritten independently of whether scoping occurred.

chunk_findings.detail: `lead.strip()` and `tail.strip()` use Python’s whitespace notion, which removes characters such as non-breaking space that POSIX shell does not treat as word separators. Given `run = "pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files\u00a0"`, `tail` is `"\u00a0"` and `tail.strip()` is empty, so `_scope_the_run` treats the run as the bare default phrase and returns it scoped with the trailing NBSP appended after `HEAD`, producing a `--to-ref HEAD\u00a0` argument. In a shell the NBSP is part of the last word, so the original command was not the bare default phrase and should have been left unchanged.

chunk_findings.detail: The new identity assertion requires `scope_to_diff` to return the command unchanged for `SKIP="$SKIP,lint" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`. That assignment is a safely quoted single shell word, and the run itself is the default phrase, yet the returned command still contains the literal `--all-files`. When executed, pre-commit still checks the entire merged tree, so the original failure mode (e.g. a pre-existing Ruff error in an unchanged file such as `tests/test_store.py:227`) can still fail the pre-push lint gate. The test therefore codifies a no-op for a realistic CI command shape rather than verifying that the `--all-files` option was scoped away.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `plain` regression assertion only checks that the command ends with ` --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`. If `scope_to_diff` were changed to append the range while leaving the original `--all-files` in place, e.g. `... --all-files --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`, this assertion would still pass even though the command still runs over all files. The test does not assert that the original `--all-files` option was removed.

chunk_findings.detail: The unquoted parser does not implement backslash escapes. In POSIX shell, a backslash outside quotes removes the special meaning of the next character, but the loop appends the backslash as ordinary text and then lets the next character hit the whitespace/operator break. For the shell source `SKIP=a\;b pre-commit run --all-files` (Python literal `"SKIP=a\\;b pre-commit run --all-files"`), the shell parses the assignment value as `a;b` and the remainder as ` pre-commit run --all-files`. `_leading_skip` instead returns `own="a\\"`, `verbatim=""`, `rest=";b pre-commit run --all-files"`. A caller that rebuilds the leading assignment from `own` will re-emit the escaped semicolon as an active command separator (and escaped spaces/newlines are split the same way: `SKIP=a\ b ...` yields own `a\` and a rest beginning with the escaped space, splitting the shell value `a b`). This changes the command’s semantics and can execute the text after an escaped operator.

chunk_findings.detail: The new loop asserts that `scope_to_diff("SKIP=$(echo lint) " + CI.DEFAULT_COMMAND, ...)` returns the source unchanged. Since `CI.DEFAULT_COMMAND` is the pre-push run containing `--all-files` (as the adjacent assertions require), the returned command still passes `--all-files` to `pre-commit`, so executing it still checks the entire merged tree and the original lint-gate failure can still occur. The leading assignment can be left verbatim while the trailing bare default run is rewritten, exactly as the same test requires for `SKIP="$SKIP,lint"` and for the quoted `$(...)` assignment; the “inseparable word” reason does not prevent scoping the run itself.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `quoted_run` assertion `assert cmd.endswith(f" --to-ref HEAD"), cmd` is an f-string with no placeholder, which default `ruff check` flags as F541; because the CI Lint gate runs Ruff over the changed files, this reintroduces a lint failure on this branch. The likely intended assertion was `f" --from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD"`, which would also verify that the scoped command uses the correct base ref rather than only checking the trailing `--to-ref HEAD`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_sub_end` counts parentheses without respecting quoting or backslash escapes inside a command substitution. For the valid shell command `SKIP=$(echo '(') pre-commit run --all-files`, the scanner sees the `(` inside the single quotes, never balances, and returns `-1`. `_leading_skip` then loses the substitution boundary and treats that `(` as an unquoted shell operator, so the returned run region begins with `(echo '(') pre-commit run --all-files` instead of ` pre-commit run --all-files`. `_scope_the_run` therefore does not see the bare default run phrase and `scope_to_diff` leaves `--all-files` in the command, so the pre-push lint still checks the whole merged tree. The same wrong end occurs for quoted close parens (`SKIP=$(echo ")") pre-commit run --all-files`, where it stops at the `)` inside the double quotes) and for escaped close parens (`SKIP=$(echo \)) pre-commit run --all-files`).

chunk_findings.detail: The new inner-quote scanner does not apply backslash escapes inside double-quoted text. Given the shell command `SKIP=$(echo "\"") pre-commit run --all-files`, the `$()` is balanced: the double-quoted argument is `"\""` (open quote, escaped literal quote, close quote), so `_sub_end` should return the index after the final `)`. Instead it opens `inner` at the first quote, closes it at the escaped second quote, reopens at the third quote, then sees the real closing `)` while `inner` is still set, leaves `depth` at 1, and returns `-1`. A valid command substitution is therefore treated as unbalanced; `_leading_skip` can lose the substitution boundary (the same failure mode as earlier finding #24) and the diff-scoping rewrite can leave `--all-files` in place.

chunk_findings.detail: Changing these hooks to `pass_filenames: true` makes ruff receive explicit file paths instead of `.`. Ruff does not apply its `exclude`/`extend-exclude` patterns to explicitly passed paths unless `--force-exclude` is supplied. The new entries (`uv run ruff check` and `uv run ruff format --check`) omit that flag. Thus, if the repository’s ruff configuration excludes a tracked Python path (e.g. `[tool.ruff] exclude = ["ddflow/_vendor"]`) and a branch modifies a file under that path, pre-commit will pass it explicitly to ruff and ruff will lint/format-check it, potentially failing the push even though the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` invocation would have skipped the excluded file.

chunk_findings.detail: The new scoping drops the environment’s `SKIP` whenever the command already carries its own leading `SKIP=` assignment. The removed implementation explicitly merged the inherited `SKIP` with the command’s own skip (`SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}..."`), because a shell command-prefix assignment overrides the inherited environment. Now, given environment `SKIP=slow-tests` and `command="SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files"` with a valid `since`, `scope_to_diff` returns `SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref <since> --to-ref HEAD`. When run through the shell, `SKIP` is exactly `lint`, so the `slow-tests` hook is not skipped even though the selected-tests plan set it; the old behavior would have skipped both `slow-tests` and `lint`. This can cause CI to run hooks that were meant to be skipped (or fail because a skipped hook now runs).

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test’s pre-commit hook will not run in the pre-push stage, so the second test fails (and the first passes vacuously). In `pre-commit`, a hook’s `stages` defaults to `[commit]` unless specified, while `CI.run`’s default command is the pre-push command `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push`. In `test_the_branchs_own_bad_python_still_fails_the_push`, the branch diff contains `mine.py` with `BAD = 2`, but the hook `changed-python-clean` is not selected for the `pre-push` stage, so pre-commit exits successfully without executing the script; `res.status` is `"passed"`, causing the assertion expecting `"failed"` to fail. If `pre-commit` is not installed, the whole file skips, so the intended regression gate may also be silently skipped.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert " --to-ref HEAD" in cmd` is an unanchored substring check, so it also matches `--to-ref HEAD~1` (or `--to-ref HEAD^`). If `scope_to_diff` returned `SKIP=frozen-workflow-files pre-commit run --from-ref base --to-ref HEAD~1`, the test would pass even though the CI diff excludes the pushed `HEAD` commit and could miss errors in the tip. The test should require the target ref to be exactly `HEAD`, not merely start with that text.

chunk_findings.detail: The new leading-`SKIP=` parser assumes the assignment value is a single non-whitespace token optionally wrapped in one quote layer. A valid shell command such as `SKIP='lint, slow' pre-commit run --all-files` with a valid `since` matches only `SKIP='lint,` because `\S+` stops at the space; `lead.end()` then leaves `slow'` in `run`. The returned command becomes `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint," slow' pre-commit run --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`, which the shell parses as an unmatched quoted word (`slow'`) instead of invoking `pre-commit`, so the CI command is corrupted rather than preserving the original quoted `SKIP`.

chunk_findings.detail: The double-quote branch of `_leading_skip` does not implement shell escaping: inside a double-quoted `SKIP` value it treats a backslash as an ordinary character and the following `"` as a closing quote. For the valid shell command `SKIP="lint\"slow" pre-commit run --all-files` with an inherited environment `SKIP=slow-tests`, the parser closes the quote at `\"`, then treats the real closing quote as opening a new quote and returns `None` because it ends inside a quote. `scope_to_diff` then emits the original assignment unchanged except for the `--all-files` rewrite, e.g. `SKIP="lint\"slow" pre-commit run --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`. The shell sets `SKIP` to `lint"slow`, shadowing `slow-tests`, so the inherited skip is not merged and the skipped hook/test runs. The same escaping bug can also split a valid command inside a quoted value (`SKIP="\" --all-files" ...`) and rewrite the `--all-files` that belongs to the `SKIP` value, producing a malformed command.

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test only checks prefixes for the `lint, slow` and empty-`SKIP` cases, and only checks the scoped suffix for the `$(echo pwn)` case; it never asserts that `--all-files` has been removed for any of the new inputs. Thus a `scope_to_diff` implementation that returned, for example, `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'lint, slow' pre-commit run --all-files` or `SKIP="" pre-commit run --all-files` would satisfy the assertions even though the command would still lint the whole tree, which is the behavior the change is supposed to prevent. chunk_findings.detail: The new double-quote scanner still does not implement shell backslash escapes. Inside `"..."` it appends a backslash as an ordinary character and then processes the following character as if it were unescaped. For the valid command text `SKIP="a\\b" pre-commit run --all-files` (two backslash characters between the quotes), the shell would resolve the assignment value to `a\b`, but `_leading_skip` returns `a\\b` with `active=False`, so the surrounding `scope_to_diff` path rebuilds a single-quoted literal containing two backslashes and the CI run receives a different SKIP value. The same branch also treats `SKIP="lint\$slow" ...` as active even though `\$` is a literal `$`, causing the inherited SKIP not to be merged. This contradicts the docstring’s “value the shell would resolve it to” and the earlier requirement to merge a parseable leading SKIP with the environment’s SKIP.

chunk_findings.detail: The new double-quote escape handling and the unquoted backslash handling do not account for backslash-newline line continuation. In shell, an unquoted `\<newline>` removes both characters, and inside double quotes a backslash also retains special meaning before a newline (not only before `$`, backtick, `"` and `\`). Given a multi-line CI command such as `SKIP=a\` + newline + `b pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell parses the assignment value as `ab` and the command as `pre-commit ...`, but `_leading_skip` appends the newline as part of the value and returns `a\nb`; `scope_to_diff` then rebuilds a single-quoted value containing a newline, changing the command. The same corruption occurs inside double quotes, e.g. `SKIP="a\` + newline + `b" ...`, where the expected value is `ab` but the parser keeps both the backslash and the newline.

chunk_findings.detail: The added double-backslash assertion only checks a prefix ending at `pre-commit run `. chunk_findings.detail: Choosing the **last** literal ` --all-files` can replace the wrong occurrence and leave an actual `--all-files` flag in the run. chunk_findings.detail: The new backslash-newline case checks only the rebuilt prefix and that `--all-files` is absent; unlike the adjacent `a\b` case, it does not check that the diff range was appended. Given the test input `SKIP="foo\<newline>bar" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, a `scope_to_diff` implementation that correctly parses the continuation but returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'foobar' pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push` (or `... --from-ref HEAD --to-ref HEAD`) satisfies all assertions for that case. CI would then not scope the run to the branch diff, potentially linting nothing, while the regression test still passes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:244

chunk_findings.detail: When `_leading_skip` declines a double-quoted `SKIP` assignment containing shell expansion, `scope_to_diff` passes the whole command (including that verbatim assignment) to `_scope_the_run`. Given `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --all-files)" pre-commit run --all-files` with a valid `since`, `run.find("pre-commit run")` matches the text inside the double-quoted assignment, and the first ` --all-files` after that match is also inside that assignment. The function returns `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD)" pre-commit run --all-files`. The operator’s assignment is no longer verbatim, and the real `pre-commit run` still receives `--all-files`, so the CI run still lints the whole tree. This is a regression from the previous last-occurrence behavior, which would have selected the real trailing flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The “first ` --all-files` after `pre-commit run`” heuristic is not quote-aware, so a quoted file argument before the real flag can capture the replacement. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files' --all-files` with a valid `since`, `at=0` and the first literal ` --all-files` in `run[at:]` is the one inside the quoted `--files` argument. The returned command is `pre-commit run --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD' --all-files`, leaving the actual `--all-files` flag on the run (so the whole tree is still checked) and inserting the diff range into a file argument. The added test only covers the opposite order, where the real flag appears before the quoted argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new “only the default phrase” logic still uses plain substring replacement: `if DEFAULT_COMMAND in run: run.replace(DEFAULT_COMMAND, ..., 1)`. That replaces the first textual occurrence of the default phrase anywhere in the command, not necessarily the actual `pre-commit run` invocation. For example, with a valid `since=abc`, input `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files 'pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files' --all-files` contains `DEFAULT_COMMAND` only inside the quoted `--files` argument. The function returns `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files 'pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref abc --to-ref HEAD' --all-files`, so the real pre-commit run still receives `--all-files` and still lints the whole merged tree (and the quoted file argument is corrupted). The added test uses only a partial quoted marker (`' --all-files'`), so it does not cover a quoted argument containing the full default phrase.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The scanner does not keep the whole shell word when a `SKIP` value contains command substitution. It marks `$`/backtick as “active” but still ends the word at the first whitespace or operator after that marker. Given `SKIP=$(echo pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files) pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, after `SKIP=` it sees `$`, then the next character `(` is in the operator set and breaks the word; `_leading_skip` returns `(None, "SKIP=$", "(echo pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files) pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files")`. The shell assignment word is the entire `SKIP=$(...)` expansion, and the untouched remainder begins only after the matching `)`. A caller that uses `verbatim` as the immune assignment and searches `rest` for the default run phrase can therefore rewrite the text inside the command substitution (or emit a truncated assignment) while leaving the real run’s `--all-files` flag in place.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: Inside a double-quoted `SKIP` value the scanner treats every inner `"` as closing the outer quote, so it does not track quoting inside a command substitution. For `SKIP="$(echo "foo bar")" pre-commit run --all-files`, the outer quote is opened, the inner quote before `foo` is seen as closing it, and the following space inside the inner quoted string triggers the word-end break. `_leading_skip` returns a `verbatim` value ending at `SKIP="$(echo "foo` and a `rest` beginning with ` bar")" pre-commit run --all-files`, even though the shell word is the whole assignment. Thus a quoted command-substitution argument containing spaces or shell operators is not kept verbatim-immune; scoping code that trusts the returned `rest` can treat text inside the substitution as the command remainder and corrupt the command or miss scoping the actual run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The quoted-run case only asserts `cmd.endswith(f" --to-ref HEAD")`, not the full `--from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD` range. For example, if `scope_to_diff` returned `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files)" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref HEAD --to-ref HEAD`, the test still passes: the prefix assertion is true, the `--all-files` count is still one, and the command ends with `--to-ref HEAD`. That would scope the CI run to an empty diff (`HEAD..HEAD`) or omit the required start ref entirely, defeating the regression test’s purpose.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_a_skip_value_with_shell_expansions_runs_as_written

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_sub_end` spanner counts parentheses inside `$( ... )` without tracking quoting inside the substitution, so it can misparse a valid shell word. For `SKIP=$(echo '(') pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files` with a valid `since`, `_sub_end` starts at `$(`, then sees the `(` inside the single-quoted `'('` and increments depth to 2; the real closing `)` only brings depth back to 1, so `_sub_end` returns `-1`. `_leading_skip` then falls back to the old word break at the following `(`, splitting the assignment after `SKIP=$` and putting `(echo '(') pre-commit...` into the rest. `scope_to_diff` therefore reconstructs a malformed command / fails to replace the real `--all-files` flag. The same quote-blindness also causes premature termination for inputs like `SKIP=$(echo ')') ...`, where the quoted `)` closes the outer substitution in `_sub_end`'s counting. The added regression probe (`SKIP="$(echo "foo bar")" ...`) has balanced unquoted parentheses and does not exercise this case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_sub_end

chunk_findings.detail: The new quote-aware scan only honours backslash escapes while `inner` is empty: the `elif c == "\\"` branch is part of the outer `if inner:` / `elif` chain, so when a double-quoted span is active a backslash is ignored. In shell, inside double quotes a backslash before `"` escapes the closing double quote. For the valid command `SKIP=$(echo "a\")b") pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, `_sub_end` starts at `$(`, opens `inner="` at the first quote, ignores the backslash, then treats the escaped `"` as closing the quote. The following literal `)` inside the quoted word is therefore seen while `inner` is empty, so it decrements depth and returns an end index at that inner `)` instead of the substitution's real closing `)` after `b"`. The caller then believes the command substitution ended early and parses the remaining `b") pre-commit ...` as the rest of the command, so the diff-scoping/rebuild can corrupt or miss the actual `pre-commit run` invocation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_sub_end

chunk_findings.detail: Changing `ruff-check` and `ruff-format` to `pass_filenames: true` makes Ruff receive explicit file paths. Ruff, by default, checks explicitly supplied paths even if they match `exclude`/`extend-exclude` or `.gitignore`; the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` respected the project’s Ruff exclusion configuration. With this change, if the repository has any intentionally excluded Python file (for example generated `*_pb2.py`, vendored code, or migrations containing an unused import), a diff-scoped run or `pre-commit run --all-files` that passes that path to `uv run ruff check` will now report the error and fail the push/CI, whereas it was skipped before. The same applies to `ruff format --check` at `.pre-commit-config.yaml:44`. Add `--force-exclude` to both entries (or otherwise filter excluded paths) to preserve the previous semantics.
chunk_findings.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml:38

chunk_findings.detail: `scope_to_diff` validates `since` with `W.rev(tree, since)` but then interpolates the original `since` directly into the shell command string: `command.replace(" --all-files", f" --from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD", 1)`. If `since` is a ref name containing shell metacharacters (for example a Git ref such as `foo$(touch /tmp/pwn)` or `foo;touch /tmp/pwn`, which can be valid ref names), `W.rev` can resolve it, so the function returns a command like `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref foo$(touch /tmp/pwn) --to-ref HEAD`. When the CI runner executes that command through a shell (as the surrounding command forms, including `SKIP=` prefixes and the previous `rc=0; ...; exit $rc` pattern, require), the shell expands/executes the injected content on the CI machine. The safe value is the commit hash returned by `W.rev`, or the ref must be quoted with `shlex.quote` before interpolation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail:
The test’s lint hook swallows non-“BAD found” grep failures. `SCRIPT` is `#!/bin/sh
if grep -q BAD "$@"; then exit 1; fi
exit 0
`, so it only exits 1 when `grep` exits 0 (marker found). If `grep` exits 2 because a passed file is missing/unreadable, or exits 127 because `grep` is not available, or misparses a filename beginning with `-` as an option, the `if` condition is false and the script falls through to `exit 0`. For example, `scripts/lint.sh deleted.py` returns 0 even though it could not check the file; a diff-scoped pre-commit run that passes a deleted or oddly named file could therefore see the hook “pass” when it did not actually lint the input.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_diff_scope.py:SCRIPT

chunk_findings.detail: The new SKIP-merging path rebuilds the leading assignment by inserting the raw captured `SKIP` value inside double quotes, so shell quoting in the original value is not preserved. Given `command = "SKIP='lint' pre-commit run --all-files"` and a resolvable `since`, `_LEADING_SKIP` captures `'lint'` and the function returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint'" pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`. When this is run through the shell, `SKIP` becomes the literal `'lint'` (or `inherited,'lint'` if `SKIP` was set), not `lint`; pre-commit therefore does not skip the `lint` hook, whereas the previous command preserved `SKIP='lint'` and did skip it. This can cause a hook the command intended to skip to run, potentially failing CI, whenever a leading `SKIP=` assignment uses single quotes or otherwise depends on shell quoting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: The new quote-stripping step only checks that the captured `SKIP` token starts and ends with the same quote character; it does not check that those quotes form a single balanced layer around the whole value. For the valid shell command `SKIP='lint','format' pre-commit run --all-files`, the captured raw token is `'lint','format'`. The code strips the first and last single quotes, producing `lint','format`, and rebuilds the command as `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}lint','format" pre-commit run ...`. When executed by a shell, pre-commit receives a `SKIP` value such as `lint','format` (or `inherited,lint','format`), which splits into hook IDs `lint'` and `'format`, not `lint` and `format`, so the intended hooks are not skipped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: After stripping a quote layer, the value is re-embedded inside double quotes, so characters that were literal inside single quotes become shell-active. Given `SKIP='$(touch /tmp/pwn)' pre-commit run --all-files`, the function returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}$(touch /tmp/pwn)" pre-commit run ...`. Executing that with a shell performs command substitution and creates `/tmp/pwn`, whereas the original single-quoted assignment would set `SKIP` to the literal string `$(touch /tmp/pwn)`. The same applies to other shell metacharacters such as backticks or `$HOME`, changing the command's semantics and potentially executing arbitrary code from a CI command/config value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: `_leading_skip` only treats quote characters as grouping, so it does not recognize an unquoted command substitution as part of the leading shell word. For the valid POSIX command `SKIP=$(echo lint) pre-commit run --all-files`, the loop breaks at the space between `echo` and `lint`, returning `own="$(echo"` and `run=" lint) pre-commit run --all-files"`. `scope_to_diff` then emits `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'$(echo' lint) pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`; when executed, the stray unquoted `)` is a shell syntax error (and, more generally, the assignment word has been cut in the wrong place). The parser should either handle command substitutions or return `None` for a word it cannot parse instead of producing a malformed command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The parser treats only whitespace as terminating the leading `SKIP=` word, not shell operators. Given the shell command `SKIP=lint;pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell parses the assignment value as `lint` and the remainder as `;pre-commit run --all-files`, but `_leading_skip` consumes the `;` and the following `pre-commit` until the next space, returning own `lint;pre-commit` and rest ` run --all-files`. `scope_to_diff` then rebuilds something like `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint;pre-commit' run --all-files`, so the actual `pre-commit` command is swallowed into the SKIP value and the command tries to run `run`. Even `SKIP=lint; pre-commit run --all-files` keeps the `;` in the literal SKIP and skips the intended merge.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The double-quoted branch does not implement shell backslash escapes. For a valid command whose characters after `SKIP=` are double quote, backslash, backslash, double quote (`SKIP="\\"` in shell source), the shell resolves the assignment value to one backslash, but the code appends both backslashes and returns own `\\`; `scope_to_diff` then re-emits the wrong literal. The same branch also treats an escaped closing double quote as closing the quote, so an unbalanced shell word such as double quote, `a`, backslash, double quote, space is accepted as own `a\` instead of returning `None` as the docstring requires.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: When `_leading_skip` returns `None`, the original leading assignment is left in the command and the existing diff-scoping step replaces the first ` --all-files` in the whole string. Given `SKIP=$(echo --all-files) pre-commit run --all-files`, the first ` --all-files` is the argument to `echo`, not the pre-commit flag, so the returned command becomes `SKIP=$(echo --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD) pre-commit run --all-files`: the pre-commit run is not scoped and the command substitution is corrupted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: The parser still ends the leading `SKIP=` word only on whitespace; it does not stop at shell operators. Given the valid shell command `SKIP=lint;pre-commit run --all-files`, the loop consumes `lint;pre-commit` as the assignment value and leaves ` run --all-files` as the rest. `scope_to_diff` then rebuilds a command like `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'lint;pre-commit' run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`, which runs `run` instead of `pre-commit` and sets `SKIP` to a value containing the command name. The new change only adds double-quote escape handling and does not address this operator boundary problem.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The visible parser still marks unquoted `$` as shell-active, so a command such as `SKIP=$(echo --all-files) pre-commit run --all-files` is declined by `_leading_skip` (or at least cannot be safely re-quoted). `scope_to_diff` then performs its global replacement of the first ` --all-files` in the whole command string, which is the argument to `echo`, producing `SKIP=$(echo --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD) pre-commit run --all-files`. That corrupts the command substitution and leaves the actual `pre-commit run` invocation unscoped. The new diff does not make the diff-scoping replacement aware of command-substitution boundaries.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: `_scope_the_run` replaces the textual *last* occurrence of `" --all-files"`, not the pre-commit run’s own flag. Given a valid command such as `run = "pre-commit run --all-files --files ' --all-files'"`, `run.rpartition(" --all-files")` selects the occurrence inside the quoted file argument and returns `pre-commit run --all-files --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD'`. The actual `--all-files` option is left in place, so the command still runs over all files (defeating the diff-scoping fix), and the file argument is corrupted. The same failure occurs with a trailing comment, e.g. `pre-commit run --all-files # --all-files`, where the flag is unchanged and only the comment is rewritten.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new anchor is still purely textual: it finds the first literal `pre-commit run` and replaces the first literal ` --all-files` after it, without parsing shell tokens or quotes. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files'` (or the same command behind a parseable `SKIP=lint;` prefix), there is no `--all-files` option for `pre-commit`; the only occurrence is a quoted file argument, yet the function rewrites it to `pre-commit run --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD'`, so a run without the flag is not left untouched. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files' --all-files`, the first textual occurrence is again the quoted file argument, so that argument is rewritten and the real `--all-files` remains, leaving the run unscoped. The same textual search also regresses the unparseable leading-assignment path: for `SKIP=$(echo pre-commit run --all-files) pre-commit run --all-files`, `_leading_skip` declines on the unquoted `$` and the whole command is scoped, but the first `pre-commit run` is inside the command substitution, so the substitution is corrupted and the actual `pre-commit run --all-files` is left unchanged. These cases contradict the docstring and the intent that the range land on the run’s own flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new scoping test is a plain substring match, so it rewrites `DEFAULT_COMMAND` wherever it appears in the shell string, not only when it is the `pre-commit run` option. For example, with `run = "pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files '" + DEFAULT_COMMAND + "'"` (the phrase is a single-quoted `--files` argument and the command has no `--all-files` option), `_scope_the_run` returns `... --files '<PRE_PUSH_RUN> --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD'`, corrupting the file argument. The same failure occurs for a declined leading assignment such as `SKIP=$(echo <DEFAULT_COMMAND>) <DEFAULT_COMMAND>`: the first match is inside the command substitution, so the substitution is changed while the real `pre-commit run` still receives `--all-files`. This can both corrupt commands and leave the run unscoped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The parser only declines shell expansions for `$`/backtick, but shell assignment values also undergo tilde expansion. For a command such as `SKIP=foo:[REDACTED:path] pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell would resolve `[REDACTED:path]` after the unquoted colon to the home directory, so `SKIP` becomes `foo:/home/<user>/bar`; `_leading_skip` instead returns the unresolved literal `foo:[REDACTED:path]`, and the caller’s rebuild single-quotes that value, leaving a literal tilde. This violates the function’s stated contract of returning “the value the shell would resolve it to” and changes the value passed to `pre-commit`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: `scope_to_diff` rewrites a parsed leading `SKIP=` assignment whenever the original command contains the substring ` --all-files`, even when `_scope_the_run` decides not to scope the run. For example, with an inherited `SKIP=ruff` and `command = "SKIP=lint; echo ' --all-files'"`, `_leading_skip` returns `own="lint"`, `_scope_the_run` returns the run unchanged because there is no default run phrase, but the function still returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint'; echo ' --all-files'"`. When executed, the shell sets `SKIP` to `ruff,lint` for subsequent commands, whereas the original command set it to `lint`. If no diff range is actually added, the command should remain as written; the `_scope_the_run` fix does not answer this because the leading assignment is rewritten independently of whether scoping occurred.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: `lead.strip()` and `tail.strip()` use Python’s whitespace notion, which removes characters such as non-breaking space that POSIX shell does not treat as word separators. Given `run = "pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files\u00a0"`, `tail` is `"\u00a0"` and `tail.strip()` is empty, so `_scope_the_run` treats the run as the bare default phrase and returns it scoped with the trailing NBSP appended after `HEAD`, producing a `--to-ref HEAD\u00a0` argument. In a shell the NBSP is part of the last word, so the original command was not the bare default phrase and should have been left unchanged.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new identity assertion requires `scope_to_diff` to return the command unchanged for `SKIP="$SKIP,lint" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`. That assignment is a safely quoted single shell word, and the run itself is the default phrase, yet the returned command still contains the literal `--all-files`. When executed, pre-commit still checks the entire merged tree, so the original failure mode (e.g. a pre-existing Ruff error in an unchanged file such as `tests/test_store.py:227`) can still fail the pre-push lint gate. The test therefore codifies a no-op for a realistic CI command shape rather than verifying that the `--all-files` option was scoped away.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:292

chunk_findings.detail: The new `plain` regression assertion only checks that the command ends with ` --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`. If `scope_to_diff` were changed to append the range while leaving the original `--all-files` in place, e.g. `... --all-files --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`, this assertion would still pass even though the command still runs over all files. The test does not assert that the original `--all-files` option was removed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:273

chunk_findings.detail: The unquoted parser does not implement backslash escapes. In POSIX shell, a backslash outside quotes removes the special meaning of the next character, but the loop appends the backslash as ordinary text and then lets the next character hit the whitespace/operator break. For the shell source `SKIP=a\;b pre-commit run --all-files` (Python literal `"SKIP=a\\;b pre-commit run --all-files"`), the shell parses the assignment value as `a;b` and the remainder as ` pre-commit run --all-files`. `_leading_skip` instead returns `own="a\\"`, `verbatim=""`, `rest=";b pre-commit run --all-files"`. A caller that rebuilds the leading assignment from `own` will re-emit the escaped semicolon as an active command separator (and escaped spaces/newlines are split the same way: `SKIP=a\ b ...` yields own `a\` and a rest beginning with the escaped space, splitting the shell value `a b`). This changes the command’s semantics and can execute the text after an escaped operator.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new loop asserts that `scope_to_diff("SKIP=$(echo lint) " + CI.DEFAULT_COMMAND, ...)` returns the source unchanged. Since `CI.DEFAULT_COMMAND` is the pre-push run containing `--all-files` (as the adjacent assertions require), the returned command still passes `--all-files` to `pre-commit`, so executing it still checks the entire merged tree and the original lint-gate failure can still occur. The leading assignment can be left verbatim while the trailing bare default run is rewritten, exactly as the same test requires for `SKIP="$SKIP,lint"` and for the quoted `$(...)` assignment; the “inseparable word” reason does not prevent scoping the run itself.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_a_skip_value_with_shell_expansions_runs_as_written

chunk_findings.detail: The new `quoted_run` assertion `assert cmd.endswith(f" --to-ref HEAD"), cmd` is an f-string with no placeholder, which default `ruff check` flags as F541; because the CI Lint gate runs Ruff over the changed files, this reintroduces a lint failure on this branch. The likely intended assertion was `f" --from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD"`, which would also verify that the scoped command uses the correct base ref rather than only checking the trailing `--to-ref HEAD`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_a_skip_value_with_shell_expansions_runs_as_written

chunk_findings.detail: `_sub_end` counts parentheses without respecting quoting or backslash escapes inside a command substitution. For the valid shell command `SKIP=$(echo '(') pre-commit run --all-files`, the scanner sees the `(` inside the single quotes, never balances, and returns `-1`. `_leading_skip` then loses the substitution boundary and treats that `(` as an unquoted shell operator, so the returned run region begins with `(echo '(') pre-commit run --all-files` instead of ` pre-commit run --all-files`. `_scope_the_run` therefore does not see the bare default run phrase and `scope_to_diff` leaves `--all-files` in the command, so the pre-push lint still checks the whole merged tree. The same wrong end occurs for quoted close parens (`SKIP=$(echo ")") pre-commit run --all-files`, where it stops at the `)` inside the double quotes) and for escaped close parens (`SKIP=$(echo \)) pre-commit run --all-files`).

chunk_findings.detail: The new inner-quote scanner does not apply backslash escapes inside double-quoted text. Given the shell command `SKIP=$(echo "\"") pre-commit run --all-files`, the `$()` is balanced: the double-quoted argument is `"\""` (open quote, escaped literal quote, close quote), so `_sub_end` should return the index after the final `)`. Instead it opens `inner` at the first quote, closes it at the escaped second quote, reopens at the third quote, then sees the real closing `)` while `inner` is still set, leaves `depth` at 1, and returns `-1`. A valid command substitution is therefore treated as unbalanced; `_leading_skip` can lose the substitution boundary (the same failure mode as earlier finding #24) and the diff-scoping rewrite can leave `--all-files` in place.
