chunk_findings.detail: The previous review’s fix intended to preserve the pre-run machine snapshot, but the `or` still does not distinguish “no snapshot was supplied” from “an empty snapshot was supplied.” `machine: dict[str, Any] | None` accepts `{}`, which is falsy, so `machine={}` causes `F.machine(repo)` to run again at build time—after `RC.check` has already executed the repro command. That can record post-run load/conditions as if they were the filing-time facts, the exact race from prior finding #1. Use `F.machine(repo) if machine is None else machine`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:out["machine"] = machine or F.machine(repo)

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-run evidence reads happen before the precomputed `check` is even retrieved, and the outer `try` still discards the sighting when those reads fail. If `log.read_all()` raises — for example a locked or corrupted event log — execution jumps to the outer `except` and returns `{"repro": {"unavailable": ...}}`; it never reaches `run = given.get("check")` or `sighting(run)`. A valid already-computed verdict is lost: calling `attach(..., given={"check": {"reproduced": True, "runs": 1, "failures": 1}})` with a `log` whose `read_all()` raises produces no `sighted`, so a failed repro is not recorded merely because the event log could not be read. It also skips `RC.check` entirely when `check` is absent. Moving `log.read_all()` inside the guard prevented the bug from escaping `attach`, but this independent ordering defect remains: the repro run/verdict must still be produced and returned when pre-run evidence collection fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: A repro command whose executable is missing is still recorded as `reproduced: "yes"`. `_one_run` only skips `shot.could_not_run`, `shot.timed_out`, or `shot.code is None`; a POSIX shell exits 127 when it cannot find the command in `line`, and `_tail_from_file` returns an existing empty tail file, so `_one_run` returns 127 and `check` reports `failures: 1`. For example, `cmd="definitely_missing_command_xyz"` reports the bug as reproduced even though the requested command never executed and therefore cannot confirm the bug. This is the prior #4 production-code defect; the triage only refuted the uv test-case by assuming uv is present in the suite, not the behavior for any other missing tool in a real repro command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The prior #3 fix assumes that an `ENOENT` on the tail file means the shell's redirect failed and the line never ran, but that is not sound: the line can run and delete the tail file before the read. The tails directory is created with the predictable prefix `ddflow-repro-*` in the default temp dir, so `cmd = "rm -r /tmp/ddflow-repro-*; false"` with `repro_runs=1` runs, deletes the current tail file, then exits 1. `_tail_from_file` returns `(None, 0)`, `_one_run` returns `(None, b"", 0)`, and `check` returns `unavailable` instead of `reproduced: "yes"`; a real non-zero run is discarded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_tail_from_file

chunk_findings.detail: All `repro_runs` executions share one `W.scratch_tree` checkout, and nothing resets it between iterations, so later runs do not see the recorded commit. A stateful command contaminates the tree: `cmd = "[ ! -e ddflow-marker ] && touch ddflow-marker"` exits 0 on the first run and creates `ddflow-marker`; because that file remains, the second run exits 1, so `check` reports `reproduced: "yes"` and `failures: 1`. In a fresh checkout per run the command would pass both times, so the failure rate is wrong and a bug can be confirmed that is not confirmable at the recorded sha.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier fix for previous finding 5 is not complete for relative redirect targets. The test parses `target` from the shell line and then calls `target.resolve()` without anchoring it to the run's `cwd` from `kw`. If `_one_run` emits a relative redirect inside the scratch checkout, such as `( ... ) > .ddflow-repro/1.out 2>&1` while `kw["cwd"]` is the scratch checkout, the shell creates the tail file inside the reproduced tree. But `Path(".ddflow-repro/1.out").resolve()` is resolved against this test process's current directory (the filing repo, via the `proj` fixture's `monkeypatch.chdir(repo)`), not against `kw["cwd"]`; the resulting `<repo>/.ddflow-repro/1.out` is not relative to `here`, so `not target.resolve().is_relative_to(here)` is true and the regression passes. The assertion should first resolve `target` against `kw["cwd"]` when `target` is relative.

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not actually pin that the idle-time message belongs to `T1`. It only asserts that the whole `doctor`/`status` output contains `"T1"` somewhere and `"no progress for"` somewhere. For example, if the surfaces print `T1: held by agent-a` and separately print `T2: no progress for 1000s`, the test passes even though the yield-requested `T1` lease's idle time is not surfaced. The same weakness applies to `"can now be broken"` at line 63 and the `status` assertion at line 67. A regression test for this intent should check the same line/section, e.g. that some line contains both `T1` and `no progress for`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new line-wise helper still does not pin that the matched line is the yield-requested surface. `_idle_line` returns any line containing both `T1` and `no progress for`; it does not require the line to appear under the `Yield requested:` section produced by `_yield_lines` or to carry the `[y]` marker. If `doctor` or `status` prints a health/warning line such as `  [!] T1: no progress for 1000s can now be broken` while the `Yield requested:` list is missing entirely, `_idle_line` returns that line and the assertions for `clock.fmt_age(AGO)` and `can now be broken` still pass. Thus the test can remain green even when the requested yield-requested lease list is not actually surfaced.

chunk_findings.detail: `overview` computes `yield_vs` once using a specific `time.time()` and `LBR.tree_activity(log.root)`, then calls `health_lines`, which now appends `LBR.doctor_notes(st, cfg, events, log.root)`. `doctor_notes` has no parameter for the already-computed `now`, tree activity, or verdicts, so it must re-evaluate them. With a yield-requested lease whose idle time is near the threshold, the first evaluation can omit it while the second includes it, or vice versa; the same lease can also be rendered twice in `ddflow status` (once in `health` from `doctor_notes`, once in `yields`/`yield_requested`) with different idle seconds. The status surfaces should share one verdict snapshot instead of recomputing independently.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/overview.py:211 (with ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:430)

chunk_findings.detail: `doctor_notes` passes `time.time()` as the current time to `verdicts`, bypassing ddflow’s `clock` abstraction that this module already imports and uses elsewhere. Given a test or runtime harness that freezes/overrides `ddflow.core.clock.now` (for example, to 1000) while lease progress timestamps are recorded through the same clock, `doctor_notes` still supplies the real wall-clock time. `verdicts` then computes an idle duration of roughly the real epoch time instead of the intended 1000 seconds, so the doctor/status idle-time assertion becomes nondeterministic or false and doctor can report a different idle time than the holder’s brief/heartbeat.

chunk_findings.detail: The new base-dict expression only emits `executed: False` when `check is None`; if a check mapping is supplied but does not contain an `executed` key, the recorded `repro_cmd` omits the field that the previous code always wrote. Since `check` is typed as `dict[str, Any] | None`, inputs such as `check={}` or `check={"reproduced": "yes", "runs": 1, "failures": 1}` are valid, and `build(..., repro_cmd="pytest", check=check)` returns `{"command": "pytest", ...}` with no boolean `executed` marker. This changes the existing `repro_cmd` schema for the checked path and can make consumers that require the field (or that treat a missing flag as “not executed”) misclassify the reproduction state; the code should default a boolean explicitly, e.g. merge over `{"executed": False}` when no check exists and over `{"executed": True}` when a check result is present.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:out["repro_cmd"]

chunk_findings.detail: When `given` contains a `repro_cmd` but no `check`, `attach` calls `log.read_all()` and `F.machine(repo)` before `RC.check`. If either of those evidence reads raises — for example a locked or corrupt event log, or a machine probe that raises — execution jumps to the outer `except` and returns `{"repro": {"unavailable": ...}}` without ever calling `RC.check`. For `bug found --repro-cmd false`, the requested repro command is therefore not run and the bug receives no `sighted` verdict, even though the function’s own contract is that evidence failures should not suppress or lose a repro verdict: a `build`/`store` failure after the run still returns `sighted`. A transient evidence-read failure thus silently suppresses confirmation/unconfirmation of the repro command.

chunk_findings.detail: The special case for “the program never ran” is too narrow: shell-level setup failures other than 126/127 are still counted as reproduction. Given `repro_runs=1` and `cmd = "true > /nonexistent_ddflow_dir/out"` (or `cd /nonexistent_ddflow_dir && true`), the outer tail-file redirect succeeds, but the inner redirection/`cd` fails before `true` is executed and the shell exits 1 (or 2). `_one_run` sees a non-126/127 code, reads the existing tail file, and returns that code; `check` then records `reproduced: "yes"` and `failures: 1` even though the repro command’s program never ran. This can mark a bug confirmed from an invalid command line rather than from a failing test.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The per-run `git reset --hard` and `git clean -xdfq` calls are made with `P.capture`, but their returned `Shot` is never inspected for failure or timeout. If either command fails, the loop still runs the next iteration in the same scratch checkout, so the “fresh checkout every run” guarantee is lost. Concrete case: `repro_runs=2` with `cmd = "[ ! -e ddflow-marker ] && { touch ddflow-marker; chmod 500 .; }"`. The first run exits 0 and leaves an untracked `ddflow-marker`; before the second run, `git clean -xdfq` cannot remove it because the directory is not writable, but `_run_at` ignores that failure. The second run sees the marker, exits 1, and `check` records `reproduced: "yes"` with `failures: 1`, even though every run in a fresh checkout would exit 0.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The updated bundle test now actually executes `uv run pytest tests/test_x.py`. In an environment where `uv` is not on `PATH` (for example, running the suite with system Python rather than through `uv`), the shell exits 127. After the fix for previous finding #3, 126/127 are treated as “could not execute” and are not counted as a repro run, so `run["executed"]` and `run["reproduced"]` will not satisfy the new `is True` / `"yes"` assertion. The prior test did not execute the command, so this change makes the test non-hermetic and dependent on an external package manager/network rather than a guaranteed failing command.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_bundle.py:78

chunk_findings.detail: The probe source passed to `python(...)` calls `sys.exit` but imports only `os`; standard `python -c` does not provide `sys` in the global namespace. Every run therefore fails with `NameError` (exit 1) before the marker-length check can run. This makes the test pass even when the scratch checkout is not reset/cleaned between runs: run 1 creates `seen` and exits 1 due to `NameError`; if `seen` survives, runs 2 and 3 also append to it and still exit 1 due to the same `NameError`, so `runs == 3`, `failures == 3`, and `reproduced == "yes"` hold without proving the fresh-checkout isolation the test claims to pin. The source needs to import `sys` (e.g. `import os, sys`) for the marker logic to decide the exit code.

chunk_findings.detail: The generated remediation command leaves the glob argument unquoted. For a live item with globs `["pkg.py"]` and tracked package files under `pkg/`, `stale_package_globs` can return `("pkg.py", "pkg/*")`, producing the note `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*`. If the operator copies and runs that command, the shell expands `pkg/*` to the files currently present in `pkg/` (or, with spaces or multiple matches, splits/mangles the argument), so `ddflow update` receives the wrong argument instead of the intended glob pattern. The command should quote the glob list (e.g. with `shlex.quote`) to be executable as printed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The remediation note emitted by `stale_glob_notes` still presents the corrected glob list as a bare shell argument, e.g. `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*`. For an item whose globs include `pkg.py` and whose tracked files now live under `pkg/`, the note can be copied by an operator; with matching files in `pkg/`, the shell expands `pkg/*` into multiple words (or mangles it if paths contain spaces), so `ddflow update` receives the wrong argument instead of the single intended glob. Moving the note generation to `leasebreak.stale_glob_notes` and adding yield-line tests does not fix the quoting problem.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The remediation command is still emitted with the glob argument unquoted, so the earlier confirmed finding remains unfixed. For a live item with `globs = ["pkg.py"]` and tracked files under `pkg/`, `stale_package_globs` can suggest `pkg/*`, producing the note line ending in `` `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*` ``. If the operator copies and runs that command in a shell, `pkg/*` is expanded to the files currently present in `pkg/`, so `ddflow update` receives one or more file paths instead of the intended glob and records the wrong globs for the item. The value should be shell-quoted as a single argument (or otherwise emitted in a non-expanding form).

chunk_findings.detail: The confirmed unquoted-glob defect is not answered by the commits shown here: the new `_idle_line` test only checks that a rendered line for `T1` contains the idle duration and `can now be broken`; it does not exercise `stale_glob_notes` or verify that the generated `ddflow update ... --globs ...` remediation command is quoted. Given a stale package glob such as `pkg/*`, the note can still be `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*`, which the shell expands or splits when copied, so `ddflow update` can receive the wrong globs. The delta therefore does not demonstrate that the confirmed issue is fixed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The remediation note is still not safe to copy into a shell. It wraps the corrected glob list in double quotes, but double quotes do not fully quote an arbitrary shell argument: they allow parameter expansion and are terminated by embedded double quotes. For example, if a live item has the glob `a$b.py` and tracked files under `a$b/`, `stale_package_globs` can produce the replacement `a$b/*`; the note then contains `ddflow update ITEM --globs "a$b/*"`. When copied into a shell, `$b` is expanded (to the environment value or, if unset, to the empty string), so `ddflow update` receives `a<x>/*` or `a/*` instead of the intended `a$b/*`. A glob containing a double quote would similarly split/mangle the argument. The generated command should be shell-quoted with `shlex.quote` (or an equivalent safe quoting method), not merely wrapped in double quotes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The added quoting regression test only asserts that the doctor note contains the substring `--globs "`; it does not assert that the glob argument is properly closed or that it is one safe shell word. For example, a note `ddflow update S1 --globs "stale/p*` (missing closing quote) or `ddflow update S1 --globs "['stale/p*']"` (Python list repr interpolated into the string) still contains `--globs "` and therefore passes, while the copied command is either a shell syntax error or passes the wrong argument to `ddflow update`. Thus the test does not actually pin the quoting fix for the previously confirmed stale-glob remediation defect.

chunk_findings.detail: The new base-dict expression only emits `executed: False` when `check is None`; if a check mapping is supplied but does not contain an `executed` key, the recorded `repro_cmd` omits the field that the previous code always wrote. Since `check` is typed as `dict[str, Any] | None`, inputs such as `check={}` or `check={"reproduced": "yes", "runs": 1, "failures": 1}` are valid, and `build(..., repro_cmd="pytest", check=check)` returns `{"command": "pytest", ...}` with no boolean `executed` marker. This changes the existing `repro_cmd` schema for the checked path and can make consumers that require the field (or that treat a missing flag as “not executed”) misclassify the reproduction state; the code should default a boolean explicitly, e.g. merge over `{"executed": False}` when no check exists and over `{"executed": True}` when a check result is present.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:out["repro_cmd"]

chunk_findings.detail: When `given` contains a `repro_cmd` but no `check`, `attach` calls `log.read_all()` and `F.machine(repo)` before `RC.check`. If either of those evidence reads raises — for example a locked or corrupt event log, or a machine probe that raises — execution jumps to the outer `except` and returns `{"repro": {"unavailable": ...}}` without ever calling `RC.check`. For `bug found --repro-cmd false`, the requested repro command is therefore not run and the bug receives no `sighted` verdict, even though the function’s own contract is that evidence failures should not suppress or lose a repro verdict: a `build`/`store` failure after the run still returns `sighted`. A transient evidence-read failure thus silently suppresses confirmation/unconfirmation of the repro command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: The special case for “the program never ran” is too narrow: shell-level setup failures other than 126/127 are still counted as reproduction. Given `repro_runs=1` and `cmd = "true > /nonexistent_ddflow_dir/out"` (or `cd /nonexistent_ddflow_dir && true`), the outer tail-file redirect succeeds, but the inner redirection/`cd` fails before `true` is executed and the shell exits 1 (or 2). `_one_run` sees a non-126/127 code, reads the existing tail file, and returns that code; `check` then records `reproduced: "yes"` and `failures: 1` even though the repro command’s program never ran. This can mark a bug confirmed from an invalid command line rather than from a failing test.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The per-run `git reset --hard` and `git clean -xdfq` calls are made with `P.capture`, but their returned `Shot` is never inspected for failure or timeout. If either command fails, the loop still runs the next iteration in the same scratch checkout, so the “fresh checkout every run” guarantee is lost. Concrete case: `repro_runs=2` with `cmd = "[ ! -e ddflow-marker ] && { touch ddflow-marker; chmod 500 .; }"`. The first run exits 0 and leaves an untracked `ddflow-marker`; before the second run, `git clean -xdfq` cannot remove it because the directory is not writable, but `_run_at` ignores that failure. The second run sees the marker, exits 1, and `check` records `reproduced: "yes"` with `failures: 1`, even though every run in a fresh checkout would exit 0.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The updated bundle test now actually executes `uv run pytest tests/test_x.py`. In an environment where `uv` is not on `PATH` (for example, running the suite with system Python rather than through `uv`), the shell exits 127. After the fix for previous finding #3, 126/127 are treated as “could not execute” and are not counted as a repro run, so `run["executed"]` and `run["reproduced"]` will not satisfy the new `is True` / `"yes"` assertion. The prior test did not execute the command, so this change makes the test non-hermetic and dependent on an external package manager/network rather than a guaranteed failing command.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_bundle.py:78

chunk_findings.detail: The probe source passed to `python(...)` calls `sys.exit` but imports only `os`; standard `python -c` does not provide `sys` in the global namespace. Every run therefore fails with `NameError` (exit 1) before the marker-length check can run. This makes the test pass even when the scratch checkout is not reset/cleaned between runs: run 1 creates `seen` and exits 1 due to `NameError`; if `seen` survives, runs 2 and 3 also append to it and still exit 1 due to the same `NameError`, so `runs == 3`, `failures == 3`, and `reproduced == "yes"` hold without proving the fresh-checkout isolation the test claims to pin. The source needs to import `sys` (e.g. `import os, sys`) for the marker logic to decide the exit code.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_verify.py:84 (`test_how_many_runs_is_a_knob_and_each_run_sees_a_fresh_checkout`)

chunk_findings.detail: A failed pre-run evidence read is not marked as failed; it is left as `None`, the same sentinel used when no pre-run read was needed. After `RC.check` has executed the repro command, `attach` retries any `None` value. Thus, if `log.read_all()` raises before the run (for example, a transient lock on the event log) but succeeds after the run, `build` receives the post-run event log as though it were the pre-run snapshot. With `given={"repro_cmd": "pytest -k flaky"}`, the repro command can write events during `RC.check`; the second `log.read_all()` then includes those post-run events, violating the stated pre-run evidence contract and potentially attributing repro-run activity to the filing context. The same pattern applies to `F.machine(repo)`: a pre-run machine probe failure followed by a successful post-run probe records load/process conditions after the repro command has run, which is misleading for flake diagnosis.

chunk_findings.detail: `overview` computes `yield_vs` once using a specific `time.time()` and `LBR.tree_activity(log.root)`, then calls `health_lines`, which now appends `LBR.doctor_notes(st, cfg, events, log.root)`. `doctor_notes` has no parameter for the already-computed `now`, tree activity, or verdicts, so it must re-evaluate them. With a yield-requested lease whose idle time is near the threshold, the first evaluation can omit it while the second includes it, or vice versa; the same lease can also be rendered twice in `ddflow status` (once in `health` from `doctor_notes`, once in `yields`/`yield_requested`) with different idle seconds. The status surfaces should share one verdict snapshot instead of recomputing independently.

chunk_findings.detail: `doctor_notes` passes `time.time()` as the current time to `verdicts`, bypassing ddflow’s `clock` abstraction that this module already imports and uses elsewhere. Given a test or runtime harness that freezes/overrides `ddflow.core.clock.now` (for example, to 1000) while lease progress timestamps are recorded through the same clock, `doctor_notes` still supplies the real wall-clock time. `verdicts` then computes an idle duration of roughly the real epoch time instead of the intended 1000 seconds, so the doctor/status idle-time assertion becomes nondeterministic or false and doctor can report a different idle time than the holder’s brief/heartbeat.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test does not actually pin the intended copy-pastable remedy. It only requires some line containing `"now the package"` to also contain the substring `--globs "`; it does not require that line to mention task `S1`, the stale glob `stale/p.py`, the corrected package glob `stale/p`, or that the shell-quoted argument is closed. For example, if `doctor` emits `S1: stale glob stale/p.py now the package, use --globs "stale/p.py` (unterminated quote) or `S1: stale glob stale/p.py now the package, use --globs "stale/p.py"` (the old stale glob, not the corrected package glob), the test still passes even though the remedy is not the required corrected, shell-safe one.

chunk_findings.detail: `overview` snapshots yield verdicts once with `LBR.verdicts(..., time.time(), LBR.tree_activity(log.root))`, then calls `health_lines`, which now appends `LBR.doctor_notes(st, cfg, events, log.root)`. Because `doctor_notes` receives no already-computed `now`, tree activity, or verdicts, it re-evaluates the same lease independently. For a lease whose idle time is within one execution interval of the yield threshold, the first evaluation can exclude it while the second includes it, or vice versa; in one `ddflow status` run this can produce a health note saying a lease is yield-requested while `data["yield_requested"]` and the `Yield requested:` section are empty, or print two different idle times for the same lease. chunk_findings.detail: The assertion does not actually pin shell quoting. On POSIX, `shlex.quote("stale/p/")` returns `stale/p/` unchanged because letters, dot, and slash are shell-safe, so the test expects the unquoted command ` `ddflow update S1 --globs stale/p/` `. Thus a doctor note that emits the corrected glob without any shell quoting passes, and the test never exercises the `pkg/*` expansion case named in its docstring; the intended “copy-pastable, shell-quoted argument” property is not pinned.

chunk_findings.detail: When `given` supplies a `check` that is the result of an already-executed repro command, `attach` skips its own pre-run evidence capture and only reads `log.read_all()` and `F.machine()` inside the bundle-building `try`. Those reads occur after the caller’s repro run, so the bundle records post-run evidence as the pre-run snapshot. For example, if a caller runs `res = RC.check(repo, sha, "ddflow event append --text from-repro", ...)` and then calls `attach(..., repro_cmd="ddflow event append --text from-repro", check=res)`, any event written by that repro command is read back by `log.read_all()` and stored in the bundle, exactly the post-run masquerade that the earlier fix was intended to eliminate; the comment’s claim that this read is “still pre-run” is false for a supplied check that actually ran.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: The unavailable records returned before any run are still missing `"executed": False`. `check(repo, "", "pytest", 1, 10, 100)` returns `{"unavailable": "repro command is empty"}`; `check(repo, "deadbeef", "pytest", 1, 10, 100)` can return `{"unavailable": "the tree sha ... is not recorded"}`; and `_run_at` returns `{"unavailable": "no scratch checkout ...", "load": ...}` when `s.path is None`. The bundle code’s current default from the earlier fix (`dict(check).setdefault("executed", check is not None)`) then turns any such check dict into `executed: True`, so a bug can be recorded as having executed a repro when no command was run or no scratch checkout was made. This is inconsistent with the later no-codes path, which explicitly records `executed: False`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:check/_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: After the shell has already reached an exit code, `_one_run` discards that exit code if the tail file cannot be opened, assuming the line never ran. The repro line itself can remove or make inaccessible its own stdout file. For example, with `tail_bytes=100` and `repro_cmd='tail=$(readlink /proc/self/fd/1); rm -f "$tail"; exit 1'`, the subshell exits 1, but `_tail_from_file` fails to open the removed tail file, `_one_run` returns `None`, and `_run_at` counts the attempt as `unreached`. Thus a run that did reach a failing exit code is not counted in `failures`; if other runs succeed, the record says `reproduced: "no"` despite a confirming failure. The same can happen if the line chmods the tail file/path or replaces it with a symlink, so the “tail file missing means the line never ran” assumption is wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The `python()` helper builds a shell command by interpolating `sys.executable` and `source` inside double quotes without shell escaping. For example, `python('print("x")')` produces `"python" -c "print("x")"`; the shell terminates the `-c` argument at the inner quote and then treats `x` as a separate command, so the intended repro snippet is not executed. The same interpolation also expands `$`, backticks, or similar shell syntax in the source or interpreter path. Because every test uses this helper to build the command that `reprocheck` runs through the shell, any natural snippet containing a double quote (or an interpreter path containing shell-active characters) yields a wrong repro command.

chunk_findings.detail: The generated remediation command leaves the glob argument unquoted. For a live item with globs `["pkg.py"]` and tracked package files under `pkg/`, `stale_package_globs` can return `("pkg.py", "pkg/*")`, producing the note `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*`. If the operator copies and runs that command, the shell expands `pkg/*` to the files currently present in `pkg/` (or, with spaces or multiple matches, splits/mangles the argument), so `ddflow update` receives the wrong argument instead of the intended glob pattern. The command should quote the glob list (e.g. with `shlex.quote`) to be executable as printed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The remediation note emitted by `stale_glob_notes` still presents the corrected glob list as a bare shell argument, e.g. `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*`. For an item whose globs include `pkg.py` and whose tracked files now live under `pkg/`, the note can be copied by an operator; with matching files in `pkg/`, the shell expands `pkg/*` into multiple words (or mangles it if paths contain spaces), so `ddflow update` receives the wrong argument instead of the single intended glob. Moving the note generation to `leasebreak.stale_glob_notes` and adding yield-line tests does not fix the quoting problem.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The remediation command is still emitted with the glob argument unquoted, so the earlier confirmed finding remains unfixed. For a live item with `globs = ["pkg.py"]` and tracked files under `pkg/`, `stale_package_globs` can suggest `pkg/*`, producing the note line ending in `` `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*` ``. If the operator copies and runs that command in a shell, `pkg/*` is expanded to the files currently present in `pkg/`, so `ddflow update` receives one or more file paths instead of the intended glob and records the wrong globs for the item. The value should be shell-quoted as a single argument (or otherwise emitted in a non-expanding form).

chunk_findings.detail: The confirmed unquoted-glob defect is not answered by the commits shown here: the new `_idle_line` test only checks that a rendered line for `T1` contains the idle duration and `can now be broken`; it does not exercise `stale_glob_notes` or verify that the generated `ddflow update ... --globs ...` remediation command is quoted. Given a stale package glob such as `pkg/*`, the note can still be `ddflow update ITEM --globs pkg/*`, which the shell expands or splits when copied, so `ddflow update` can receive the wrong globs. The delta therefore does not demonstrate that the confirmed issue is fixed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The remediation note is still not safe to copy into a shell. It wraps the corrected glob list in double quotes, but double quotes do not fully quote an arbitrary shell argument: they allow parameter expansion and are terminated by embedded double quotes. For example, if a live item has the glob `a$b.py` and tracked files under `a$b/`, `stale_package_globs` can produce the replacement `a$b/*`; the note then contains `ddflow update ITEM --globs "a$b/*"`. When copied into a shell, `$b` is expanded (to the environment value or, if unset, to the empty string), so `ddflow update` receives `a<x>/*` or `a/*` instead of the intended `a$b/*`. A glob containing a double quote would similarly split/mangle the argument. The generated command should be shell-quoted with `shlex.quote` (or an equivalent safe quoting method), not merely wrapped in double quotes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:stale_glob_notes

chunk_findings.detail: The added quoting regression test only asserts that the doctor note contains the substring `--globs "`; it does not assert that the glob argument is properly closed or that it is one safe shell word. For example, a note `ddflow update S1 --globs "stale/p*` (missing closing quote) or `ddflow update S1 --globs "['stale/p*']"` (Python list repr interpolated into the string) still contains `--globs "` and therefore passes, while the copied command is either a shell syntax error or passes the wrong argument to `ddflow update`. Thus the test does not actually pin the quoting fix for the previously confirmed stale-glob remediation defect.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_yield_surfaces.py:test_doctor_quotes_the_remedy_for_a_stale_package_glob

chunk_findings.detail: The new “quoting” regression test does not actually pin a quoted unsafe glob. It creates the package `stale/p/` and then asserts the note contains `` `ddflow update S1 --globs {shlex.quote('stale/p/')}` ``. But `shlex.quote('stale/p/')` returns the string unchanged (`stale/p/`), so the assertion accepts an unquoted `--globs stale/p/` argument and does not require an open and closed shell word. The glob that motivated the fix is the package glob form (`pkg/*` / `stale/p/*`), which `shlex.quote` renders as `'stale/p/*'`; using `stale/p/` means the test either fails against a note that correctly quotes `stale/p/*` or passes without exercising the shell-expansion case it claims to cover. The pin should force/assert the unsafe suggested glob, e.g. expect `shlex.quote('stale/p/*')` (`'stale/p/*'`) or otherwise assert the argument is one balanced quoted shell word containing `*`.

chunk_findings.detail: `overview` evaluates the yield verdicts once with `LBR.verdicts(st, cfg, events, time.time(), LBR.tree_activity(log.root))`, then calls `health_lines`, which now appends `LBR.doctor_notes(st, cfg, events, log.root)`. `doctor_notes` receives no already-computed `now`, tree activity, or verdicts, so it must re-evaluate the same lease verdicts with a fresh clock. A `ddflow status` run for a lease whose idle time crosses the yield threshold between those two evaluations can therefore be internally inconsistent: the first evaluation may produce no `data["yield_requested"]` and no `yields` line, while the `health` notes produced by `doctor_notes` say the lease is yield-requested; or the reverse can happen. When both evaluations include the lease, the same lease is surfaced twice in status with potentially different idle times. The earlier refutation that status evaluates verdicts once does not answer this diff, because the added `doctor_notes` call is inside `health_lines` (visible after `ordered = wait_order(...)`), and `overview` calls `health_lines`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` only rejects exit codes 126/127 as “the shell answered before the line’s program ran”, but a failing redirection or failing builtin before the intended program does the same thing and is still counted as a reproduced failure. For example, `check(repo, sha, "true > /nonexistent/ddflow-repro/out", 1, 10, 100)` creates the outer tail file, the inner redirection fails before `true` runs, the subshell exits non-zero with the shell’s “cannot create” error in the tail, `_one_run` returns that non-zero code, and `_run_at` records `reproduced: "yes"` even though no repro program ran.

chunk_findings.detail: Repeated runs share one scratch checkout and are “reset” only with `git reset --hard` and `git clean -xdfq`, which do not clear local git config or other `.git` state, so an earlier run can poison a later run and fabricate a failure. With `repro_runs=2` and `repro_cmd='git config --get repro.poison >/dev/null && exit 1 || { git config repro.poison 1; exit 0; }'`, the first attempt exits 0 and writes `.git/config`; the reset/clean between attempts does not remove that marker; the second attempt exits 1, so `check` records `reproduced: "yes"` and `failures: 1` even though on a fresh checkout at the recorded sha the command would always exit 0.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The `python()` helper still embeds `sys.executable` inside double quotes instead of using `shlex.quote(sys.executable)`. Double quotes do not prevent shell expansion of `$` or backticks, and a double quote in the path breaks the command. For example, if `sys.executable` is `/tmp/a$HOME/python`, `python("import sys; sys.exit(1)")` produces `"/tmp/a$HOME/python" -c 'import sys; sys.exit(1)'`; the shell expands `$HOME`, runs the wrong path or fails to find the interpreter, and tests such as `test_a_run_that_fails_is_the_sighting_that_reproduces` can record an unavailable/no-repro run instead of the intended `reproduced: yes`. This makes the new tests environment-dependent and only partially answers the earlier shell-escaping finding.

chunk_findings.detail: The repro run is not bound to the bug’s recorded sha. When `repro_cmd` is supplied, `attach` reads `F.tree(repo).get("tree_sha", "")` once and passes that sha to `RC.check`, but it does not return that sha in the sighting, nor does it use the bug’s already-recorded sha (despite having `bid` and `st`). If the HEAD changes while the repro command is running, the bug can be recorded as confirmed at a different sha than the one on which the command actually ran. For example, HEAD is `A`; `bug found --repro-cmd "sleep 10"` starts the repro run at `A`; another agent commits `B` during the sleep; the handler then records the bug at current sha `B` with `sighted={"reproduced": true, ...}`. The bug is marked confirmed by a run at `A`, while `bug fixed` and later lists treat it as a bug at `B`. The same problem occurs if `attach` is called for an existing bug: it still runs at the current tree sha instead of the bug’s recorded sha.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: For a caller-supplied `check`, the code reads the event log and machine facts after the repro run has already happened. The comment claims this is “still pre-run,” but if the handler performs the check itself and passes the result, `log.read_all()` and `F.machine(repo)` are called after that command completed. For example, a handler runs `RC.check(repo, sha, "ddflow note during-repro", ...)` and then calls `attach(..., check=run, repro_cmd="ddflow note during-repro")`; the note event written by the repro command is then included in the bundle’s event snapshot as if it had existed before the repro command. Likewise, load/xdist conditions captured by `F.machine` are post-run, not the conditions during the flaky run, corrupting the recorded failure-rate context.

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` treats any failure to open the tail file as “the line never ran”, but the line can delete or replace the harness tail file after it has already run and produced an exit code. For example, on a default Linux setup, `check(repo, sha, 'rm -rf "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}"/ddflow-repro-*; exit 1', 1, 10, 100)` causes the outer shell to create the random tail file, the line then removes the whole `ddflow-repro-` temp directory, and the subshell exits 1. `P.run_shell` returns exit code 1, but `_tail_from_file` gets `ENOENT`, `_one_run` returns `None`, and `_run_at` records the run as unreached/unavailable instead of `reproduced: yes`. This is wrong under the module’s own rule: the run reached an exit code, so it must be counted even if the output cannot be recovered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The per-run reset does not actually return the scratch checkout to the recorded sha because `git clean -xdfq` does not remove nested Git repositories; Git requires `-ff` for that. With `repro_runs=2` and `cmd='mkdir nested && git init -q nested && exit 0'`, the first run exits 0 and leaves `nested/` containing `.git`. Before the second run, `git clean -xdfq` skips `nested` instead of deleting it, so the second run’s `mkdir nested` fails and exits 1. `_run_at` then records `failures: 1` and `reproduced: yes` for a failure that only exists because the scratch tree was not reset. The `.git/config` snapshot added in response to the earlier poisoning finding does not address this untracked-state contamination.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to pin that the tail budget bounds the run itself, but its assertions are also satisfied by an implementation that redirects the whole command output to an outside scratch file and then reads the entire file into memory to slice the tail: the recorded shell line still starts with `(`, contains ` > ` and ` 2>&1`, the extracted target resolves outside `cwd`, and the returned output is still the last eight `x` bytes. Thus a repro command that emits gigabytes could still exhaust this process’s memory (or the test’s own memory when reading the tail file) and the test would pass; it only proves redirection to an external file, not that capture/readback is bounded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_verify.py:test_the_capture_is_a_scratch_file_not_an_in_process_buffer

chunk_findings.detail: The repro run is not bound to the bug’s recorded sha. When `repro_cmd` is supplied, `attach` reads `F.tree(repo).get("tree_sha", "")` once and passes that sha to `RC.check`, but it does not return that sha in the sighting, nor does it use the bug’s already-recorded sha (despite having `bid` and `st`). If the HEAD changes while the repro command is running, the bug can be recorded as confirmed at a different sha than the one on which the command actually ran. For example, HEAD is `A`; `bug found --repro-cmd "sleep 10"` starts the repro run at `A`; another agent commits `B` during the sleep; the handler then records the bug at current sha `B` with `sighted={"reproduced": true, ...}`. The bug is marked confirmed by a run at `A`, while `bug fixed` and later lists treat it as a bug at `B`. The same problem occurs if `attach` is called for an existing bug: it still runs at the current tree sha instead of the bug’s recorded sha.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: For a caller-supplied `check`, the code reads the event log and machine facts after the repro run has already happened. The comment claims this is “still pre-run,” but if the handler performs the check itself and passes the result, `log.read_all()` and `F.machine(repo)` are called after that command completed. For example, a handler runs `RC.check(repo, sha, "ddflow note during-repro", ...)` and then calls `attach(..., check=run, repro_cmd="ddflow note during-repro")`; the note event written by the repro command is then included in the bundle’s event snapshot as if it had existed before the repro command. Likewise, load/xdist conditions captured by `F.machine` are post-run, not the conditions during the flaky run, corrupting the recorded failure-rate context.

chunk_findings.detail: When a caller supplies `given["check"]` (the code explicitly supports this path and uses it to compute the sighting), the pre-run event/machine capture is skipped and `log.read_all()` / `F.machine(repo)` are read only in the inner `try`, i.e. after the supplied check has already run. If the check is the result of the repro command—as the `sighting` use implies—the recorded bundle contains post-run state, not the “state at that moment” snapshot the comment claims. For example, `run = RC.check(repo, sha, "stress --cpu 8", ...)` followed by `attach(..., repro_cmd="stress --cpu 8", check=run)` records `F.machine(repo)` after the load-generating command has exited, so a flaky failure caused by high load can be stored with low/absent load, and any events emitted during the repro run can be included as if they were pre-filing evidence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: The loop's inter-run isolation is not actually achieved. It runs `git reset --hard` and `git clean -xdfq` *before* it restores the saved `.git/config`, and it never clears stale `.git` locks. With `[bugs] repro_runs=2` and `--repro-cmd 'touch .git/index.lock; exit 1'`, the first run is recorded as a failure, but the second iteration's `git reset --hard` fails because the lock exists, so the second attempt is counted `unreached` and the record says `runs=1` rather than running both attempts and recording the true failure rate. Similarly, a first run that writes `.git/config` (e.g. `git config alias.reset false`) affects the next iteration's own `git reset` before the pristine config is written, contradicting the stated guarantee that every run sees the checkout as the first did.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The modified assertion requires `run["reproduced"] == "yes"` for `uv run pytest tests/test_x.py` purely because the file is absent and pytest exits non-zero. This makes any non-zero exit—missing test file, missing `uv`/`pytest`, broken venv, usage error, etc.—count as a confirmed repro. For example, filing a bug with `--repro-cmd "uv run pytest tests/test_x.py"` in a checkout where that test file has not been added records `executed: true, reproduced: yes`, so the bug is treated as confirmed even though no test ran and no bug was reproduced. The test therefore locks in a false-positive confirmation path that contradicts the intent that a bug remain unconfirmed until a real repro command fails at the recorded sha.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_bundle.py:85

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named for “not offered before confirmed work,” but it only asserts membership in the result of `bug_items(...)`: `ok_bug.fix_task in ids and bad_bug.fix_task in ids`. If `bug_items` returns an ordered scheduling list such as `[bad_bug.fix_task, ok_bug.fix_task]` (unconfirmed before confirmed), every assertion in the test still passes: both fix tasks are present, neither bug id is present, and `bad_bug.reproduced == "no"` is true. Thus the test passes while the unconfirmed bug’s fix task is offered ahead of confirmed work, which is the exact behavior the change is supposed to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_verify.py:test_an_unconfirmed_bugs_fix_task_is_not_offered_before_confirmed_work

chunk_findings.detail: `sighting` decides whether a run produced a verdict solely from the presence of a `reproduced` key, so it returns a sighting for records that reached no exit code. Its own docstring says an unavailable run is no sighting, but `sighting({"reproduced": None, "runs": 0, "failures": 0})` returns a non-empty dict. Because `attach` explicitly supports a caller-supplied `given["check"]`, such a record can be written into the bug event as `sighted`; the fold may count a sighting that did not happen or try to derive a failure rate from `failures`/`runs` with `runs == 0`. It should reject zero-run or unavailable records (for example by requiring `runs > 0` and a real verdict) instead of trusting the key’s presence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:sighting

chunk_findings.detail: The per-run `.git/config` restore follows symlinks: `(s.path / ".git" / "config").write_bytes(pristine_cfg)` opens the path with the default `O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC` semantics. With `[bugs] repro_runs=2`, a first repro run can replace that regular config file with a symlink to a writable file outside the scratch checkout, e.g. `--repro-cmd 'ln -sf [REDACTED:path] .git/config; exit 1'`. The second iteration’s “restore pristine config” step then writes through the symlink and truncates/overwrites `[REDACTED:path]` with the scratch config bytes. This is the same class of symlink poisoning the module explicitly guards against for the tail file (`O_NOFOLLOW` in `_tail_from_file`), but the config restore has no such guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The loop’s inter-run isolation still lets state left inside `.git` bleed into the next run. The code only restores `.git/config` and unlinks `index.lock`/`HEAD.lock`; `git clean -xdfq` does not clean `.git`, and no other `.git` files are removed. With `repro_runs=2`, a repro line such as `[ -e .git/poison ] && exit 1; touch .git/poison; exit 0` makes the first run exit `0` and leave `.git/poison`, then the second run sees that marker and exits `1`. `_run_at` records `executed: true`, `reproduced: yes`, `failures: 1`, even though the second failure is caused by the first run’s contamination, not by the bug at the recorded sha. The earlier fix for stale `index.lock`/`HEAD.lock` does not answer this broader `.git` marker bleed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to pin that an unconfirmed bug’s own item is excluded from `bug_items`, but it never establishes that `P1.CARRY` would otherwise be offered. Given a `bug_items` implementation that never returns plain non-fix tasks (for example, it returns only bugfix branches, or it filters tasks with no matching `carry/*` files), the assertions still pass: `P1.CARRY` is present in `state(proj).items`, `P1.CARRY not in ids` is true, and `carry.fix_task == ""` is true. Thus the test would pass even if the unconfirmed/reproduced condition had no effect, or if the item were excluded for unrelated reasons, so it does not actually demonstrate the claimed exclusion of the bug’s own item.

chunk_findings.detail: `_merge_sighted` treats `sig["reproduced"] == "yes"` as sufficient to set `bug.reproduced = "yes"` even when the record shows no failing run. The earlier fix to `reprobundle.sighting` only requires a yes/no verdict and `runs > 0` (per the triage), so an inconsistent caller-supplied or malformed check such as `{"reproduced": "yes", "runs": 1, "failures": 0}` (or with `failures` absent) is still accepted as a sighting and folded into the bug. In that case `_merge_sighted` sets `bug.reproduced = "yes"` and then records `bug.repro_failures = 0`; `bug_list` will therefore leave the bug open rather than marking it `unconfirmed`, so the bug is treated as confirmed even though its recorded repro had zero failures. This violates the stated rule that a bug whose repro did not fail remains unconfirmed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/knowledge.py:_merge_sighted

chunk_findings.detail: The new `executed` default is inferred from the mere presence of a `reproduced` key, not from whether a repro run actually occurred. Given a caller-supplied check such as `{"reproduced": None, "runs": 0}` — a record that reached no run/exit code and is reachable through the existing `attach` support for `given["check"]` — the returned `repro_cmd` becomes `{"command": repro_cmd, "reproduced": None, "runs": 0, "executed": True}`. That records the repro command as executed even though it was not, contradicting the original meaning of `executed` and the comment that an unavailable/no-run check must have `executed: False`. The separate `sighting` fix requiring a yes/no verdict and `runs > 0` does not correct this `executed` field, so anything trusting `executed` can treat evidence from a nonexistent run as real.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:build

chunk_findings.detail: `sighting` calls `int(run.get("runs", 0))` without guarding against a non-integer `runs` value. Because `sighting` accepts `Any` and `attach` explicitly accepts a caller-supplied `given["check"]`, a check such as `{"reproduced": "yes", "runs": None}` (or `runs: "x"`) passes the `reproduced` yes/no test and then raises before `sighting` can return `{}`. In `attach`, that exception is caught by the outer `except`, so the call returns `{"repro": {"unavailable": "TypeError: ..."}}` and omits `sighted`. The intended degradation for a record with no usable runs is to produce no sighting while still preserving the repro evidence/verdict; instead the whole repro link is replaced by an unavailable marker and the recorded verdict is lost.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:sighting

chunk_findings.detail: The per-run config restore still uses a predictable staging file inside `.git` and opens it with `Path.write_bytes`, which follows symlinks and blocks on FIFOs. With `[bugs] repro_runs=2`, a first repro line can create `.git/.ddflow-pristine-cfg` as a symlink to any writable file outside the scratch checkout, e.g. `ln -sf "$HOME/.bashrc" .git/.ddflow-pristine-cfg; exit 1`. On the second iteration, `staged.write_bytes(pristine_cfg)` truncates/overwrites that target with the scratch `.git/config` contents, and then `os.replace` moves the symlink into `.git/config`; `git reset --hard` then runs against the poisoned config node. If the line instead creates a FIFO at that path (`mkfifo .git/.ddflow-pristine-cfg; exit 1`), the second iteration’s `write_bytes` opens the FIFO for writing with no reader and no timeout and hangs `ddflow bug found`. The previous `os.replace` fix protects the `.git/config` node, but not the staging path (or `.git` itself) used to restore it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` treats a missing or unreadable tail file after the run as proof that the line never ran, but the line can make its own tail file unreadable or delete it after the shell has opened it. For example, with `tail_bytes > 0` and default `TMPDIR=/tmp`, a repro line such as `chmod 000 /tmp/ddflow-repro-*/* 2>/dev/null; exit 1` (or `rm -f /tmp/ddflow-repro-*/*; exit 1`) runs in the scratch tree, exits 1, and then `_tail_from_file` fails to open the path and returns `None`. `_one_run` converts that to “no run”, so with one run `_run_at` records `executed: false` and `unreached: 1` instead of `reproduced: yes`, even though the run reached an exit code. This undercounts failures and can turn a reproducible bug into an unavailable/unconfirmed one merely because the command removed its optional output file.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to pin that the repro command is run in a scratch checkout of the recorded sha, but the command used (`touch ran.txt`) only requires any writable working directory, and the only sha-related assertion is that `run["at"]` is truthy. If `_run_at` regressed to execute the command in an empty `tempfile.mkdtemp()` directory and set `at` to any non-empty value, the test would still pass: `touch ran.txt` exits `0`, no `ran.txt` is created in `proj`, `run["executed"]` is true, and `run["reproduced"] == "no"`. Thus the test would not catch a regression where repro commands are not run in a checkout of the recorded sha at all.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_bundle.py:test_repro_cmd_is_run_at_the_recorded_sha_in_a_scratch_checkout

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to pin that an unconfirmed bug’s fix task is not offered ahead of confirmed work, but it only checks membership in `ids` (`ok_bug.fix_task in ids`, `bad_bug.fix_task in ids`, bug ids absent). It never checks the order of `ids`. If `bug_items` returns an ordered list that places `bad_bug.fix_task` before `ok_bug.fix_task`, every assertion still passes, so the test would pass an implementation that offers the unconfirmed bug ahead of confirmed work.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_verify.py:test_an_unconfirmed_bugs_fix_task_is_not_offered_before_confirmed_work

chunk_findings.detail: The new unconfirmed filter only recognizes `reproduced == "no"` as unconfirmed. A bug that has never produced a repro run — e.g. `bug found` without `--repro-cmd`, or with a repro command that could not be executed — has `Bug.reproduced == ""` (the new default in `ddflow/core/records.py`) and, after the filing, `sightings == 1`. In `bug_branch_ids`, the condition `b.reproduced == "no" and b.sightings < SIGHTINGS_THAT_CONFIRM` is therefore false, so the code still adds `b.item` and `b.fix_task` to the bug-branch set. That makes such a bug count as confirmed bug work and eligible to be scheduled/offered ahead of confirmed bugs, even though it has neither a failing repro run nor a second sighting. Under the stated rule that a bug is unconfirmed until its repro command fails (or a second sighting/confirming run confirms it), the filter should treat an open bug with `reproduced != "yes"` and fewer than two sightings as unconfirmed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py:bug_branch_ids

chunk_findings.detail: The new `real` calculation still performs an unguarded `int(check_dict.get("runs", 0) or 0)` conversion. Because `attach` accepts a caller-supplied `given["check"]` and `build` now receives that `check`, a record such as `{"reproduced": "yes", "runs": "x"}` (or `runs=[1]`) raises `ValueError`/`TypeError` before `build` can return the bundle. The earlier fix only guarded `sighting`’s parsing of `runs`/`failures`; it does not protect this `int()` call in `build`, so the repro command/verdict evidence can be lost, or the filing call can fail if `build` is reached outside the outer attach guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:build

chunk_findings.detail: `sighting` validates counts by converting them with `int()` but then discards the parsed integers and returns the original values, and it only checks `runs > 0` plus `failures > 0` for a `yes` verdict. It never enforces that the recorded counts are whole, non-negative numbers with `failures <= runs`. Because `attach` accepts a caller-supplied `given["check"]`, a check such as `{"reproduced": "yes", "runs": 1.5, "failures": 2}` passes the guard (`int(1.5)` is 1, `int(2)` is 2) and `sighting` returns the record unchanged. The fold then treats the bug as confirmed while the event records 2 failures in 1.5 runs; similarly `{"reproduced": "no", "runs": 1, "failures": -1}` is accepted and records a negative failure count. The earlier fix only rejected a yes verdict with `failures <= 0`, so fractional and out-of-range counts are still folded as valid sightings.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:sighting

chunk_findings.detail: The guard around `int(run.get("runs", 0) or 0)` catches only `TypeError` and `ValueError`, but an uncountable numeric value can raise `OverflowError`. For example, `attach(..., check={"reproduced": "no", "runs": float("inf"), "failures": 0}, capture="")` makes `int(float("inf"))` raise `OverflowError`; this escapes `sighting`, is caught by `attach`’s outer handler, and returns `{"repro": {"unavailable": "OverflowError: ..."}}`. The documented behavior for a runs value that cannot count is to return `{}` from `sighting` and continue (with capture off, the result should be `{}`), not to turn the repro link into an unavailable marker.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:sighting

chunk_findings.detail: `_prime_scratch` assumes the scratch `.git` directory and its lock files remain ordinary, removable files, but it catches only `FileExistsError` from the staging `open`. If the first repro line poisons the scratch tree (for example `rm -rf .git; exit 1`, or `mkdir .git/index.lock; exit 1`), the second iteration raises `FileNotFoundError` / `IsADirectoryError` from `Path.unlink` or `os.open` instead of returning `False`. With `[bugs] repro_runs=2` and the `rm -rf .git` line, the first run’s exit code `1` is already in `codes`, but the exception escapes `check`, so the caller never receives the record with `reproduced: yes` (or the filing crashes); the module’s stated contract that a run which reached an exit code is kept and an unresettable scratch only makes later runs `unreached` is violated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_prime_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` redirects the whole repro line to a tail file but never bounds how many bytes the shell may write; `repro_tail_bytes` only bounds the read-back in `_tail_from_file`. With `repro_tail_bytes=4096` and a repro command such as `dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=100000`, the shell writes about 100 GB to the tail file under `/tmp/ddflow-repro-*` until the timeout, filling the filesystem. A verbose or runaway repro command can therefore DoS the machine even though the stored output is tiny; the harness needs to cap the written bytes (e.g. via `head -c` / a size limit), not just the bytes it reads back.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The git commands in `_prime_scratch` and the repro shell in `_one_run` are run only with `cwd=scratch`; they do not set or clear `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, `GIT_INDEX_FILE`, or related git environment variables. If ddflow is invoked from a git hook or any tool that exports an absolute `GIT_DIR` / `GIT_INDEX_FILE`, `git reset --hard sha` and `git clean -xdfq` act on that inherited gitdir instead of the scratch checkout, and the repro command can see or modify the filer’s real repository. For example, with `GIT_DIR=[REDACTED:path]` and `repro_runs=2`, the first run’s scratch modifications are not undone by the second `_prime_scratch`, so the second run does not execute in a clean checkout of the recorded sha even though the returned record still says `at=sha` and `executed=true`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_prime_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: `_prime_scratch` runs `git reset --hard sha` before `git clean -xdfq`. If a previous run leaves an untracked directory where the target sha has a tracked file, the reset can fail; the subsequent clean may remove that directory, but `_prime_scratch` still returns `False`, so that run is counted as `unreached`. With `repro_runs=2`, a first run that exits `0` and creates such a directory (e.g. `rm -f tracked_file && mkdir tracked_file && exit 0`) causes the second run to be lost; a flaky failure that would have occurred on the second run is missed and the recorded failure rate is wrong. Cleaning before reset, or retrying reset after clean, would avoid losing the run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_prime_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: The list still treats only `b.reproduced == "no"` as unconfirmed. A bug filed without `--repro-cmd`, or whose repro bundle produced no `sighted` evidence, keeps the new empty-string `Bug.reproduced` default while `_h_bug_found` increments `bug.sightings` to 1. Since `"" != "no"`, `bug_list` leaves `row["state"]` as the normal open state and `row["reproduced"]` empty, so an unreproducible single-sighting bug is displayed as confirmed/open. This contradicts the intended/accepted rule that any open bug with `reproduced != "yes"` and `sightings < SIGHTINGS_THAT_CONFIRM` should be shown as unconfirmed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_list.py:122

chunk_findings.detail: The new `executed` logic only applies when the `executed` key is absent: `check_dict.setdefault("executed", real)`. Therefore a caller-supplied `executed: True` bypasses the “no-run / uncountable-run is not executed” rule entirely. For example, `build(..., repro_cmd="pytest", check={"reproduced": "", "runs": 0, "executed": True})` (or `{"reproduced": "yes", "runs": "x", "executed": True}`) computes `real == False` but still emits `out["repro_cmd"]["executed"] == True`. That contradicts the stated invariant that an unavailable/no-run check “never really executed” and lets an unexecuted or invalid repro be recorded as executed when the check dict carries an explicit flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:build

chunk_findings.detail: `sighting` accepts a coherent-looking check whose verdict contradicts its failure count: for `check={"reproduced": "no", "runs": 1, "failures": 1}` it returns `{"reproduced": "no", "runs": 1, "failures": 1}` as a sighting. The validation only rejects `reproduced == "yes"` with `failures <= 0` and `failures > runs`; it does not reject `reproduced == "no"` with `failures > 0`. Given the stated rule that a bug is unconfirmed until its repro command fails, this input records a repro that failed the only run as a non-yes sighting, so the schedule can still treat the bug as unconfirmed even though the repro command failed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:sighting

chunk_findings.detail: `_countable` validates counts by converting them to `float`, so it silently loses precision for large integer inputs. For example, `sighting({"reproduced": "yes", "runs": 10**20, "failures": 10**20 + 1})` converts both `runs` and `failures` to the same floating value, so the `failures > runs` guard sees equal counts and accepts the record, even though the stored/original `failures` is greater than `runs`. This violates the function’s stated contract that “failures beyond runs” is not a sighting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:_countable

chunk_findings.detail: `_prime_scratch` trusts that `scratch/.git` is still a real directory. With `[bugs] repro_runs=2`, a repro command such as `rm -rf .git && ln -s [REDACTED:path] .git && exit 0` can poison the scratch tree after the first run. Before the second run, `_prime_scratch` resolves `scratch/.git/index.lock`, `scratch/.git/config`, and the staging path through that symlink; `os.replace` can write the pristine config into the operator’s real `.git/config`, and the subsequent `git clean`/`git reset` calls run against that gitdir, so they can clean or reset the real repository. The `except OSError` guard added for poisoning does not prevent this because the symlinked paths are valid and the operations succeed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_prime_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `run["executed"] is True and run["at"] == head and run["reproduced"] == "yes"` treats any non-zero shell exit as a successful reproduction. Given the same test in an environment where `uv` is not on `PATH` (or where the repro command is a typo), `/bin/sh -c "uv run pytest tests/test_x.py"` exits with 127 before `pytest` ever starts; the test still passes and the filing records the bug as confirmed. That is wrong: `executed` should mean the repro command actually ran, and a command-not-found/environment failure should not confirm a bug nor let a test that claims “pytest exits non-zero” pass when pytest never ran.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_bundle.py:test_basic_bundle

chunk_findings.detail: The added `int(value)` conversion is tried for every value and only `TypeError`/`ValueError` are swallowed. This makes non-integral floats count as truncated integers and lets `OverflowError` escape. For example, `sighting({"reproduced": "no", "runs": 1, "failures": 0.5})` calls `_countable(0.5)`, which returns `0`; the new `failures > 0` contradiction guard therefore sees no failure and accepts the record as a sighting, even though a `"no"` verdict cannot have a positive/fractional failing count. The same `int()` route also breaks the documented “None when it cannot count anything” contract: `_countable(float("inf"))` raises `OverflowError` from `int(float("inf"))` because the `except` tuple omits `OverflowError`, whereas the previous float path returned `None`. A check carrying `runs=float("inf")` (or a non-integral float count) can crash `build`/`sighting` or record an invalid count instead of being rejected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:_countable

chunk_findings.detail: The new `sightings` counter defaults to `0` and the diff adds no backfill for pre-existing `Bug` records, but `schedule.bug_branch_ids` now requires either `reproduced == "yes"` or `sightings >= SIGHTINGS_THAT_CONFIRM` before an open bug contributes its `item`/`fix_task`. On upgrade, an old open bug record that has no `sightings` key loads with `sightings=0` and `reproduced=""`, so the function skips it and the item/fix_task are no longer returned as bug branches, whereas before the change every open bug contributed. Since the record's original filing was already a sighting (the field comment says “1 is the filing”), a historical open bug should be backfilled to at least `1` (or missing treated as `1`); otherwise it needs two new `bug.found` events to regain its previous scheduling priority.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/records.py:sightings

chunk_findings.detail: `_countable` returns negative integers and negative digit strings unchanged, and `sighting` only rejects `runs <= 0` and `failures > runs`; it never rejects `failures < 0`. Thus `sighting({"reproduced": "no", "runs": 1, "failures": -1})` (or `failures: "-1"`) returns `{"reproduced": "no", "runs": 1, "failures": -1}` instead of `{}`. That records a valid-looking sighting with a negative failing-run count, contradicting the function's own rule that negative counts are not sightings and allowing a bug's stored failure rate/folded counts to become negative (or cancel real failures when sightings are summed).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:sighting

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` treats any failure to open the tail file after the run as proof that the repro line never ran, but the line can delete its own tail file after it has already run. With `[bugs] repro_tail_bytes > 0`, a repro command such as `rm -f "$(readlink /dev/fd/1)"; exit 1` runs in the subshell whose fd 1 is the tail file, removes that file, then exits 1. `_tail_from_file` then gets `ENOENT` on open, returns `(None, 0)`, and `_one_run` discards the exit code as `None`; `_run_at` counts the run as `unreached` and, if all runs do this, records `unavailable` instead of `reproduced: "yes"`. The run reached exit code 1, so this violates the stated rule that only runs that never reached an exit code are counted apart and lets a failing repro avoid confirmation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: When `tail_bytes` is 0, `_one_run` returns the shell exit code without any evidence that the repro line itself ran. A malformed repro command that makes `/bin/sh` fail to parse, e.g. `echo hi &&`, exits with code 2; because `keep` is 0, `_one_run` returns that code directly and `_run_at` puts it in `codes`, producing `reproduced: "yes"`. The same malformed command with `tail_bytes > 0` is treated as no-run because the tail file is never created, so the `tail_bytes=0` path silently turns a shell syntax error into a confirmed reproduction.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: `_prime_scratch` restores the working tree and `.git/config`, but not `HEAD` or refs, so git-metadata side effects persist between runs. With `repro_runs=2`, a repro command such as `git rev-parse --verify -q probe >/dev/null || { git checkout -b probe; exit 1; }; exit 0` exits 1 on the first run because branch `probe` is absent, then creates it. Before the second run, `git clean -xdfq` and `git reset --hard <sha>` do not delete branch `probe` or restore the pristine detached HEAD, so the second run sees `probe` and exits 0. The record reports one failure in two runs even though every fresh checkout of the recorded sha would have failed, making the flaky failure rate wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_prime_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: The priming only rejects a symlink at `scratch/.git` itself, but it still trusts symlinks inside the git dir, so a poisoned first run can make the next ddflow `git reset` write outside the scratch tree. For example, with two runs, a first repro command like `rm -rf .git/refs && ln -s [REDACTED:path] .git/refs && git checkout main && exit 0` leaves `.git/refs` pointing at the operator’s real refs and HEAD on `main`; the second `_prime_scratch` then runs `git reset --hard <sha>`, and git updates `[REDACTED:path]` through the symlinked refs directory. This is the “reroute the resets onto the operator’s tree” case the code says it prevents, but the new check does not cover.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_prime_scratch

chunk_findings.detail: The tail-file path is extracted with `line.split(" > ", 1)[1].split(" 2>&1", 1)[0].strip("'\"")`, which strips quote characters before stripping whitespace. The split on `" 2>&1"` leaves a trailing space (and, for a quoted path, a trailing quote that is not stripped because the space blocks it). For a correct wrapped line such as `(cmd) > /outside/link 2>&1`, this sets `target` to `/outside/link ` rather than `/outside/link`. The test then resolves that bogus path, so it does not follow the actual final symlink component; if `/outside/link` is a symlink into the scratch checkout, the real tail file is inside `here`, but the bogus path resolves outside and the assertion passes. Thus the test can fail to detect a tail file that actually lives inside the checkout.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repro_verify.py:test_the_capture_is_a_scratch_file_not_an_in_process_buffer

chunk_findings.detail:
The earlier fix for the unguarded `.git/config` read is incomplete. `_run_at` first reads `(s.path / ".git" / "config").read_bytes()` inside a `try`, but then immediately executes the same read again outside any `except`:

```python

```

That second read is the value actually passed to `_prime_scratch`. If it fails (for example, a concurrent cleanup or filesystem race removes/replaces `.git/config` between the two reads, or permissions change), the `OSError` propagates out of `check` instead of producing the promised `unavailable` record. The `finally` removes the tails directory, but it does not convert the exception into a degraded record, so the filing can still raise.

chunk_findings.detail: `_tail_from_file` returns `(None, 0)` for any `os.open` failure, and `_one_run` treats `None` as “the tail file was never created,” discarding the run’s exit code. But the tail file can be created by the shell and then removed or made unreadable by the repro line itself. Because the tail path is present in the shell’s argv, a repro command can discover it and do, for example, `rm -f "$tail"; exit 1` or `chmod 000 "$tail"; exit 1`. `_tail_from_file` then gets `FileNotFoundError`/`PermissionError`, returns `None`, `_one_run` returns `None`, and `_run_at` counts the failed run as `unreached`. The docstring says an unreadable-but-present file should yield `(b"", size)`, so the exit code should still count with no output; as written, a failing repro can be marked unconfirmed merely because it deleted or obscured its own output file.

chunk_findings.detail: `_prime_scratch` only rejects `scratch/.git` being a symlink; it never verifies that `scratch` itself is still a real directory on each run. A repro run can end with `d=$PWD; cd /; rm -rf "$d"; ln -s "$HOME/repo" "$d"; exit 0`. With `repro_runs=2`, the second call to `_prime_scratch` follows the replaced `scratch` symlink, sees `scratch/.git` is not a symlink, writes the pristine config into the operator repository’s `.git/config`, and runs `git clean -xdfq` / `git reset --hard <sha>` in that operator tree; `_one_run` then executes the repro command there as well. This is the exact “poisoned run reroutes resets onto the operator’s tree” failure the function claims to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: The tails directory is created once and never revalidated. A run can discover its tail path (e.g. `readlink /proc/self/fd/1`) and replace the tails directory with a symlink; for example, with `repro_runs=2`, the first run can do `t=$(readlink /proc/self/fd/1); d=$(dirname "$t"); rm -rf "$d"; ln -s "$HOME" "$d"; exit 0`. The second run’s shell redirect `> /tmp/ddflow-repro-.../<random> 2>&1` follows the parent-directory symlink and creates the tail file outside the throwaway dir (or inside the scratch if symlinked there), and `_tail_from_file` reads it because `O_NOFOLLOW` protects only the final component, not the parent directory. This defeats the stated guarantee that the tail file lives in a throwaway dir outside the checkout and never changes the reproduced tree.

For example, an old open bug `B1` with `item=I123` and `fix_task=F456` but no repro command now stops being treated as a bug branch and loses its prior scheduling treatment, even though no repro command ever ran and the constant/docstring say the filing itself was the first sighting.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier fix only changes `executed`; it does not suppress the verdict or failure evidence when there are no countable runs. For example, `build(..., repro_cmd="pytest", check={"reproduced": "yes", "failures": 1})` has no `runs` key, so `r` becomes `0`, `executed` becomes `False`, but the returned `repro_cmd` still contains `reproduced: "yes"` and `failures: 1` (with `runs: 0`).
