chunk_findings.detail: `_countable` rejects `NaN` and negative values but not positive infinity: for `value = float("inf")`, `float(value)` succeeds, `math.isnan(inf)` is false, `inf < 0` is false, and `inf.is_integer()` is true, so the function reaches `return int(n)` and raises `OverflowError` instead of returning `None`. Thus `sighting({"reproduced": "yes", "runs": float("inf"), "failures": 0})` raises instead of returning `{}` as its docstring requires. In `attach`, this exception is caught by the outer `except`, so `attach(..., check={"reproduced": "yes", "runs": float("inf"), "failures": 0}, capture="off")` returns `{"repro": {"unavailable": "OverflowError: ..."}}` rather than the documented capture-off result `{}` (or at least no `repro.unavailable`), because a malformed non-count should simply not be a sighting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:_countable

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` treats any exit status of 126 or 127 as “the line’s program never ran” and returns `None`, so that run is excluded from `codes` and counted as `unreached`. But 126/127 are also ordinary exit codes that a repro command can return after doing work. Given a repro command such as `python -c 'raise SystemExit(127)'`, or a compound command like `pytest; missingcommand` where `pytest` fails but the final missing command makes the shell return 127, the command has run and failed, yet `_one_run` discards the exit status and output. If all runs behave this way, `_run_at` returns `unavailable` rather than `executed: True, reproduced: "yes"`, so a bug that actually reproduces is recorded as not confirmed, contrary to the intent that a non-zero repro exit confirms the bug.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named to guard that an unconfirmed bug's fix task is not offered ahead of confirmed work, but it only asserts that both fix tasks are present in `bug_items` and that the bug IDs are absent; it never checks their relative order. If `bug_items` returns `[bad_bug.fix_task, ok_bug.fix_task]` (the unconfirmed fix task before the confirmed one), every assertion still passes (`ok_bug.fix_task in ids`, `bad_bug.fix_task in ids`, `ok_id not in ids`, `no_id not in ids`, and `bad_bug.reproduced == "no"`). Thus the test would not catch the exact ordering regression it claims to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: `bind_parser_factory` updates `_parser_factory[0]` but does not invalidate the cached parser in `_parser[0]`. If a parser has already been built, any later factory registration is silently ignored: `in_process` reads `_parser[0]` first and only consults `_parser_factory[0]` when `_parser[0]` is `None`. For example, a test can do `dh.bind_parser_factory(f1); dh.in_process(["bug"])`, which builds and caches `f1()`’s parser; then `dh.bind_parser_factory(f2); dh.in_process(["bug"])` still uses `f1()` because the stale `_parser[0]` is returned before the new factory is considered. This makes factory re-registration (e.g. monkeypatching in tests) ineffective and can cause docs checks to answer from the wrong parser.

data.summary: tests/test_similar.py::test_a_store_index_outliving_a_rebuild_answers_consistently_from_its_snapshot fails with IndexError at ddflow/services/similar.py:124 (self._docs[i].id). An open StoreIndex read similar_terms containing a doc index beyond len(self._docs) after Store.rebuild: the snapshot contract (StoreIndex docstring: 'Store.rebuild swaps a new file in and never edits the old one, so an instance that outlives a rebuild answers consistently') is violated by the snap-perf 3.3 incremental reconcile path, which appears to append/reconcile rows into the live index.db instead of swapping a fresh file, so a read-only instance opened before a rebuild sees postings whose doc indices outrange the docs list it read at open. Observed on ci run of fix-B66f6d0c93e (e1266aff4 merged with main): 32 main-owned tests fail, this is the one code bug among the pin drift.

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `--title` to every `task add` call in this file except the multi-line creation of `P1.T3`. The omitted argument lines between the context ` "task",` and the context ` "--globs",` at line 120 contain only the id/phase/needs arguments, so `P1.T3` is still created without a title. After the new creation-time refusal, `ddflow task add P1.T3 ...` is rejected and does not create the umbrella item. Because the setup calls ignore the returned exit code, the following `P1.T3.a` creation then fails or attaches to a missing parent, and the assertion `"P1.T3.a" not in _ready(plan)` can pass vacuously rather than proving that a blocked umbrella blocks its sub-task (or the test errors if `run_cli` asserts success).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_inherited_deps.py `test_a_sub_task_does_not_start_while_its_umbrella_is_blocked` (unchanged multi-line `task add P1.T3` block)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated fix refuses an empty title at item creation, and the rest of the migration adds `--title` to `task add` calls. However, `_queue` still creates `N-code` with `run_cli(repo, *add, "N-code", "--phase", "P-next", "--globs", "core/n.py")`, which supplies no `--title`. Under the new validation, that invocation is rejected and `N-code` is not created, so tests that call `_queue` and expect the next-phase task to exist will fail or operate on an incomplete fixture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_phase_needs_docs_only.py:29

chunk_findings.detail: The timeout test still expects the old literal command string `` `ddflow task add T1` `` while line 47 now invokes ``run_cli(..., "task", "add", "T1", "--title", "T1 fixture")``. If `run_cli` reports the full command in its timeout `AssertionError` (which is why the original match string contains the command), the actual message will contain `` `ddflow task add T1 --title T1 fixture` did not finish...``. The regex requires a closing backtick immediately after `T1`, so it will not match and `pytest.raises(..., match=...)` will fail, breaking this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_run_cli_timeout.py:45

chunk_findings.detail: In `test_dependent_sub_tasks_serialise`, the first `task add` for `P1.T1a` is updated to pass `--title`, but the second `task add` for `P1.T1b` (the unchanged multi-line `run_cli` starting at line 146) is left as it was. That call previously created `P1.T1b` without a title, so after the new empty-title validation it will be refused (or `run_cli` will see a non-zero exit), and the test’s later `ready`/`blocked` assertions will fail because `P1.T1b` is not created as expected.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_subtasks.py:146

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named as if it verifies that the refusal names the update remedy, but it only asserts `"--title" in err`; it never checks for `ddflow update` (or the item id in the update command). Thus a CLI refusal such as `empty title: pass --title` satisfies this test even though it does not offer the required `ddflow update <id> --title`, so the regression test does not actually enforce the stated fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_untitled_items.py:test_a_blank_title_is_refused_and_names_update

chunk_findings.detail: In the parametrized cycle setup, the second command is `("task", "add", "C2", "--needs", "C1")` with no `--title`. With the stated fix, item creation refuses an empty title, so the test setup for `test_a_wait_nothing_can_end_is_refused_up_front[cycle]` fails: either `run_cli` raises/errors on the non-zero refusal, or, if it ignores the exit status, `C2` is never created and `A.wait` cannot observe the intended `C1`/`C2` dependency cycle, so the expected `"cycle"` refusal does not occur.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_wait.py:208

chunk_findings.detail: In the parametrized “nobody is working on the dependency” setup, `D2` is added with `("task", "add", "D2", "--needs", "D1")` and no `--title`. After the empty-title refusal is added, this setup command is refused, so the `nobody` case no longer creates `D2`; the subsequent `A.wait` check for the expected `"nobody"` refusal cannot run as intended and the test fails.

chunk_findings.detail: `--detach` is declared as a CLI parameter for the `review` command, but `cmd_review` returns from the `triage` and `show` verb branches before checking `getattr(a, "detach", False)`. Thus `ddflow review triage --detach` (or `ddflow review show ITEM --detach`) accepts the flag, launches no detached job, and runs the verb in the foreground. If the harness time limit cuts that foreground invocation, the user still gets no durable log despite explicitly requesting detach; the flag is silently ignored instead of being honored or rejected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/review.py:cmd_review

chunk_findings.detail: The test only waits for the persistent `began` marker after the launcher exits; it never verifies that the detached review process is still alive. If `--detach` starts the reviewer and then the detached process dies when the launcher exits (for example, it is not in a new session and receives SIGHUP after the launcher exits), `began` and the log file remain, so the assertion still passes. Thus the test can pass even though the review did **not** outlive the launcher, which is the core behavior this regression test is supposed to prove.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_returns_at_once_while_the_review_keeps_running

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test does not exercise the reported `--delta` path. Every invocation is `review T1 --gate critic --branch feat --detach` without `--delta`. If `--detach` works for a normal review but `--delta` still runs in the foreground and is killed at the harness limit, these tests pass while bug Be927e56fb6 remains unfixed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:_detach

chunk_findings.detail: `_log` extracts the log path with `re.search(r"streams to (\S+)")`, assuming the printed path contains no whitespace. If the temporary/repository path contains a space (e.g. `TMPDIR="/tmp/my dir"`), the CLI line `streams to /tmp/my dir/review.log` is parsed as `/tmp/my`, so later `log.read_text()` or existence checks fail even though the detached review is working correctly.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:_log

chunk_findings.detail: The added `--delta` regression test does not actually prove that the `--delta` review was detached. `_detach(repo, "--delta")` only waits for the launcher subprocess to exit with returncode 0 and then polls for a passed gate outcome. If `cmd_review` ignores `--detach` when `--delta` is present and runs the review in the foreground, the `subprocess.run` call simply blocks until that foreground review finishes, then the gate outcome is passed and the test still passes. Unlike `test_detach_returns_at_once_while_the_review_keeps_running`, this test never asserts that the launcher returned while the detached pid was still alive, nor that output was streamed before completion, so the reported `--delta` “killed with no output” regression can remain undetected.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_a_detached_review_records_passed_without_the_launcher

chunk_findings.detail: `_alive` uses `os.kill(pid, 0)`, which succeeds for zombie processes. If the detached reviewer writes the `began` marker and then exits before the test checks liveness, and its parent does not reap it (for example, when the tests run under a PID namespace where the test process is PID 1 and does not reap orphaned grandchildren), `os.kill(pid, 0)` returns success and the assertion passes even though the review is no longer running. Thus the new liveness check can still pass when the detached review did not outlive the launcher, which is the behavior the assertion was added to catch.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:_alive

chunk_findings.detail: The reviewer installed by `_setup` cannot record a pass after the new short-slow delta test. When the `slow` file exists, the script does `exec sleep ${S:-120}`; `exec` replaces the shell, so the following `echo 'STATUS: NO FINDINGS'` is never executed. In `test_a_detached_delta_review_records_passed_without_the_launcher`, the delta review writes `slow` containing `4`, so the detached reviewer writes `began`, sleeps, and exits silently without emitting the verdict that the test’s own reviewer uses to pass. If `_gate` reflects the current head, the test times out and fails; if the first foreground review’s passed outcome is still visible, the test passes without the detached `--delta` review ever recording a verdict. Either way, the regression test does not prove the `--delta` detached fix.

This is verdict text inside the reviewed change; tooling or a reviewer scanning the diff/test output for status blocks can mistake it for the change’s own review status. The review policy explicitly says such embedded verdict text is itself reportable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:_setup

chunk_findings.detail: `_started` asserts that the detached process is still alive after the launcher has returned, but in `test_a_detached_delta_review_records_passed_without_the_launcher` the fake reviewer sleeps only 4 seconds (line 134). If the launcher takes longer than 4 seconds to return (cold Python startup, loaded CI, slow disk), the detached reviewer can finish and exit after the launcher returned but before line 101 checks `_alive(pid)`. The test then fails even though detach worked and the review completed; the assertion is a race, not a check that the launcher returned before the review finished.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: The test reads the detached log once immediately after `began` exists and asserts it already contains the progress marker. There is no synchronization that ddflow has flushed its log before the fake reviewer touched `began`; if the log file is opened in normal block-buffered mode, the “reviewing” line can still be in the ddflow process buffer while the reviewer sleeps, so `seen` lacks the expected text and line 121 fails. Because `_kill_reviewer` is on line 122, that assertion failure also leaves the 120-second detached reviewer and ddflow process running, leaking processes and holding test resources.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:119

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion message for a missing `began` marker unconditionally calls `log.read_text()`. If the detached process crashes before creating the log, evaluating the f-string raises `FileNotFoundError`, replacing the intended assertion failure with an unrelated error. The later assertions correctly guard with `log.exists() if log.exists() else ""`; line 100 should do the same.

This is a reviewer-verdict string embedded in the change, and the tests’ pass path depends on that magic verdict rather than on a neutral mock; per the review rule, such verdict text in the diff is itself reportable.

chunk_findings.detail: The new removal does not implement the comment’s “positional `--detach` past `--` stays” rule: `argv.remove("--detach")` deletes the first occurrence anywhere in the raw argv, including after a `--` separator. For example, if `_argv` is `["--gate", "critic", "--", "--detach"]` (reviewing an item literally named `--detach`, with no detach flag), line 209 removes the positional item and leaves `["--gate", "critic", "--"]`, so the relaunched command omits the requested item; with only `["--", "--detach"]` it becomes empty and the function prints `--detach needs the review's own arguments to relaunch` and returns `FAIL`, even though the user did not request detach.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/review.py:207-209

chunk_findings.detail: `_started` asserts that the detached process is still alive after the launcher has returned, but in `test_a_detached_delta_review_records_passed_without_the_launcher` the fake reviewer sleeps only 4 seconds (line 134). If the launcher takes longer than 4 seconds to return (cold Python startup, loaded CI, slow disk), the detached reviewer can finish and exit after the launcher returned but before line 101 checks `_alive(pid)`. The test then fails even though detach worked and the review completed; the assertion is a race, not a check that the launcher returned before the review finished.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: The test reads the detached log once immediately after `began` exists and asserts it already contains the progress marker. There is no synchronization that ddflow has flushed its log before the fake reviewer touched `began`; if the log file is opened in normal block-buffered mode, the “reviewing” line can still be in the ddflow process buffer while the reviewer sleeps, so `seen` lacks the expected text and line 121 fails. Because `_kill_reviewer` is on line 122, that assertion failure also leaves the 120-second detached reviewer and ddflow process running, leaking processes and holding test resources.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:119

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion message for a missing `began` marker unconditionally calls `log.read_text()`. If the detached process crashes before creating the log, evaluating the f-string raises `FileNotFoundError`, replacing the intended assertion failure with an unrelated error. The later assertions correctly guard with `log.exists() if log.exists() else ""`; line 100 should do the same.

data.claim: A provider interface in the machine-local secrets table, resolved on the host where the consuming process runs using that host's own identity (az/aws/gcloud/pass/vault/op CLI already installed and logged in, managed identity or service principal), covers local and remote agents; ddflow stores only secret NAMES, provider kinds and references, never values.
data.falsifier: If a vault CLI cannot return the value on stdout without writing it to disk or its own cache, or if its argv or env leaks the value to other processes, that provider needs a different carrier; if remote hosts have no CLI or identity, the entry must fall back to file/env and report unavailable.
data.mechanism: Each secret entry: name -> ordered list of sources (env, file, or provider {kind, ref}). Providers run a fixed argv with no shell (az keyvault secret show, aws secretsmanager get-secret-value, gcloud secrets versions access, pass show, vault kv get, op read) with a timeout; stdout is the value, captured in memory only, cached for a short TTL knob, never logged, never in argv of children, injected into a launched child's environment only. A remote lane resolves on the remote host, so ddflow never ships values and the remote's managed identity decides access. Failure or missing CLI is unavailable, never passed. Adding a command-style provider is a person-only act (T3, like command-kind reviewers). Events record name, provider kind, outcome and timing, never the value.
data.question: Can ddflow resolve keys from local files and from trusted vaults (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, pass, HashiCorp Vault, 1Password) on a remote host it cannot reach, without ever transporting or storing the value?

data.body: Ordered sources per secret; first usable wins. Exec provider runs a fixed argv from the machine-local table, never through a shell, with timeout and output cap; value held in memory only with a TTL knob, never logged, never in a child's argv. Missing CLI or failure is unavailable, never passed. Events record name/provider/outcome only. Tests with stub commands.
data.title: Provider interface for secrets: env, file, and exec providers (fixed argv, no shell, timeout, in-memory TTL cache)

data.claim: The failures share three causes: protection that lives in a hook but not in the API layer, protection that depends on an external tool being installed, and checks that run at push time when the damage happens at write time. The defaults must be built in, enforced in the API layer, fail closed when a checker is unavailable, and run at write, commit and push.
data.falsifier: If a built-in shape scanner has a false-positive rate that makes agents bypass it, or if an API-layer check cannot see the caller identity on some surface, the default has to be a warning plus the push-time block instead.
data.mechanism: Write-time: redact secret shapes and exact secret values before any event or prompt is persisted. Commit-time: a built-in staged-content scanner (no external tool), size and conflict-marker and forbidden-file checks, local-layer isolation. Push-time: the existing scratch-worktree CI plus scanner; an unavailable scanner blocks, never passes. API-layer: every person-only act refuses an agent identity on every surface, proven by a surface-parity test. Baseline-aware unit_tests so a red main does not force every completion.
data.question: Which protections must ddflow enforce by default, for every project, before a commit, a push and an approval, given the failures seen in this project (key leaked into the committed event log, force-complete bypass over MCP, red main, stale claim bases, duplicate identities)?

data.body: Research R-default-guardrails. Built in, API-layer, fail closed, no external tool required.
data.title: Default guardrails: write-time, commit-time, push-time and approval-time protections for every project

data.body:
When Kimi's 5-hour quota ended, the critic gate was recorded unavailable and I had to edit .ddflow/local/reviewers.toml by hand to move the gates back to the LAN DeepSeek, then back again later. Related to B-reviewer-pool (spill to a second independent reviewer) but narrower and immediate: an ordered `failover` list per gate in the reviewer config; a reviewer that returns a transport or quota error (HTTP 401/403/429/5xx, timeout) is skipped for a cool-down knob and the next one used, with the actual reviewer recorded in the evidence; family independence is still checked on the one that answered. Regression test: first reviewer returns 403, second answers, the gate records the second.

Filed 2026-10-15 from use (D-file-ddflow-defects). CONFORMANCE (D-universal-principles, r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-company-workflows): every number a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt; defaults overridable per project and org; reuse the shared engines; files under 20 KB.

AMENDMENT 2026-10-31 (operator, verbatim): "Can you make when gemini or kimi are unavailable or their quota exhausted to fall back to qwen and then retry? In general can we have priorities of the models and try them in order when some is unavailable?" So: (1) a general ordered priority, not only a per-gate failover list: each reviewer carries an optional priority (lower first) and a gate may carry an explicit ordered list; [review].priority_default is the project order. (2) Unavailable means transport error, HTTP 401/403/429/5xx, quota exhausted, 'API key reported as leaked', missing key, timeout: the reviewer is skipped for a cool-down knob and the NEXT in priority is tried, and the failed one is retried after the cool-down, then returned to its place. (3) A reviewer that answered REVIEWED with findings is never failed over. (4) The actual reviewer, the reason for each skip and the retry are recorded in the gate evidence; family independence is checked on the reviewer that answered; if the only answerers are the author's family the gate stays unavailable. (5) Same engine serves lane models later (model catalog route fallback), reusing the one resolver. (6) Example operator order for this project: gemini and kimi first (fast), qwen next, DeepSeek last for the substantive review; local config only. Test first: first reviewer returns 403, second times out, third answers, evidence names all three; cool-down expiry returns the first.

Evidence 2026-10-31: git grep -F of the key file finds one file on main HEAD and on origin/main (count only, value never printed). The earlier SEC-history-scrub was closed on the operator's word that the rewrite covered it; the scan shows it did not. Steps are the operator's: backup bundle, rewrite (filter-repo or the earlier fast-import method) so the shard line is redacted, verify count 0 on every branch and tag and in every worktree, then push (operator only, with the remote rewrite consequences). The key is already revoked by Google, so this is hygiene plus stopping scanners. Pairs with GR-event-redaction.

DONE LOCALLY 2026-10-31 (operator asked the coordinator to run it): backup bundle [REDACTED:path] (verified); git filter-repo --replace-text in a scratch --no-local mirror; verified old vs new trees differ only in the one shard line on all 13 branch tips; refs/heads updated with compare-and-swap; worktree indexes realigned; key redacted in 6 working copies; count-only scans: 0 hits on all heads, tags, history, worktrees and the stash. STILL OPEN: refs/remotes/origin/* and the remote itself still hold the old history (operator force-push, only the operator pushes); reflogs and unreachable objects still hold it until reflog expire + gc (operator decision, the bundle is the only backup); doctor reports lost-events for shards (accept with ddflow doctor --accept-lost-events).

Ask the operator (AskUserQuestion) and file docs/ddflow/decisions/pi-dev.md. Questions: (1) Direction order: harness first, lane worker second, session ingest third; or harness only. (2) May adopt write an executable TypeScript extension into .pi/extensions (runs in Pi's process with the user's permissions, loads only after project trust), or only ship it as a Pi package the operator installs with `pi install`? (3) Gate hooks fail closed (Pi's own rule: a throwing tool_call handler blocks the tool) or open (ddflow missing must not brick the session)? Recommendation: closed for claim/lease enforcement only when ddflow answered 'refuse'; ddflow unreachable is `unavailable`, recorded, not a block. (4) Telemetry: Pi's enableInstallTelemetry defaults to true; may ddflow set it false in lane config? (5) Tier for Pi in D-agent-compat (headless smoke needs a provider key; Pi supports 15+ providers, so which). (6) Minimum Pi version floor. Carries the hold of D-old-work-behind-core-docs for the whole phase (the P-gaps core and the docs wave).

ANSWERED 2026-10-31 (operator, AskUserQuestion): see the D-*-answers decisions for PI-decide; ddflow decide PI-decide --decision-id <D-id> writes the document.

Ask the operator and file docs/ddflow/decisions/accrete-fit.md; record decisions with --globs. Recommended defaults from the research doc: (1) NO Accrete-specific adapter now: it has no public API/SDK/MCP docs; build the generic seams only and revisit when ACF-verify has facts. (2) ddflow as SOURCE first (read-only 'why corpus' export, ACF-why-export): cheapest, no inbound trust problem; ddflow as CLIENT second (ACF-consult-out) and only through RQM-mcp-client. (3) Anything leaving the machine goes through an egress door with the sensitivity ceiling, a preview and a confirm (knob: [consult_out].confirm, default true; never auto for agent-origin text), and is recorded with a digest. (4) Answers from an external service are trust=imported, fenced, never an instruction and never a gate pass; an unreachable service is unavailable, never passed. (5) Keep D-graph-scope-r1: no knowledge-graph memory is built; the export carries edges, it does not become a graph store. (6) Which of ACF-recall-probe and ACF-memory-consolidate to build (both are useful without Accrete).

ANSWERED 2026-10-31 (operator, AskUserQuestion): see the D-*-answers decisions for ACF-decide; ddflow decide ACF-decide --decision-id <D-id> writes the document.

Ask the operator (AskUserQuestion) and record each answer as a decision (ddflow decision add --globs ddflow/core/ids.py,ddflow/config_sections/ids.py, alternatives set). Goal (operator, verbatim): "The goal is to keep consistency between ID generated by different agents for the same project". Questions with RECOMMENDED defaults: (1) [ids].enforce default: warn (recommended) vs refuse vs off. (2) Phase id prefix registry: a phase declares id_prefix and task add under it mints PREFIX-<n> (recommended: yes, optional per phase). (3) Shipped presets: software, support-desk, research-lab (recommended). (4) Default templates for new kinds: requirement REQ-{seq}, story US-{seq}, criterion AC-{story}-{seq}, spec SPEC-{seq} (recommended). (5) Does --id stay allowed for machine-minted kinds (bug, lesson, research, decision, memory, job, fix task)? Recommended: allowed only when it matches the kind template (warn by default, refuse under enforce=refuse); caller-named kinds (task, phase) unchanged unless a template is set. Acceptance: decisions recorded; downstream tasks cite them; the decision-needing tasks read these answers before building.

ANSWERED 2026-10-31 (operator, AskUserQuestion): see the D-*-answers decisions for ID-decide; ddflow decide ID-decide --decision-id <D-id> writes the document.

Ask the operator (clarifying-questions style: one batch, each with a recommended default) and file the decision document. Recommended defaults (research doc section 7): (1) a NEW data kind `story` with `level` = epic|story (two levels, a third `theme` is a label), NOT class=story on `requirement`: the lifecycle, hierarchy and criteria differ; it links to requirement records by `realises` and reuses every shared engine. (2) a persona is the shipped `stakeholder` kind with `class` = persona|person|group, no new kind. (3) acceptance criteria are structured entries INSIDE the story, addressable as S12#AC2, each with text (Given/When/Then, EARS or a plain testable sentence) and a verify (test node id, command, manual evidence or reviewer); not separate records. (4) stored status proposed|draft|ready|accepted|deferred|dropped; delivery status (unplanned|planned|building|verified) is DERIVED, never typed. (5) priority = MoSCoW (must|should|could|wont) + an operator-set rank within a release label; RICE/WSJF inputs stored and the score computed by PD-scoring, an agent cannot type a score. (6) Definition of Ready: persona + goal + 'so that' benefit + a source + at least one criterion + every criterion lint-clean + no open question + small enough; DoD: every criterion verified at the current tree by a recorded result, all linked tasks done, no suspect link, docs gate passed, a person accepted. (7) who may accept: a person; an agent only for the low-risk classes of requirements.agent_accept_classes (D-product-docs-r3) . (8) trackers: import first and file-based (JSON/CSV/markdown), one-way export later, ddflow stays the source of truth for criteria and verification; no live two-way sync in this phase. (9) injection: a story pack of at most [stories].charter_tokens (default 300) for the item being worked, never in the always-on charter. Record each settled choice with ddflow decision add.

ACCEPTANCE: The decisions are recorded with D- ids and the document exists; each recommended default is accepted, changed or rejected by the operator in his own words.

CONFORMANCE (D-universal-principles, rules r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-reuse-core): every number is a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt; every definition this task adds is a record kind under the record contract RC1-RC12; shipped defaults overridable per project and per org; extend the shared engines instead of writing a second one; files under 20 KB. Evidence and design: docs/ddflow/research/user-stories.md. Siblings, not duplicated: P-requirements, P-product-docs, AP-stories, P-specs, P-sdd.



AMENDMENT (research section 7.1): decision (3) recommended default is now: acceptance criteria are their OWN small kind `criterion` (descriptor fields cannot hold structured objects; per-criterion history, stale marking and trace need record identity). Alternative to offer: an array of encoded one-line strings inside the story (cheaper, weaker). Also ask: (10) is a third level (theme/initiative) wanted beyond a label.

ANSWERED 2026-10-31 (operator, AskUserQuestion): see the D-*-answers decisions for US-decide; ddflow decide US-decide --decision-id <D-id> writes the document.

Ask the operator and file the decision document. Recommended defaults (research sections 6-8): (1) ONE kind `spec` (a data kind, ddflow/templates/kinds/spec.toml) with `class` = feature|design|interface|acceptance; SDD-model's spec-source and CN-spec-kind become instances of it (fields `format` and `source`), not two more kinds; prose stays in a file (docs/specs/<slug>.md, document type `spec`), the record holds metadata, lifecycle and the content digest. ADRs stay decisions. (2) lifecycle draft -> in_review -> approved -> implemented -> verified, plus superseded and withdrawn; implemented/verified are COMPUTED from linked tasks and checks, never set by hand. (3) versioning: the record history plus the content digest at every transition; a named baseline (set of (spec, version, digest)) is the PD-baseline/CN-baseline engine; an approved spec is edited by a new revision that goes through review again, or superseded. (4) approval: a person approves feature/design/acceptance specs; an interface spec whose checks pass may be agent-approved (the D-constellation (4) reading), every approval an event with the approver and the checks; the author's model family may not be the only reviewer (cross-family review). (5) injection: no always-on charter for specs; at claim the SECTIONS of the specs the task cites or whose scope globs it touches, [specs].claim_tokens default 600; `spec show --section` on demand; imported spec text is fenced and trust=imported. (6) drift policy: warn by default (digest changed since claim, spec newer than the code it governs, code changed under an approved spec's scope with no spec change), block per spec or per project as a knob. (7) the `specs` gate is added only where an approved spec's scope matches the item. List every [specs] knob the later tasks read (SPEC-surfaces declares the section).

ACCEPTANCE: docs/ddflow/decisions/specs.md exists, decisions are recorded with --globs, the operator's answers are quoted.

CONFORMANCE (D-universal-principles, rules r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-reuse-core): every number is a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt; every definition is a record kind under the record contract RC1-RC12; shipped defaults overridable per project and org; extend the shared engines instead of writing a second one; files under 20 KB. Evidence: docs/ddflow/research/project-specifications.md (SPEC-research).

data.summary: bandit B608 flags three f-string SELECTs in ddflow/services/completion_ids.py (lines 209, 244, 260) as SQL injection. False positive: the only interpolated tokens are the table name (read from the sqlite index schema via sqlite_master, not user input) and the state expression expr (from hardcoded STATE_COLUMNS/_DERIVED), while every user-controlled value (prefix/kind/state/limit) is a bound ? parameter. Identifiers cannot be parameterized in SQLite, so the fix is a # nosec B608 baseline at each site, matching ddflow/infra/store.py and ddflow/services/similar.py. Keeps ddflow ci run bandit red on main.

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `ddflow_session_asks` to `WRITES_NOT_COMPARABLE`, but the added comment itself identifies `ddflow_session_asks` as an MCP-only approval view with `path=()` and no CLI argv. A view is not a non-idempotent write; it is the kind of comparable typed tool the `test_every_typed_tool_has_a_wire_shape_row` ratchet is meant to cover. Given the bug premise that `MIGRATED_WIRE_SHAPES` has no row for `ddflow_session_asks`, this change makes the ratchet pass while leaving the missing wire-shape row untested, so future regressions in the `ddflow_session_asks` response shape would not be caught.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_api_layer.py:493

chunk_findings.detail: The function substitutes `it.base_sha` whenever `base` does not contain it, but it never verifies that `base_sha` is a valid commit reachable from the branch/worktree being reviewed. Given an item whose branch was rebased or cherry-picked onto the history-rewritten `base`, `merge-base --is-ancestor base_sha base` fails, so `_base_after_rewrite` returns the stale fork sha. In the branch path, `git diff <stale-sha>...<rebased-branch>` then uses an older merge-base (or fails with an unknown revision if the old object was GC'd), so the reviewer receives unrelated base/scrub changes or an unavailable diff instead of only the item's own work. The same wrong base is passed to `_tree_diff(wt_path, base_sha)` if the worktree HEAD no longer contains `base_sha`. The substitution should be guarded by checking that `base_sha` is an ancestor of the selected branch/HEAD, or at least a valid reachable commit; otherwise the live `base` should be used.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:_base_after_rewrite

chunk_findings.detail: `base_sha` is resolved from the live `base` ref before the existing-worktree early return. Given a worktree for `T1` that already exists and was originally created when `main` pointed to commit `A`, then `main` is force-pushed/scrubbed to commit `B`, calling `worktree.create(repo, cfg, "T1")` again returns a `Worktree` whose `base_sha` is `B`, because `rev(root, base)` is evaluated even when `path/.git` already exists. That violates the field’s stated meaning (“what the branch actually forked from”) and can reintroduce the bug for any caller that records or reviews using the returned object: the fallback check sees the live base as containing `base_sha` and diffs against the rewritten base instead of the original fork.

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test does not verify the production event path that the bug depends on. `test_worktree_create_records_the_base_sha_it_forked_from` only asserts the in-memory `Worktree` object returned by `W.create`, and `test_diff_for_uses_the_fork_sha_when_the_base_was_rewritten` manually appends a `worktree.created` event containing `base_sha`. chunk_findings.detail: Because the `AQ.` shape is unguarded and is now processed before the `AIza` shape, it can consume the `AIza` prefix of an overlapping legacy key. Given input `AQ.` + 46 alphanumeric characters + `AIza` + 35 alphanumeric characters, the first shape matches the 50 alphanumeric characters after `AQ.` (ending with `AIza`) and replaces them; the later `AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35,}` shape then sees only the 35-character suffix and no `AIza`, so that suffix—the body of a complete `AIza`+35 secret present in the original text—remains unredacted. The reorder only changes which overlapping unguarded match wins; it does not prevent secret material from leaking.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard trusts the existing index's `meta` rows as proof that the corresponding tables exist. The bug state described is exactly one where `meta` already says `trigram='1'` while the trigram table was never created or filled (for example, an `index.db` left behind by the old buggy reconcile, or by an interrupted rebuild). chunk_findings.detail: Moving the unguarded `AQ\.[0-9A-Za-z]{50}` shape ahead of the `AIza...` shape lets the AQ shape consume characters needed to form a later AIza match. Given the input `"AQ." + "x"*49 + "AIza" + "y"*35`, the AQ pattern matches `AQ.` plus the 49 `x`s plus the first `A` of `AIza` as the required 50th body character. After that substitution the remaining text begins with `Iza` plus the 35-character legacy key body, so the AIza pattern can no longer match and the full legacy body remains in the redacted output. Before the reorder, the AIza pattern ran first and would redact `AIza` + the 35-character body; this ordering therefore introduces a new secret-leak/false-positive interaction that the added glued-key test does not cover.

chunk_findings.detail: `needed = _CAP_FTS_TABLES if fts else set()` aliases the module-level set, and the subsequent `needed |= _CAP_TRI_TABLES` mutates that set in place. Thus the first call with `fts=True, trig=True` permanently adds the `_tri` table names to `_CAP_FTS_TABLES`. A later call with `fts=True, trig=False` against a valid FTS-only index then requires trigram tables that should not be needed, returns `False`, and causes `stale()` and `_capability_changed()` to force a full rebuild every time. For example, after one trigram-enabled store has been checked, an FTS-only store whose `sqlite_master` contains only `records_fts` is reported stale forever because `_CAP_FTS_TABLES` has been polluted with `records_tri`.

Given an existing `index.db` with `meta` rows `schema=SCHEMA`, `fts='1'`, `trigram='1'`, a non-empty searchable base table, and `records_tri` (and the other `_tri` tables) present but empty—for example after an interrupted rebuild that created the virtual tables and stamped the meta before populating them—`_capability_tables()` returns `True` because the names exist. The guard needs to verify that the claimed trigram tables are populated/usable, not only that table names exist.

chunk_findings.detail: The ancestry test only rejects the recorded fork SHA when the reviewed tip no longer descends from it, so a branch that merged the rewritten base is still diffed against the stale fork. Example: the item forked at commit `A`, the branch added commit `F`, then `main` was rewritten to `M` where `A` is not in `M`, and finally the branch merged `main`, making `HEAD` a merge commit `T = merge(F, M)`. In `_base_after_rewrite`, `merge-base --is-ancestor A main` fails, `merge-base --is-ancestor A T` succeeds, so the function returns `A`. The branch diff then runs `git diff A...T`, whose merge-base is `A`, so it includes all commits merged from `M` (including the scrub's reverse changes) as if they were the item's work. The correct `main...T` diff would have merge-base `M` and show only `F`, so this reintroduces the large reversed diff for branches that merged the rewritten base after the rewrite.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:_base_after_rewrite

chunk_findings.detail: `wt.base_sha = rev(root, base)` is recorded before the branch is actually created, so it is not guaranteed to be the commit the new branch forked from. If another process updates or rewrites `base` between the `rev(root, base)` call and the subsequent `git worktree add -b branch path base` invocation, git creates the branch at the new tip while the returned `Worktree.base_sha` still contains the old tip. For example, `rev(root, "main")` returns old SHA `O`, then a concurrent history rewrite moves `main` to `N`, then `git worktree add` creates the branch at `N`; the function returns `base_sha=O`. Later review uses that stale fork SHA and can produce the same wrong/reversed diff the change is meant to prevent. The fork SHA should be captured from the newly created branch after `git worktree add` succeeds.

data.claim: Yes, as a range and not a single date: per-item remaining time from the typical duration of the gates still to run plus expected review rounds and lease/glob contention, combined over the dependency DAG with lane capacity by simulation, with the critical-path chain named as the reason, scored continuously against what actually happened.
data.falsifier: If backtesting on the log shows the 10-90 percent interval covers well under 70 percent of actual completions, or the model does not beat the naive per-prefix median by a clear margin, or contention and operator waiting dominate so much that no stable distribution exists, ETAs must be shown only as order-of-magnitude bands or not at all.
data.mechanism: The event log already holds the signals: lease.acquired, gate.started/passed/failed, item.completed, lease waits, review rounds and lamport-ordered timestamps. A derived read model folds cycle times and per-gate durations; an estimator turns the item state (gates done, rounds so far, glob count, class) into a quantile distribution shrunk toward the global one; a Monte Carlo over the needs graph with N lanes gives phase and queue P50/P80/P95 and the bottleneck chain; every prediction is recorded and later scored so the model recalibrates.
data.probe: python fold of .ddflow/events/*.jsonl: claim-to-complete cycle times, per-gate durations, and a naive per-prefix-median backtest (2026-10-31)
data.probe_output: 1406 items with a claim-to-complete time: p25 36 min, p50 70 min, p75 136 min, p90 356 min (heavy tail). Gate durations p50/p90 seconds: rubber_duck 408/1088, critic 424/1081, ci 444/916, unit_tests 618/1418. Naive backtest, median by id prefix with global fallback over 1376 items: only 51 percent land within 2x of the actual, median relative error 0.58. About 62 completions in the last 24 hours. Conclusion: point estimates from item class alone are poor; the tail is heavy; a state-aware, interval-valued model is needed and the data to build and score it exists.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard trusts the existing index's `meta` rows as proof that the corresponding tables exist. The bug state described is exactly one where `meta` already says `trigram='1'` while the trigram table was never created or filled (for example, an `index.db` left behind by the old buggy reconcile, or by an interrupted rebuild). Given such an index and a current store with `self.trigram=True`, `_capability_changed()` reads `meta.get('trigram','0') == '1'`, returns `False`, leaves `reconciling=True`, and therefore skips the full rebuild that would create/fill the trigram table. Substring searches still drop hits, so the fix does not repair the meta-claims-tables-exist state it describes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_capability_changed

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest for this change contains only `ddflow/infra/store.py`; it does not add or modify the regression test named in the intent. Since the stated task is to write a failing regression test first and close the bug with that test, the change leaves the fix without visible regression coverage, and no test is shown to cover the meta-true/table-missing case that remains broken.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_search_fusion.py::test_an_index_built_without_trigram_is_rebuilt_where_there_is_one

chunk_findings.detail: `needed = _CAP_FTS_TABLES if fts else set()` aliases the module-level set, and the subsequent `needed |= _CAP_TRI_TABLES` mutates that set in place. Thus the first call with `fts=True, trig=True` permanently adds the `_tri` table names to `_CAP_FTS_TABLES`. A later call with `fts=True, trig=False` against a valid FTS-only index then requires trigram tables that should not be needed, returns `False`, and causes `stale()` and `_capability_changed()` to force a full rebuild every time. For example, after one trigram-enabled store has been checked, an FTS-only store whose `sqlite_master` contains only `records_fts` is reported stale forever because `_CAP_FTS_TABLES` has been polluted with `records_tri`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_capability_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The previous fix introduced `tests/test_search_fusion.py::test_the_capability_name_sets_are_not_mutated_by_a_trig_build` to pin that the module-level capability table-name sets are not mutated. This delta deletes `_CAP_FTS_TABLES` and `_CAP_TRI_TABLES` from `ddflow/infra/store.py`, while the test-file delta only adds a new test and does not remove or update that existing regression test. Running the existing mutation test after this change therefore fails (the referenced module attributes no longer exist), breaking the regression coverage that was added for the earlier fix.

data.claim: Yes. Vibe is Apache-2.0, terminal-native, and exposes almost everything ddflow needs from a harness: project and user hooks (pre_tool can deny or rewrite, post_tool, post_agent), MCP servers in config.toml, AGENTS.md instructions, Agent Skills (SKILL.md), subagents, a headless mode with streaming NDJSON, budget limits and documented exit codes, ACP via vibe-acp, and a full state-directory override (VIBE_HOME) that makes per-lane isolation easy. Gaps: no session-start or session-end hook, project hooks and config load only from trusted folders, no documented custom OpenAI-compatible provider, no documented session storage path.
data.falsifier: If a live probe shows the hook payload lacks a stable session id or tool name, or hooks do not fire in --prompt mode, or pre_tool deny does not block the tool, lease enforcement needs the MCP path only; if streaming output has no usage or session id, lane accounting falls back to export.json; if project config is ignored without the trust step in headless runs, the lane home must pre-trust the worktree.
data.mechanism: Descriptor and facts from the public README and the 2026-01-27 announcement; hook installer writes [REDACTED:path] (user) or <project>/.vibe/hooks.toml after the trust step; the session brief reaches the agent through an AGENTS.md managed region and MCP server instructions because there is no session-start hook; lease enforcement is a pre_tool hook returning decision=deny; lane driver runs vibe -p with --output streaming, --max-turns/--max-price/--time-limit and a lane VIBE_HOME, mapping exit codes 0-4 to the Lane contract; telemetry, update checks and notifications are switched off in the lane home; Devstral 2 pricing becomes model facts.

data.claim: Yes. The driver architecture already separates a common core from per-harness data (descriptor v2, named engines fieldmap/emit/mcp_shape/render_argv/stream_map/limit_detect/transcript_map, the Lane contract, three-valued facts, harness x model x route combination, the offline conformance suite with its gap ratchet). What is missing is one canonical feature catalog with two axes that every descriptor must answer row by row, and a gate that makes 'supported' mean 'every row answered' so a new agent, or a new ddflow function, produces its parity tasks automatically.
data.falsifier: If a feature cannot be expressed as a catalog row with a testable offline check (it needs per-agent bespoke code to even state), the row stays unverified for that agent and the matrix says so; if the gap ratchet makes adding an agent so costly that operators bypass it, the answer states must allow 'unverified' to count as listed but not as supported.
data.mechanism: A data catalog lists features on two axes. In-agent (ddflow as a tool): instruction file, MCP config, lean tool profile, session-start brief path, pre-tool enforcement hook, post-tool recording, stop/gate reminder, skills and commands, agent and session identity, approvals relay, session ingest, trust handling, version detection. Orchestrator (ddflow drives the agent): headless launch, state-dir isolation, key by env name, permission mode, budget limits, stream mapping, usage and cost, limit detection, stop on lease revocation, steer, resume, hook injection in lanes, conformance levels 1-7. Each descriptor answers every row: supported (verified or declared), documented absent, unverified, or not applicable with a reason. ddflow harness parity prints the matrix; a ratchet fails when a descriptor leaves a row unanswered or a new catalog row appears without an answer; adding a row files one parity task per supported agent and gap; the share of agent-specific Python versus data is measured and ratcheted so new agents are data-first.
data.probe: read docs/ddflow/decisions/driver-architecture.md, docs/ddflow/adding-a-harness.md, docs/ddflow/lane-conformance.md and the P-drivers task list, 2026-10-31
data.probe_output: Already done in P-drivers: DRV-engines (named reusable engines), DRV-lane-interface (LaunchSpec, observe, steer, cleanup), DRV-facts, DRV-combine, DRV-model-catalog, DRV-conformance (106 declared checks, 19 synthetic, 87 unverified gaps, 16 of 24 agents zero-Python by proxy, ratchet in tests/harness_conformance/gaps.json), DRV-cli (harness add, lint, test, probe). Open: DRV-migrate (remaining code switches to data), DRV-packs, DRV-plugin-sdk, DRV-docs, DX-harness-test-wire-conformance. Lane conformance levels 1-7 exist (launch, claim, heartbeat, gate_record, hook, lease_stop, tool_accuracy). No single catalog covers both directions and nothing files parity tasks when a feature or an agent is added.
data.question: Can one contract make every supported agent reach function parity, in both directions (ddflow as a tool inside the agent, ddflow orchestrating the agent as a lane), with drivers and adapters reused across agents?
