chunk_findings.detail: The recovery code is moved into the `ddflow.services.leases` package, but the deferred completion import in `_note_landed` still uses `__package__` to build the module name. In the old top-level `ddflow/services/leases.py`, `__package__` was `ddflow.services`, so `importlib.import_module(f"{__package__}.completion")` imported `ddflow.services.completion`. In `ddflow/services/leases/recovery.py`, the same expression names `ddflow.services.leases.completion`, which is not part of this change and does not exist. Running `ddflow recover` (or any code path calling `scan`) over an expired lease whose worktree is clean and whose merge commit is on the base reaches `_note_landed`, executes that import, and raises `ModuleNotFoundError` instead of returning the completion advice. The import must target the parent service package explicitly (for example `ddflow.services.completion` or `importlib.import_module(".completion", package="ddflow.services")`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/recovery.py:_note_landed

chunk_findings.detail: The lazy re-export table omits `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim`, even though the manifest states that `ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py` adds that name. Because `__getattr__` only resolves names listed in `_SUBMODULE_OF`, `from ddflow.services.leases import lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` or `ddflow.services.leases.lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` hits the `sub is None` branch and raises `AttributeError`; `dir(ddflow.services.leases)` also omits it. This breaks the stated “public API unchanged” invariant for a public, non-underscore lifecycle helper.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/__init__.py:60-72 (_SUBMODULE_OF lifecycle block)

chunk_findings.detail: The live-holder early return bypasses the glob/resource conflict checks even when the re-claim changes those fields. If item A is held live by agent H with no globs, and item B is held live by another agent with globs covering `src/x.py`, then H calling `acquire(log, cfg, "A", holder=H, globs=["src/x.py"])` reaches the `existing.live(...) and existing.holder == holder` branch, calls `_record_claimed_globs` and `_renew_in_place`, and returns before the later `glob_clash` / `_break_idle` block. The renewed lease for A now covers `src/x.py`, creating two live claims over the same file. The same path skips the resource-capacity check, so `--resources gpu:8` on a live own lease can also overcommit when another live lease already holds the capacity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/claim.py:_acquire_locked

chunk_findings.detail: `_renew_in_place` records a new note in the `lease.renewed` event (`if note: upd["note"] = note`) but never assigns it to the mutated `Lease` object. For example, re-claiming your own live lease with `note="new"` logs the new note, while the `Lease` object returned by `acquire` (and the in-memory `existing`) still reports the old `note`. The returned public lease object is therefore inconsistent with the event log.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/claim.py:_renew_in_place

chunk_findings.detail: In `_live_pairs`, when the held glob `b` contains a wildcard, the pair is kept if any changed path matches the requested glob `a`; it does not require that changed path to also be covered by the held glob `b`. Given the same release line and no shared globs, suppose another item has an active wildcard lease `src/*` and its worktree has changed only `tests/x.py`, while the caller requests `*/*`. `conflicts` returns the pair `('*/*', 'src/*')` because both globs match `src/y.py`; `holder_changed_paths` returns `['tests/x.py']`; `GL.match('tests/x.py', '*/*')` is true, so `_live_pairs` keeps the pair and `_clash_text` drops/refuses `*/*`. But `src/*` does not cover `tests/x.py`, so the wildcard lease has no real changed work overlapping `*/*`; the claim should not be refused. The wildcard case should require a changed path to match both `a` and `b` (or at least `b`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/common.py:_live_pairs

chunk_findings.detail: `_same_clone` treats an absent current clone id as matching every named clone: `return not (theirs and clone and theirs != clone)` is true whenever `clone` is empty, although the docstring only says a claim without a clone is this clone's. `lost_contests` calls `log.clone_id(create=False)` (line 106), which can return an empty/`None` id in a repository or clone that has not created a clone id. Given a log containing an acquisition for item `X` with `data={"holder": "alice", "clone": "other-clone"}` and a later `lease.released` for `X` with `data={"holder": "alice", "lost_contest": True, "event": <acquisition id>}`, `_ours` (line 94) returns true because the current clone id is empty, so `lost_contests` reports item `X` as a contest this clone lost. The function's own contract says a release of another clone's claim under the same name is not ours; a caller using the returned winner/branch will act on another clone's lost contest.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/contests.py:88 (_same_clone)

chunk_findings.detail: `renew` mutates the local log before it checks the remote claim. It first calls `_transition(...)`, which appends a `lease.renewed` event when the local lease is mine and not quieted, and only afterwards returns `not _remote_renew(...)`. The comment immediately above that return says that if the remote claim was taken over, the lease “is not renewed” and the function should return `False`. Given remote claims enabled and a remote claim already held by another holder, this input makes the function append a local renewal (unless the renewal was quieted) and then report failure: the fold now shows the lease extended/renewed while the caller is told the renewal did not happen. If `_remote_renew` uses the opposite boolean convention, the same ordering is still wrong because the local append happens before any remote decision.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py:renew

chunk_findings.detail: The dataclass declares `salvageable: bool | None = False` immediately after saying `False` means *measured clean* and `None` means *could not measure*, and warns that collapsing unknown into clean lets `sweep(apply=True)` remove unmeasurable trees. But because the field has a default, any valid construction that omits `salvageable`—e.g. `Recovery(item="i", holder="h", kind="orphan_worktree", worktree="/tmp/w")`—produces `salvageable is False`, which the flag's own semantics interpret as a completed measurement showing the tree is clean. If a recovery path cannot measure the worktree and fails to pass `salvageable=None` (or if a new caller omits it), `sweep(apply=True)` will treat it as safe to remove. The default should be `None` (or the field should be required) to preserve the three-valued invariant.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/model.py:43 (Recovery.salvageable)

chunk_findings.detail: `scan` classifies an expired lease whose worktree is clean and fully merged as `salvageable=False`, and then `_note_landed` rewrites the advice to say the item must be completed, not released (explicitly citing Ba2eff5726b). `sweep(apply=True)` still only checks `rec.kind == "expired_lease" and rec.salvageable is False`, so for a non-terminal, non-adopted item whose merge gate passed and whose `merged_sha` is reachable from the base, it calls `expire(log, rec.item, ...)`. That clears/expires the claim instead of completing the item, returning it to the queue to be claimed/merged again—the exact behavior the comment says is wrong. The sweep path should skip or mark unsweepable the recoveries that `_note_landed` identifies as landed-on-base.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/recovery.py:sweep

chunk_findings.detail: The split moves the code into `ddflow.surfaces.registry`, one package deeper than the old `ddflow.surfaces.registry` module, but the stated plan keeps the old relative imports (`from ..config_sections._compat import ...` and `from .argtypes import ...`) “as before.” From inside `ddflow.surfaces.registry._aliases` (and likewise `__init__.py`), `..` resolves to `ddflow.surfaces`, so those imports look for `ddflow.surfaces.config_sections._compat` and `ddflow.surfaces.registry.argtypes`, not the original `ddflow.config_sections._compat` and `ddflow.surfaces.argtypes`. Importing the package/submodule then raises `ImportError` as soon as any command/param/alias is loaded; the correct forms from the package are `...config_sections._compat` and `..argtypes` (or absolute imports).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry/_aliases.py

chunk_findings.detail: The call to `super().error(...)` is indented inside the `for a in self._actions` loop, so it is executed on the first action rather than after scanning all actions. For a normal parser with `add_help=True`, `self._actions[0]` is the help action; when an unknown command triggers a message like `argument cmd: invalid choice: 'foo'`, the loop immediately calls `super().error(glob_list_hint(message, self._argv))` with the unmodified message and exits. The `_did_you_mean` suggestion is therefore never added unless the matching subparsers action happens to be first, and if a parser somehow has no actions, `error()` can return without exiting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry/__init__.py:151 (SuggestingParser.error)

chunk_findings.detail: `used_aliases` merges deprecated flag tables from every parser on the command path and then scans all of `argv` without tracking which parser actually consumed each token. If a parent parser has a deprecated `--old` flag (`_compat_flags = {"--old": Alias("flag", "--old", "--global-new", "0.1", "1.0")}`) and a chosen subcommand parser defines its own non-deprecated `--old` flag, argv `["sub", "--old"]` parses the subcommand’s flag, but the function still returns the parent’s deprecated `Alias` because the parent entry remains in `flags`. Conversely, if the subcommand also deprecates `--old` with a different `Alias`, argv `["--old", "sub"]` uses the parent flag before the subcommand, yet the subcommand’s entry overwrites the parent entry and the parent alias is missed. This violates the function’s contract to return the aliases actually used by the parsed command line and can emit wrong or missing deprecation notices.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry/_aliases.py:used_aliases

chunk_findings.detail: `exclusive_required` is validated and documented as making the mutually exclusive group required, but `add_to` creates the group with `parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()` and never passes `required=True` (nor can it retroactively make an already-created group required). For example, `Param("a", exclusive="g")` and `Param("b", exclusive="g", exclusive_required=True)` added to the same parser with a shared `groups` dict produce an optional mutually exclusive group, so `parser.parse_args([])` succeeds even though the documented behavior requires exactly one of `--a` or `--b` to be supplied.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry/_param.py:Param.add_to

chunk_findings.detail: `array_schema` determines the shape from `payload` alone, while `result_shape` gives `text` precedence over `payload`. `result_schemas` calls `output_schema(..., text=text)` but calls `array_schema(command, payload)` without `text`. Given a tool-table entry such as `{"ddflow_x": {"payload": "hits", "text": "doc"}}`, `result_schemas` records `shape == "text"` (because `text` is truthy), but `array_schema` returns a non-`None` array schema because `"hits"` is in `ARRAY_PAYLOADS`. This violates the documented contract that `array_schema` is `None` for any shape other than `array` and produces an inconsistent schema row (a text result carrying an array schema).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry/_schemas.py:array_schema / result_schemas

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-31 (AskUserQuestion, ADP-decide 4-7), own words: (4) ports: 'Next to their adapters in ddflow/adapters (Recommended)': port Protocol, default implementation and registry in one package; every layer imports only ddflow.adapters. (5) fakes: 'ddflow/adapters/fakes, shipped (Recommended)': a ratchet requires every port to have a fake. (6) ManagedFile: 'Backup next to the file, consent once per file kind (Recommended)': a .ddflow-bak copy before the first write, ownership markers on every ddflow-owned key, consent once per kind of file (for example user-level Vibe hooks), not per write. (7) config formats: 'TOML only for ddflow's own config, other formats only for managed files (Recommended)': JSON, JSONC and YAML are handled only in ManagedFile for other tools' files. Completes D-adapters-answers.
data.title: Adapters: ports and fakes live in ddflow/adapters, ManagedFile backs up next to the file with consent once per kind, own config stays TOML-only

data.body:
Decide and document the pattern once: ports (Protocols) in core or services, default adapters in infra homes, fakes in a tests helper package, registration through core.registry.Registry[T] where a family has several adapters (forge, CI, notify, supervisors already plan this). Waits on the reconciled layer contract so the new contracts land on one model. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section. Operator questions in ADP-decide. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, D-unify strangler with ratchets): port = Protocol, one default implementation in its home module, a fake for tests; baseline ignore lists only shrink; no behaviour change for callers; files under 20 KB.

OPERATOR 2026-10-31 (D-adapters-answers): adapters live in a NEW ddflow/adapters package at the bottom of the layer contract (core uses only our adapters); this task also produces the ONE reconciled layer contract (folds B-arch-layer-contracts: test_layering vs .importlinter, 9 core->config, 2 services->views, 9 surfaces->infra baseline entries) and marks B-arch-layer-contracts done by reference. Existing infra homes (proc, git, fsio, tomlcfg, digest) migrate under ddflow/adapters behind re-exports (see ADP-migrate-homes).

OPERATOR 2026-10-31 (D-adapters-answers-2): ports (Protocols) live next to their adapters in ddflow/adapters, not in core; fakes in ddflow/adapters/fakes (shipped) and a ratchet requires every port to have a fake.

73 modules in services and infra call json load or dump and about 8 write managed regions (adopt, compat_refs, enforce hooks and views, export ops, readme tools, fsio); every harness installer merges its own settings its own way. One ManagedFile port with format adapters (json, jsonc, toml via tomlkit, yaml, markdown region): idempotent merge of only ddflow-owned keys with an ownership marker, drift detection, backup, atomic write, clean removal, never touching unmanaged text; the content shape stays in the descriptor engines (mcp_shape, emit). Existing installers move onto it family by family; new agents (Vibe, ZCode) use it from the start. Tests first with fixtures of messy real-world files. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, D-unify strangler with ratchets, D-adapters-answers): port = Protocol in ddflow/adapters, default implementation, a fake for tests; baselines only shrink; no behaviour change; files under 20 KB.

OPERATOR 2026-10-31 (D-adapters-answers-2): a .ddflow-bak copy next to the file before the first write; ownership markers on every ddflow-owned key; consent once per file kind (not per write); JSON, JSONC and YAML are handled ONLY here.

Today config.py, config_sections/_layers.py, config_shadow.py, configwrite.py and configcompat.py each handle part of it. One ConfigStore port: resolve (layered, with the source of every value and the explain log), set (to the right file, comment-preserving through the TOML adapter), unset, validate; sources are adapters (file, local file, env, session overrides, org pack) in a registry so a new source (a company pack, a remote store) is one adapter. Core is handed its knobs (no core to config imports; folds the 7 baseline entries). Tests first with an in-memory fake store. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, D-unify strangler with ratchets, D-adapters-answers): port = Protocol in ddflow/adapters, default implementation, a fake for tests; baselines only shrink; no behaviour change; files under 20 KB.

OPERATOR 2026-10-31 (D-adapters-answers-2): ddflow's own config stays TOML only; other formats exist only in ManagedFile for other tools' files; a new config SOURCE (org pack, remote store) is an adapter, a new FORMAT is not.

Questions with defaults: (1) adapters live in ddflow/infra/<family> (default) vs a new ddflow/adapters package. (2) strangler: migrate a family when its task runs and ratchet baselines only shrink (default) vs one big-bang move. (3) order: http, sqlite, toml, filesystem/shutil, templates, third-party singles, clock/env (default). Not in needs on purpose (L-needs-on-decide-tasks). CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, D-unify strangler with ratchets): port = Protocol, one default implementation in its home module, a fake for tests; baseline ignore lists only shrink; no behaviour change for callers; files under 20 KB.

ANSWERED 2026-10-31 (operator): see D-adapters-answers and D-adapters-answers-2; ddflow decide ADP-decide --decision-id D-adapters-answers writes the document (cite both).

chunk_findings.detail: The `clock-env` family is mapped to the entire `os` root module, although the stated family is time/uuid/random/os.environ. Because `_external_roots` records only import roots, any module that does `import os` or `from os import path` for `os.path` is placed in `clock-env.importers`; since `clock-env` has no declared home, `FamilyReport.violations` lists it. For example, adding `ddflow/foo.py` containing `import os` and using `os.path.join("a", "b")` makes `ddflow.foo` a `clock-env` violation even though it never touches `os.environ`. This misclassifies ordinary path use as clock/env/randomness dependency and can make the ratchet baseline grow for code that should not belong to the `clock-env` family.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:37

chunk_findings.detail: `_external_roots` swallows `SyntaxError` and `OSError` and returns no imports. A file that cannot be parsed or read is silently treated as having no dependencies, so a forbidden import in that file is invisible to the census. For example, create `ddflow/foo.py` containing `import subprocess` followed by a syntax error such as `def f(:`; `_external_roots` catches the `SyntaxError` and returns `()`, so `scan(repo)` reports no `subprocess` importer and no violation, allowing a new importer outside the family’s home to evade the ratchet. The census should fail or report the unparsable/unreadable file rather than omit it from the dependency census.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:101-104

chunk_findings.detail: The command registers itself under `tool="ddflow_archdeps"`, i.e. a new tool named after the command, even though the stated intent and D-unify require this to be an action on the existing tool/view surface (consistent with `family="ddflow_view"` and `help_group="view"`). Loading `COMMANDS` therefore either fails registry validation against the existing tool set or creates a second tool; in either case the `archdeps` action is not added to the existing tool’s action surface, violating the strangler/ratchet requirement [D-unify].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/arch_deps.py:22

chunk_findings.detail: The ratchet test cannot enforce “baseline ignore lists only shrink” because it compares the scan against the same editable `BASELINE` literal in the test file. Given a change that adds a new module outside a family’s declared home, e.g. `ddflow.foo` importing `sqlite3` outside `ddflow.infra.docindex`, and the same change appends `"ddflow.foo"` to `BASELINE["sqlite3"]`, `test_ratchet_violations_match_baseline` sees `got == want` and passes; `test_default_scan_reports_every_family` also passes because `"sqlite3"` is already in the family set, and `test_violations_are_importers_outside_the_home` still passes for `http`-style no-home families because violations equal importers. This contradicts the stated ratchet requirement that a new importer outside a home fails and that baselines only shrink.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py:test_ratchet_violations_match_baseline

chunk_findings.detail: `_external_roots` promises to return `None` when a file “cannot be read or parsed,” but it only catches `OSError` and `SyntaxError`. A file that cannot be decoded as UTF-8 raises `UnicodeDecodeError` from `path.read_text`, and a file containing a null byte raises `ValueError` from `ast.parse`; neither is caught, so `scan` crashes instead of putting the module in `Census.unparsed`. For example, adding `ddflow/foo.py` with invalid UTF-8 bytes (or `b"\x00"`) makes the census fail outright rather than reporting the file as unparsed, contradicting the stated “never skipped” behavior and the ratchet’s need to know when dependency data is unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:_external_roots

chunk_findings.detail: The added `write_text` calls put unescaped newlines inside ordinary single-quoted string literals (e.g. `write_text("import subprocess` followed by a real line break and then `")`). This makes `tests/test_arch_deps.py` itself syntactically invalid: importing/collecting the test module raises `SyntaxError: unterminated string literal`, so the new test cannot run and the whole test file fails collection.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py:test_unparsable_file_is_reported_not_skipped

evidence.diff_source: delta review of 1 commit since d55645016c

chunk_findings.detail: The `clock-env` family is keyed on the import root `os`, but the intent and the module’s own description say the family is `os.environ`. Given a new `ddflow/foo.py` containing `import os.path`, `_external_roots` returns `("os",)`, `member_of` classifies it as `clock-env`, and because `STDLIB_HOMES` has no `clock-env` home, `ddflow.foo` appears in `violations`. The ratchet would then fail a new module that imports no `os.environ`, only path helpers, so the census/ratchet is wrong for ordinary `os.path` imports.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:STDLIB_FAMILIES["clock-env"]

chunk_findings.detail: The third-party detector classifies any import root not in `sys.stdlib_module_names` and not `ddflow` as third-party. `sys.stdlib_module_names` is documented as excluding built-in modules, so given `ddflow/foo.py` containing `import builtins`, the root `builtins` is put into `third_party` and reported as a third-party family/violation. `builtins` is a built-in module, not an external third-party dependency, so the census reports a false dependency family.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:AstArchDepsCensus.scan

chunk_findings.detail: The ratchet test only iterates over the keys already present in `BASELINE`, so it cannot fail when a new external dependency family appears outside any declared home. For example, if `A.scan(ROOT)` reports a new family `rich` with violations because some module imports `rich`, the loop `for name, base in BASELINE.items()` never examines `rich`; the test passes. The full suite may catch that through `test_default_scan_reports_every_family`, but the test named as the ratchet is not itself a complete ratchet and passes if run alone or if the other test is skipped.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py::test_ratchet_violations_match_baseline

chunk_findings.detail: The new change adds a CLI/JSON view (`ddflow/api/arch_deps.py` adds `archdeps` and `render`, `ddflow/surfaces/declared/arch_deps.py` adds `_text`), but this test file never imports or exercises those surfaces. `FakeArchDepsCensus` is only tested by `test_fake_returns_the_reports_it_is_given`, which merely asserts the fake returns the object it was constructed with. Therefore a broken action or renderer—e.g. malformed JSON, omitted families, or ignoring the injected census—would not be caught here, despite the fake-for-tests requirement in [D-unify].
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py (FakeArchDepsCensus)

chunk_findings.detail: The test creates both `ddflow/ok.py` (`import subprocess`) and `ddflow/broken.py`, but only asserts that `census.unparsed == ("ddflow.broken",)`. If `A.scan` records the unparsable file and then aborts or skips the rest of the `ddflow` package, returning no families, the test still passes even though the valid `import subprocess` from `ok.py` is lost. The test should also assert that the valid module is still counted, otherwise it does not prove scanning continues after an unparsable file.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py::test_unparsable_file_is_reported_not_skipped

chunk_findings.detail: The `http` family is keyed on the import root `urllib`, but the stated intent is the network family `urllib.request` / `http.client` / `socket`. Given a new `ddflow/foo.py` containing `from urllib.parse import urlparse`, `_external_roots` returns `("urllib",)`, `member_of` classifies it as `http`, and because `STDLIB_HOMES` has no `http` home, `ddflow.foo` appears in `violations`. The ratchet then fails a module that introduces no HTTP/network dependency, only URL parsing, so the census over-reports `urllib.parse` as an external `http` family importer. This is not covered by the documented `os`/`os.path` root-granularity exception.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:STDLIB_FAMILIES["http"]

chunk_findings.detail: The tests still do not exercise the public view/action surface added by the change. `test_api_view_carries_families_and_unparsed` calls `ddflow.api.arch_deps.render` directly and only asserts that the output contains the substrings `"hashlib"` and `"unparsed"`; it never calls the `archdeps` action, never exercises the declared CLI surface `_text` listed in the manifest, and never injects `FakeArchDepsCensus` into a consumer. Consequently, an `archdeps` action that ignores an injected census and always calls the real scan, or a CLI/JSON renderer that returns a constant string containing `"hashlib"` and `"unparsed"` but omits the census’s home/violations/importers, would still pass the suite. The earlier probe only added this substring render test, so it does not answer the still-uncovered action/CLI view or the missing home/violations assertions [r-reuse-core].
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py::test_api_view_carries_families_and_unparsed

chunk_findings.detail: Given a valid Python source file `repo/ddflow/legacy.py` that begins with PEP 263 `# -*- coding: latin-1 -*-`, imports `hashlib`, and contains a non-ASCII latin-1 string such as `s = "caf\xe9"`, `_external_roots` calls `path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")`. The byte `\xe9` is invalid UTF-8 here, so `UnicodeDecodeError` is raised, caught as `ValueError`, and the function returns `None`; `AstArchDepsCensus.scan` then records `ddflow.legacy` in `Census.unparsed` and omits the `hashlib` import from the `hashlib` family. The same file parses successfully with `ast.parse(path.read_bytes())` because `ast.parse` honors the PEP 263 coding cookie, so the file is not “unparsable” and the dependency must be reported, not hidden from the census that drives the ratchet.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:_external_roots

chunk_findings.detail: `sys.stdlib_module_names` is the running interpreter’s *current-platform* stdlib set. On Linux it does not contain Windows-only stdlib modules such as `winreg` or `msvcrt`, while on Windows it does. Given a valid source file `ddflow/win_compat.py` with `if sys.platform == "win32": import winreg`, scanning on Linux hits the `elif` branch and records `winreg` as a third-party family with `ddflow.win_compat` as a violation; scanning the same file on Windows records nothing. The module docstring says the census “agrees on every platform,” and the ratchet would fail spuriously on one OS for a standard-library module. A platform-independent stdlib classification is needed, or platform-specific stdlib roots must be enumerated in `STDLIB_FAMILIES`.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/archdeps.py: AstArchDepsCensus.scan (`stdlib = frozenset(sys.stdlib_module_names)` and `elif root != "ddflow" and root not in stdlib`)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py: AstArchDepsCensus.scan (`stdlib = frozenset(sys.stdlib_module_names)` and `elif root != "ddflow" and root not in stdlib`)

titles: ddflow/services/archdeps.py: AstArchDepsCensus.scan (`stdlib = frozenset(sys.stdlib_module_names)` and `elif root != "ddflow" and root not in stdlib`)

chunk_findings.detail: The census family is specified as `time/uuid/random/os.environ`, but the implementation keys it on the `os` import root. A file such as `ddflow/core/pathutil.py` containing `from os.path import join` is recorded as an importer of the `clock-env` family because `_external_roots()` returns `("os",)`, and `AstArchDepsCensus.scan` then adds that module to `stdlib_importers["clock-env"]`. Since `clock-env` has no declared home, `FamilyReport.violations` reports every importer as a violation. This is an ordinary stdlib filesystem-path import, not an `os.environ` external dependency, and the ratchet would fail on it. The in-code comment says this over-reporting is “not a defect,” but that documents the wrong row rather than correcting it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py: STDLIB_FAMILIES["clock-env"] / AstArchDepsCensus.scan classification

chunk_findings.detail: The moved `update` treats a `O.nothing` result from `_landed_paths_fields` as a fatal outcome, so a no-op `--landed-paths` request aborts the whole edit even when other fields were valid and planned. For example, given an item whose `landed_paths` is already `["a"]`, calling `update(..., ItemEdit(title="new", landed_paths=["a"]))` makes `plan_edit` return `{"title": "new"}`, but `_landed_paths_fields` sees `paths == it.landed_paths` and returns `O.nothing(...)`; `update` then returns that outcome before `_record_update`, so the title is not changed. The same happens when `landed_paths=[]` is passed to “clear” a restriction that does not exist while other fields are also being updated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update

chunk_findings.detail: The package makes `_load` and `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` plain attributes of `ddflow.api.items`, but the actual functions are defined in submodules. If a test first imports a public function, e.g. `from ddflow.api.items import update`, the lazy `__getattr__` imports `_edit` at that time. If `_edit` obtains `_load`/`DEFAULT_PRIORITY` by normal static import from the package or from `.._base`, those names are bound into `_edit`'s module globals. A later `monkeypatch.setattr(items, "_load", fake)` or `monkeypatch.setattr(items, "DEFAULT_PRIORITY", fake)` changes only the package namespace, not the already-imported submodule's globals, so `update`/`task_add` still call the original `_load`/priority. In the old single module, the function's globals were the package/module globals, so patching `items._load` was observed at call time. This breaks the monkeypatch behavior the docstring explicitly promises.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/__init__.py:18-33

chunk_findings.detail: The body of `_add_ports` is malformed: `pid = f"{item}@{ln}" IT.add_task(` is not valid Python because two expressions are juxtaposed with no operator, separator, or assignment target. Importing this module/package will raise `SyntaxError` at parse time. Even if the line were repaired by inserting a newline/semicolon, the shown loop then passes `port` to `IT.add_task` and checks `added.ok`, but neither `port` nor `added` is assigned in the shown code; the expected `port = replace(...)` and `added = IT.add_task(...)` assignments are missing. Any import of `ddflow.api.items` that reaches this submodule fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:140 (`_add_ports`)

chunk_findings.detail: The generated-port clash check ignores `readd` and treats removed tombstones as existing. The state clearly includes removed items: `_port_of_lines` checks `origin.removed` and filters `not o.removed` from `st.items.values()`. Therefore, if a previous multi-line task created port `X@release` and that port was removed, a later call such as `task_add(repo, "X", lines="main,release", readd=True)` (with `X` itself absent or removed so the main `IT.taken(..., readd=True)` check passes) reaches line 248, sees `f"{item}@{ln}" in st.items` as true for `X@release`, and returns failed `"X@release already exist"`. This contradicts the documented behavior that `readd` lets a removed id come back, and it also contradicts the later call to `_add_ports(..., readd=readd)`, which indicates generated ports should honor `readd`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:248 (`task_add`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `_line_frozen` body contains a malformed line: `ports = [o.id for o in st.items.values() if o.port_from ==terminal or it.lease:` is not valid Python (unclosed list comprehension and a colon after an assignment). As written, importing `ddflow/api/items/_edit.py` raises `SyntaxError`, so `update`, `plan_edit`, and everything re-exported through the new package fail before any item can be updated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:_line_frozen

chunk_findings.detail: `_landed_paths_fields` returns `O.nothing` when the requested `landed_paths` are already the current restriction, or when clearing an already-empty restriction, and `update` returns that outcome unconditionally even when other fields were planned. For example, on an item with no existing `landed_paths`, calling `update(repo, id, ItemEdit(title="new", landed_paths=[]))` puts `title` into `fields`, then `_landed_paths_fields` sees no restriction to clear, returns `O.nothing`, and `update` returns before `_record_update`, so the title change is silently dropped. The same happens with `ItemEdit(title="new", landed_paths=current_paths)`; an unchanged `--landed-paths` argument should not veto other requested edits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update

chunk_findings.detail: The split drafts do not propagate the parent item's dependencies, and the `needs` argument is applied only to the first part. For an item `A` that already needs `X`, `split(A, into=["B", "C"])` creates `B` and `C` with `needs=[]` (unless the caller also passes `needs`, in which case only `B` gets it and `C` still needs nothing). Those children are the work that replaces `A`, but they can be claimed before `X` is done, so the parent's dependency constraint is lost even though `globs` and `priority` are inherited.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_split.py:118

chunk_findings.detail: The re-export mechanism only makes the package attribute resolve to the submodule object on first access. It does not propagate rebinding of private helpers back into the submodule globals where the public functions look them up. Concretely, existing callers/tests that do `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.redact, "_marker", fake)` and then call `ddflow.core.redact.redact_text(...)` used to see `fake` in the old single-module `ddflow.core.redact` globals; in the split package, `redact_text` runs in `ddflow.core.redact.engine` and resolves `_marker` from `engine`’s globals, which the package-level assignment did not change. This breaks the stated no-behavior-change and the docstring’s “monkeypatch … exactly as before” invariant for these patch-covered private names.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/__init__.py:73

chunk_findings.detail: `repo_root` with a trailing slash prevents the repo-root path redaction from matching normal rooted paths. The regex is `re.compile(re.escape(root) + r"(?![\w.-])")`; for `redact_text("[REDACTED:path]", secret_patterns=[], repo_root="[REDACTED:path]")`, the regex consumes `[REDACTED:path]` and then the lookahead sees `f`, which is in `[\w]`, so the match fails. The root is not redacted as a path even though the function contract says `repo_root` is removed, leaking the repository root path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:redact_text

chunk_findings.detail: The mask fallback leakes the first token of a two-token matched secret. `mask_secrets("hunter2 swordfish", ["hunter2 swordfish"])` matches the full string; `_mask` reaches `parts = s.split(None, 1)` and returns `f"{parts[0]} [REDACTED]"`, `hunter2 [REDACTED]`. Because the caller declared the entire matched text a secret, preserving the first half of the secret is an under-redaction leak. It should return `[REDACTED]` unless the first token is recognized as a key/context.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_mask

chunk_findings.detail: The idempotence guard only skips matches that are exactly a full `_MARKER` (`_MARKER.fullmatch(m.group(0))`), while `whole=True` scans through markers. Given `redact_text("[REDACTED:secret]", secret_patterns=[r"REDACTED"])`, the pattern matches `REDACTED` inside the marker and replaces it with `[REDACTED:secret]`, yielding `[[REDACTED:secret]:secret]`. This corrupts already-redacted text and violates the module's promise that a marker is never scanned again.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_secrets

chunk_findings.detail: Given input `kind="bug.fixed"` and `data={"item": "bug_2026-10-15_01", "lesson": "..."}`, `redact_event_data` redacts the `item` id. `"item"` is not in `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS["bug.fixed"]` (`"lesson", "changelog", "regression_verify"`), is not in `LOG_VERBATIM_NAMES`, and `("bug.fixed", "item")` is absent from `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`, so the function falls into the `else` branch and replaces the item id with a redaction marker. Since other bug-lifecycle payloads that reference an item explicitly preserve it (for example `("bug.found", "item")` is in `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`), `bug.fixed` item ids should also be preserved; the committed `bug.fixed` event data is corrupted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/log.py:LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS

chunk_findings.detail: When both inline `ID:DIGEST` forms and a positional `digests` list are supplied, positional digests are aligned to the original `ids` index, not to the IDs that actually need a digest. For example, `approvals_approve_bulk(repo, ["A:aaaa", "B"], digests=["bbbb"])` builds `target` as `[("A", "aaaa"), ("B", "")]`: the digest intended for `B` is silently dropped, so `B` is approved without the provided digest check and its full digest is recorded as a read receipt. With `["A:aaaa", "B", "C"]` and `["bbbb", "cccc"]`, `B` receives `cccc` (the digest intended for `C`) and `C` receives no digest. The function should either reject mixed forms or compact the positional digests for IDs that do not carry an inline digest.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/approvals_answer.py:approvals_approve_bulk

chunk_findings.detail: When both inline `ID:DIGEST` forms and a positional `digests` list are supplied, positional digests are aligned to the original `ids` index, not to the IDs that actually need a digest. For example, `approvals_approve_bulk(repo, ["A:aaaa", "B"], digests=["bbbb"])` builds `target` as `[("A", "aaaa"), ("B", "")]`: the digest intended for `B` is silently dropped, so `B` is approved without the provided digest check and its full digest is recorded as a read receipt. With `["A:aaaa", "B", "C"]` and `["bbbb", "cccc"]`, `B` receives `cccc` (the digest intended for `C`) and `C` receives no digest. The function should either reject mixed forms or compact the positional digests for IDs that do not carry an inline digest.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/approvals_answer.py:approvals_approve_bulk

chunk_findings.detail: `_split_ids` treats any string containing a colon as an inline `ID:DIGEST`, even when the part after the colon is empty. Thus `approvals_approve_bulk(repo, ["A:"], digests=[])` (or `["A:", "B:bbbb"]`) produces `("A", "")` rather than rejecting the malformed pair or falling back to the bare-id path. Because the bulk loop accepts an empty digest as “no prefix check” (as the prior confirmed finding showed), an operator who types `approve A:` intending to supply a digest but omits it will have request `A` approved without the read-receipt prefix being checked or prompted, while the equivalent `approve A` would go through `_digest_or_ask` and prompt. This silently weakens the digest semantics for malformed inline pairs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/approvals_answer.py:_split_ids

chunk_findings.detail: When an `update` changes some fields but the `landed_paths` value is a no-op, the code returns the landed-paths outcome and discards the other requested changes. For example, given item `X` that already has `landed_paths=["a.py"]` and `globs=["a.py"]`, call `update(repo, "X", ItemEdit(globs=["b.py"], landed_paths=["a.py"]))` (CLI equivalent: `ddflow update X --globs b.py --landed-paths a.py`). `plan_edit` correctly returns `{"globs": ["b.py"]}`; `update` then calls `_landed_paths_fields`, which sees `paths == it.landed_paths` and returns `O.nothing(... already restricts ...)`. Because `update` returns immediately on any `O.Outcome` from `_landed_paths_fields`, the `globs` edit is never recorded, even though it was valid and requested. The same abort also happens for a no-op clear (`--landed-paths ""` when no restriction exists) and can prevent a `--worktree` rebind requested in the same edit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update / _landed_paths_fields

chunk_findings.detail: The new submodule does `from ddflow.api import items as _items` while it is itself part of `ddflow.api.items`. Because the new `__init__.py` re-exports the public API by importing this module, this line runs during initialization of `ddflow.api.items`, before the parent package `ddflow.api` has an `items` attribute set. The first `import ddflow.api.items` or `from ddflow.api.items import task_add` therefore raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'items' from partially initialized module 'ddflow.api'`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:9

chunk_findings.detail: The multi-line clash check ignores `readd` and removed items: `clash = [f"{item}@{ln}" for ln in wanted if f"{item}@{ln}" in st.items]`. Given an existing removed port `T@dev`, calling `task_add(repo, "T", lines="main,dev", readd=True)` fails with `T@dev already exist`, because `st.items` contains removed items (the same file relies on this in `_port_of_lines` when it tests `origin.removed`). This contradicts the documented `readd` behavior that a removed id may come back; `_add_ports` would pass `readd` to `IT.add_task`, but the premature clash check returns before that happens.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:task_add

chunk_findings.detail: `plan_edit` treats a no-op add/remove fold as “nothing to change” even when `edit.worktree` is set. `_nothing_to_change` only inspects the `needs`/`tags`/`globs` folds, and `update` only ignores a `NOTHING` outcome from `plan_edit` when `edit.landed` or `edit.landed_paths` is present. Given an item whose tags already include `bug`, `update(repo, id, ItemEdit(add_tags=["bug"], worktree="/linked/wt"))` folds `tags` back to the current list, `_nothing_to_change` returns a “nothing to change” message, `plan_edit` returns `O.nothing`, and `update` returns that outcome without calling `_update_and_rebind`; the requested `--worktree` rebind is silently skipped. The same path also bypasses the intended empty-worktree refusal for `worktree=""` when combined with a no-op fold.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:plan_edit/_nothing_to_change

chunk_findings.detail: `update` aborts on any outcome returned by `_landed_paths_fields`, including `O.nothing`, even when other fields are set. Given an item with a landed range and `landed_paths=["a.py"]`, `update(repo, id, ItemEdit(title="New", landed_paths=["a.py"]))` makes `_landed_paths_fields` return `O.nothing` because the restriction is unchanged; `update` returns that immediately, so the title is not recorded. Likewise, `ItemEdit(landed_paths=[])` on an item with no path restriction returns nothing and discards any other fields or a `worktree` rebind. A redundant or no-op path-restriction edit should not suppress the rest of the update.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update

chunk_findings.detail: `_refile_problem` validates each proposed new id against the current state with `IT.taken(st, nid, readd=False)`, but it never checks that the proposed ids are distinct from each other. For a contested item with two losing definitions, a call such as `resolve(..., keep=..., refile_as="new1,new1")` passes validation: both occurrences of `new1` are seen as unused in the pre-transaction `st`. `_apply_resolution` then zips `new_ids` with the two lost definitions and appends two `{family}.added` events for the same id `new1`, creating duplicate item ids / a bogus refiled contest instead of refusing the invalid input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_resolve.py:_refile_problem

chunk_findings.detail: This module is a submodule of the package it imports at top level. The package `ddflow/api/items/__init__.py` is described as re-exporting the public API, so it must import this module to expose `split`. When that happens, `ddflow.api.items` is already in `sys.modules` but has not yet been set as an attribute on `ddflow.api`; the top-level `from ddflow.api import items as _items` therefore executes during initialization and raises an ImportError for a partially initialized module. Using `_items._load` only inside functions does not save it, because the import statement itself fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_split.py:7

chunk_findings.detail: `needs` is applied only to the first child (`needs=csv_list(needs) if i == 1 else []`). Given `split(repo, A, into=["B", "C"], needs="X")`, child `B` depends on `X` but child `C` has no needs. If `A` was blocked by `X`, or if the caller expected the supplied `needs` to apply to every split part, `C` can be claimed before `X` completes, bypassing the dependency. The parent’s own needs are also never copied to any child, so splitting a blocked item can make its sub-tasks unblocked.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_split.py:118

evidence.reviewed_for_holder: [REDACTED:hostname]-ddflow-7267fe reviewed ci-splitter's split api.items to a <30k package

chunk_findings.detail: `_fail_fast("pytest -xq")` returns False because `shlex.split` leaves combined pytest short options as the single token `-xq`, which is not detected by `t in ("-x", "--exitfirst")`. In `_rerun_failed_tests`, that makes the fail-fast guard false for a rerun that actually stopped at the first failure, so tests after the first are wrongly marked as `flaked` and written to the flake log even though the rerun never ran them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_run.py:_fail_fast

chunk_findings.detail: When `cwd` was removed by `merge` while the gate was still running, the function sets `asked = cwd if cwd.is_dir() else repo` so ancestry checks use the repository, but the subsequent `for newer, what in ((G.tree_identity(cwd), ...), ...)` still calls `G.tree_identity(cwd)` on the now-missing directory. The git call therefore fails and raises out of `_execute` instead of reaching `G.superseded_by(..., asked, ...)` and returning the documented “could not tell keeps the record” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_run.py:_superseded_run

chunk_findings.detail: An ordinary `ddflow ci run` command with no `--timeout`, no bare `--`, and no quoted/backslash text makes `_CI_WORDS.finditer(command)` yield no matches. The `for ... else` block then executes with `m` unbound and raises `UnboundLocalError`. For example, `_with_run_timeout(cfg, gdef, 60, "item", "gate")` with `gdef.command == "ddflow ci run pytest"` passes the `_CI_VERB.match` guard but crashes instead of returning `ddflow ci run --timeout 60 pytest`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_timeout.py:_ci_command_with_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: When the command contains an old `--timeout` and no later bare `--`, the tail is rebuilt starting at `m.start()` before the old option, not after it, so the old option remains in the result. `_ci_command_with_timeout("ddflow ci run --timeout 5 echo hi", 60)` returns `"ddflow ci run --timeout 60 --timeout 5 echo hi"` instead of `"ddflow ci run --timeout 60 echo hi"`, so the timeout override does not actually replace the CI budget and can make the command invalid or use the old value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_timeout.py:_ci_command_with_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The first branch `if it.worktree:` honors a stored worktree without checking `cfg.worktree.enabled`. Given an item that already has a worktree and `[worktree].enabled` is later set to `false` (the lone-agent switch), and the item has not merged, `item_tree` returns that linked worktree instead of the primary. This contradicts the function's own contract that with worktrees off the primary stays the answer, and a worktree-gated run will execute in the stale linked worktree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_tree.py:item_tree

chunk_findings.detail: `_evidence_fields` uses `if evidence.ci_scope:` to decide whether to record the caller-supplied CI scope. `ci_scope` is typed `dict[str, Any] | None`, so an empty dict `{}` is a valid provided value meaning “the `ci run` selected no tests,” but it is falsy and is not recorded in `ev`. Given input `Evidence(ci_scope={})`, the event loses the fact that a CI scope was supplied; downstream cannot distinguish that from “no `ci_scope` provided.” It should use `if evidence.ci_scope is not None:`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_vet.py:_evidence_fields

The behavior the finding describes is pre-existing in the single-file module; this no-behavior-change split does not introduce or alter it.

chunk_findings.detail: The package re-exports patch-covered private names such as `_mask`, `_marker`, `_coerce`, and `_secrets` from submodules, but assigning to `ddflow.core.redact._mask` only sets that name in `ddflow.core.redact.__dict__`. Functions such as `redact_text` resolve `_mask` from `ddflow.core.redact.engine`'s module globals, not from the package globals, so the patch is ignored. Previously both the function and the patched private lived in `ddflow.core.redact`'s single module namespace, so `unittest.mock.patch("ddflow.core.redact._mask", fake)` would change `redact_text` behavior. This contradicts the docstring's claim that monkeypatching still "re-binds the name on THIS module exactly as before."
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/__init__.py:_SUBMODULE_OF

chunk_findings.detail: `_secrets` runs the user regex over the whole text (`whole=True`), but `settled` only keeps a match when the entire match equals a marker. A valid pattern that matches text inside a produced marker breaks idempotence: `redact_text("secret", secret_patterns=[r"secret"])` first returns `[REDACTED:secret]`; a second identical call matches the `secret` suffix inside that marker and returns `[REDACTED:[REDACTED:secret]]`. This violates the pass's documented idempotence and corrupts already-redacted output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_secrets.settled

chunk_findings.detail: `_mask` treats any two blank-delimited words as `key value` and returns `f"{parts[0]} [REDACTED]"`. When a caller supplies a pattern that matches an actual multi-word secret, this leaks the first word: `mask_secrets("hunter2 launch", [r"hunter2 launch"])` returns `"hunter2 [REDACTED]"`, leaving part of the secret visible. Since `_secrets` accepts arbitrary regexes, this can defeat redaction for phrase-style secrets.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_mask

chunk_findings.detail: `("job.started", "cwd")` is classified as `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`, so `redact_event_data` keeps that field with only `redact_network` applied. Given input `redact_event_data("job.started", {"cwd": "[REDACTED:path]"}, redactor, lookup_network=True)`, the returned dict still contains `"cwd": "[REDACTED:path]"` because `redact_network` masks private IPs/hostnames, not filesystem paths. That commits a home path unredacted even though this same module explicitly redacts `session.started.cwd` in `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` and documents that a home path must never be committed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/log.py:LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS / redact_event_data

chunk_findings.detail: `_loop` calls `_parse(m.group(1), ip_type).is_loopback` without the `try/except ValueError` guard that `_is_private` uses. `_IPV4` is only a syntactic pattern, so it legitimately matches invalid dotted quads such as `999.1.1.1`; `_loop(_IPV4.search("999.1.1.1"), ipaddress.IPv4Address)` raises `ipaddress.AddressValueError` instead of returning `False`. Any caller that iterates `_IPV4`/`_IPV6` matches and passes them to `_loop` will crash on that ordinary input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/pattern.py:_loop

chunk_findings.detail: After `python -m` is processed, `leading` is left `False`, and the special case that appends the wrapped program (`elif tok in _PROGRAMS and out[-1] == "-m":`) does not restore `leading = True`. For `redact_argv(["python", "-m", "ddflow", "view"], subcommands=["view"])`, the result is `["python", "-m", "ddflow", "<arg>"]`, but `view` is an allowed leading subcommand and should be kept according to the function’s own docstring. The special case needs to reset the leading context once it has recognized `ddflow`/`ddflow-mcp` as the real program after Python’s `-m`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/profiles.py:redact_argv

chunk_findings.detail: The exemption is moved to `ddflow/core/redact/pattern.py:_MIN_TERM`, but in the split `_MIN_TERM` is the minimum-term-length constant that belongs with the term machinery in `ddflow/core/redact/engine.py` (`engine.py` adds `_term`/`_marker`). The constants-exemption checker will look for `_MIN_TERM` in `pattern.py`, fail to find it there, and then flag the real `_MIN_TERM` in `engine.py` as an unexplained magic constant.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/constants-exemptions.toml:184

chunk_findings.detail: The function signals every integer it finds in a `daemon.<pid>.json` file without validating that it is a positive, plausible process id. A stale or corrupt runtime file such as `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.0.json` containing `{"pid": 0}` is accepted by `_daemon_pid`, then `os.kill(0, signal.SIGTERM)` is executed. In POSIX, pid `0` means “all processes in the current process group,” so this can kill the pytest runner and its child processes before the scratch `HOME` teardown finishes. Negative pids have the analogous process-group meaning, and a huge integer can also escape the caught exception types as `OverflowError`, aborting teardown.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py `terminate_suite_daemons`

chunk_findings.detail: The documented return value is “how many were terminated,” but the implementation returns `len(pids)`, i.e. how many pidfiles were parsed. For example, if a daemon exited earlier and left `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.4321.json`, `os.kill(4321, SIGTERM)` raises `ProcessLookupError`, the process is not alive, and the function still returns `1` even though it terminated nothing. Any caller or regression test that uses the return value to prove that suite daemons were actually cleaned up will get a false positive.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py `terminate_suite_daemons`

chunk_findings.detail: The cleanup identifies daemons solely by pidfile location plus `kill(pid, 0)` existence, with no check that the signaled process is still the daemon that wrote the pidfile. If a suite-started roborev daemon crashes and leaves `daemon.4321.json`, but pid `4321` is later reused by an unrelated subprocess started by the test suite, teardown will see `_alive(4321) == True` and send `SIGTERM`/`SIGKILL` to that unrelated process. This can abort cleanup subprocesses or otherwise corrupt the test session.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py `terminate_suite_daemons`

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test calls `ISO.terminate_suite_daemons` directly instead of exercising the sandbox teardown path (`_teardown`) that actually caused the orphan-daemon bug. A change can therefore add a working `terminate_suite_daemons` helper while leaving `_teardown` not calling it, calling it with the wrong directory, or deleting the scratch `HOME` before killing daemons; this test would still pass because it never invokes `_teardown`. That gives false confidence that B7d61f8c094 is fixed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:test_teardown_kills_a_daemon_the_suite_spawned_under_its_scratch_home

chunk_findings.detail: Port selection and readiness are racy. `_free_port()` releases a port, then `_spawn()` starts a daemon that tries to bind it; another process can bind the same port in the interval, causing daemon startup to fail and the test to fail nondeterministically. Separately, `_pid_under()` returns as soon as a pidfile exists, then the test asserts `_held(port)` only once. If the daemon writes its pidfile before binding the address, or binding is delayed under load, `_held(port)` returns `False` and the test fails even though the daemon is starting normally. The test needs a deterministic readiness wait or a fake daemon.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:_free_port/_held

chunk_findings.detail: `_held()` leaks the probe socket whenever `bind()` fails: the `except OSError` branch returns `True` without closing `probe`. In the normal successful test path, the daemon holds the port, so this call leaks one file descriptor; repeated calls or failures can accumulate leaked sockets.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:_held

chunk_findings.detail: The cleanup sends `SIGTERM`/`SIGKILL` to any live PID returned by `_pid_under()` from a pidfile under `home`, without verifying that the PID is the daemon spawned by the test. If the daemon exits and its PID is reused by another process before cleanup, or a stale pidfile remains, the test can signal an unrelated process and corrupt the test environment.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:finally cleanup

chunk_findings.detail: The new identity check only tests whether `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` contains the substring `roborev`. A stale pidfile under the scratch runtime whose pid has been recycled by any roborev-named test process is therefore treated as the daemon. For example, a suite-started daemon crashes leaving `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.4321.json`; later the suite starts a subprocess such as `python -m pytest tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py` and that subprocess receives pid 4321. `terminate_suite_daemons` parses 4321, `_is_roborev_daemon` returns True because the test filename contains `roborev`, and teardown SIGTERMs/SIGKILLs the unrelated test process. This is the same pid-reuse defect from the previous review; the substring check does not prove the process is the daemon that wrote the pidfile under `home`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_is_roborev_daemon

chunk_findings.detail: `_daemon_pid` does not catch `OverflowError` when converting a JSON pid field to int. A corrupt pidfile such as `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.1.json` containing Python-JSON-valid `{"pid": Infinity}` (or `{"pid": 1e999}`) makes `json.loads` return `float('inf')`; `int(inf)` raises `OverflowError`, which is not in the `except (OSError, ValueError, KeyError, TypeError)` tuple. The exception propagates out of `_daemon_pid` into `terminate_suite_daemons` and `_teardown`, so teardown fails before `shutil.rmtree`, contrary to the function's contract that invalid pidfiles yield `None`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_daemon_pid

chunk_findings.detail: The test selects a port with `_free_port()`, closes the probe socket, and then starts `roborev` on that port, so the port is not reserved between selection and daemon bind. If another process binds the same port in that window—for example, a second pytest-xdist worker running this same test and getting the same ephemeral port—the daemon’s bind fails and the loop times out, producing a nondeterministic failure of `assert _held(port)`. The readiness probe itself makes this worse because `_held()` also binds the target port while the daemon is trying to start, creating a self-race in which the daemon can see `EADDRINUSE` during a probe bind.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:_free_port / test_teardown_kills_a_daemon_the_suite_spawned_under_its_scratch_home

chunk_findings.detail: The identity check still treats any process whose `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` merely contains the substring `roborev` as the suite daemon. If a stale pidfile under the scratch runtime survives a crashed daemon, e.g. `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.4321.json`, and the PID is later recycled by an unrelated test process whose command line contains `roborev` — for example `python -m pytest tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py`, which is the new test file itself — `terminate_suite_daemons` will SIGTERM that unrelated process. The visible change only replaces the rmtree atexit registration with `_teardown`; it does not tighten daemon identity, so the suite can kill arbitrary test processes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_is_roborev_daemon

chunk_findings.detail: `_daemon_pid` still converts the JSON pid field with `int(...)` while catching only `(OSError, ValueError, KeyError, TypeError)`. A corrupt pidfile such as `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.1.json` containing `{"pid": Infinity}` is accepted by Python’s `json.loads`, which returns `float('inf')`; `int(float('inf'))` raises `OverflowError`, which is not caught. The exception escapes `_daemon_pid` into `_teardown`, and because `_teardown` is now registered as an atexit handler, teardown can abort before the scratch HOME is removed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_daemon_pid

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test still selects a port by opening a probe socket, closing it, and then starting `roborev` on that port. Between close and daemon bind the port is unreserved, so another process can bind it — a concrete case is two pytest-xdist workers running the same test and receiving the same ephemeral port. One daemon bind then fails and the test fails nondeterministically; worse, `_held()` can pass because an unrelated process holds the port, so the test may not actually verify that the spawned daemon held it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:_free_port

chunk_findings.detail: The identity check uses only `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and never verifies that the process belongs to the scratch `home`. If a suite-spawned daemon dies and leaves `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.4321.json`, and before teardown pid 4321 is reused by any live `roborev daemon ...` process (for example the operator’s real daemon, or a daemon from another parallel suite), `_is_roborev_daemon(4321)` returns true and `terminate_suite_daemons` sends `SIGTERM`/`SIGKILL` to that unrelated daemon. This contradicts the function’s stated intent that the operator’s real daemon under the real `HOME` is left alone; the pidfile’s location under the scratch home does not prove that the current owner of the pid is the suite’s daemon.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_is_roborev_daemon

chunk_findings.detail: A corrupt pidfile such as `{"pid": 999999999999999999999999}` is parsed by `json.loads()` as a Python integer, so `_daemon_pid()` returns that huge positive value without hitting the `OverflowError` path. In `terminate_suite_daemons`, the initial `SIGTERM` loop catches `OverflowError`, but the later `ours_alive()` call invokes `_alive()`, whose `os.kill(pid, 0)` raises `OverflowError` uncaught. That aborts `_teardown()` before `shutil.rmtree()`, leaving the scratch `HOME` and potentially the daemon state behind. This violates the docstring’s promise that a corrupt pid must never reach `os.kill`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_alive

chunk_findings.detail: The cleanup block is keyed to the wrong process handle: it never kills the daemon pid it discovered via `_pid_under`, and it stops using HOME-based termination once `_teardown(home)` has removed the scratch directory. If `roborev daemon run` daemonizes or spawns a worker child (the orphan case this test is meant to prevent), `_pid_under` can return the child pid while the direct `Popen` object refers to a CLI parent that has already exited. On the unfixed teardown, `ISO._teardown(home)` deletes the scratch HOME but leaves the child alive; `proc.wait()` returns, `assert not _alive(pid)` fails, then `finally` sees `home.exists()` is false so it does not call `terminate_suite_daemons(home)`, and `proc.poll()` is not None so it does not call `proc.kill()`. The test therefore exits with the known-alive `pid` still running under a deleted HOME, creating the very orphan the regression test is supposed to catch.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:65

chunk_findings.detail: `_is_roborev_daemon` can still terminate an unrelated process: it only checks that a pid named by a scratch-HOME pidfile has a first cmdline token containing `roborev` and some later exact `daemon` token, and never checks that the process was started under `home` (or that it is the daemon `run` subcommand). If a crashed suite daemon leaves `home/.roborev/runtime/daemon.4321.json` and pid 4321 is later reused by the operator’s real `roborev daemon run` daemon, or by another parallel suite’s daemon, or by a client such as `roborev daemon status`, `_is_roborev_daemon(4321)` returns True and `terminate_suite_daemons` SIGTERMs/SIGKILLs that unrelated process. The earlier daemon-token probe does not answer this because the recycled process can also carry a `daemon` token; the `except OSError: return True` path makes the same false kill possible whenever `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is unreadable (e.g. `/proc` is not mounted), touching a process whose command line is unknown.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_is_roborev_daemon

chunk_findings.detail: The cleanup in `finally` is keyed to the `Popen` handle, not to the daemon PID discovered by `_pid_under`. If `roborev daemon run` daemonizes or forks a worker (so `proc` is a CLI parent that has already exited) and `_teardown(home)` deletes the scratch `HOME` without killing the live daemon—the unfixed behavior this regression test is supposed to catch—then the test fails at `assert not _alive(pid)`, but its cleanup cannot remove the orphan: `home.exists()` is false, so `terminate_suite_daemons` is not called, and `proc.poll()` is not None, so `proc.kill()` is skipped. The live daemon survives the failed test, which is the exact orphan condition B7d61f8c094 is meant to prevent; the earlier unix-socket refutation does not answer this because it changes the bind address, not the cleanup key, and the discovered `pid` is still never killed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_isolation_roborev_daemon.py:67-72

chunk_findings.detail: The change only manufactures a textual reason from all reviewed results; it does not make those non-best findings part of the persisted gate record. The record path still derives finding rows from the single `best` result (`_finding_rows(best)` is unchanged, and the `_record` call in `gate.py` was not changed to pass `results`). In the exact scenario added by the test, `best` is the clean reviewer and the `finder` reviewer returns one `FINDING`; after the fix the round persists as `outcome=failed` with reason `"1 finding(s)"`, but no finding row for `y.py:1` is recorded. That is wrong: the persisted failed round claims a finding count that does not correspond to any recorded finding/held state, so the blocking finding is not actually persisted and can be silently lost or cleared by a later delta. The test only checks that `rec.reason` is non-empty, so it passes despite this inconsistent record.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/records.py:_reason_of

chunk_findings.detail: The guard intended to avoid killing a recycled pid is inverted when `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` cannot be read: `except OSError: return True`. The same environment where this can happen is explicitly anticipated elsewhere in the change (`_pid_max` falls back “where /proc is unavailable”). Given a scratch `HOME` whose runtime directory contains a stale or recycled `daemon.<pid>.json` file and `/proc` is unavailable (or the cmdline read fails), `_is_roborev_daemon(pid)` returns `True` for any positive pid. `terminate_suite_daemons` will then send `SIGTERM` and possibly `SIGKILL` to whatever process currently owns that pid (e.g. a user’s editor, another daemon, or PID 1 in a container), even though the docstring says unrelated processes must be left alone.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:_is_roborev_daemon

chunk_findings.detail: `terminate_suite_daemons` sends `SIGKILL` to survivors and returns immediately; `_teardown` then calls `shutil.rmtree(home, ignore_errors=True)`. Process termination after `SIGKILL` is not synchronous. If a spawned roborev daemon ignored or was slow to process `SIGTERM` and is still alive when the `SIGKILL` is delivered (for example, blocked in uninterruptible I/O, or simply not yet scheduled), it still holds the port and SQLite fd while `_teardown` deletes the scratch `HOME`/database. That recreates the original failure mode: the next gate can see port 7373 held by a process whose DB file has just been deleted. The teardown path should wait after `SIGKILL` until `_alive(pid)` is false, or otherwise synchronize with process exit, before removing the scratch home.
chunk_findings.title: tests/_isolation.py:terminate_suite_daemons

chunk_findings.detail: The `finally` cleanup can leave the daemon spawned by the test alive, recreating the exact orphan failure B7d61f8c094. It only calls `ISO.terminate_suite_daemons(home)` when `home` still exists, and only kills the direct `Popen` process. If `ISO._teardown(home)` deletes the scratch `HOME` but fails to kill a detached daemon worker (or the `roborev` parent process exits after writing a pidfile for the real daemon), the test can fail at `assert not _alive(pid)` while the known `pid` is still alive. At that point `home.exists()` is false, so `terminate_suite_daemons` is not called, and `proc.poll()` may be non-`None` because the parent exited, so `proc.kill()` is not called either. The cleanup should unconditionally kill/terminate the known `pid` if `_alive(pid)` reports it alive.

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes the reason and recorded finding count consider findings from every reviewed reviewer, but `_link_refuted` is still called only with `best.findings`. In a delta round where `best` has no findings but another reviewed reviewer has a finding that is refuted/fixed by the commits, `_link_refuted` sees no finding and does not reduce `held`; `_reason_of(best, results)` then returns a non-empty count such as `"1 finding(s)"`, so `_record` persists the round as failed. The intended clean delta round still does not become clean and the gate can remain failed with an unresolved finding, because the refutation path was not updated to the same “any reviewed reviewer” set the new `_reviewed_findings` rationale says the gate blocks on.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_link_refuted(..., _reviewed_findings(results))` call does not mirror the new `results is None` fallback just added to `_reason_of` in `records.py`. If `_record_round` is called with `results=None` and `best.findings` containing a finding that the commits refute (the call shape the new `_reason_of` code explicitly supports), this line calls `_reviewed_findings(None)` before `_reason_of` can synthesize the reason. If `_reviewed_findings` requires an iterable—as the old `results or []` guard suggests—it raises instead of recording the round; if it tolerates `None` by returning an empty collection, the refuted `best.findings` are never linked, `held` is not reduced, and the delta round remains failed even though `_reason_of` now counts `best.findings`. The gate should use the same fallback as `_reason_of`, e.g. `_reviewed_findings(results) if results is not None else best.findings`.

ddflow cannot push to a running agent, but every agent already calls ddflow regularly and runs hooks. Compute drift = commits on the base since the branch's merge base, split into RELEVANT (touch the item's globs, its pin files, the files its diff changed, or add/supersede a decision governing them) and unrelated. Surface it as one line on: heartbeat/lease renew replies, `ddflow brief`, gate_status, and the UserPromptSubmit/PostToolUse hook context (once per change of base sha, not every call): 'main moved: 14 commits, 3 touch your files (ddflow/services/ci.py ...); run ddflow sync'. Knobs [sync].notify = off|relevant|all, [sync].relevant_commits (default 1), [sync].block_commits for the claim/merge side. Shares its drift calculation with RR-freshness (task-vs-repo drift) so there is one implementation. Filed from the operator's 2026-10-17 question about drift (D-file-ddflow-defects). BASE BRANCH (operator 2026-10-17, D-item-base-branch): drift is measured against the item's recorded base (core.flow.target_branch), never a literal main/default branch; gitflow develop, a version line or a phase branch all work the same.

data.falsifier: A replay of the real event log in which v2 does not reduce lease wait or merge conflicts against v1, or lengthens makespan beyond the guard, or two runs on the same input differ.
data.mechanism: One OptimizerPort in ddflow/adapters (order, cut, explain) whose default adapter v1 is today's algorithm moved unchanged; a v2 adapter adds lane-aware scoring: cost = earliest finish minus capped affinity bonuses (glob/file overlap through an inverted file-to-task index, text similarity from the existing Matcher, co-change coupling from git history, declared affinity tags) plus aversion penalties, with a critical-path floor, an age bonus and a makespan guard that falls back to v1. Tags: affinity:<key>[@weight] and aversion:<key>[@weight] as plain strings, weight 1-100 default 50, preferred only.
data.question: Can the task selector and orderer prefer tasks that share files, overlap in globs or read alike (and affinity tags) in the same lane, keep averse tasks parallel, and sit behind one swappable optimizer adapter?

data.body: Research R-affinity-scheduling. Reduce lease waits, merge conflicts and duplicated work by ordering, not by new locks. Builds on SW-score (done), SW-pull, DX-lease-real-overlap, ETA-simulate, the similarity matcher and MV-path-moves. data.body: Adapter 'affinity-v2' behind OptimizerPort. Order ready items by critical-path rank (fill Item.critical from the chain length; today never filled), then place each for the asking lane: cost = earliest start minus capped affinity bonus (lane's recent and running tasks vs this one: file overlap, similarity, coupling, tags) plus aversion penalty (an averse pair should be offered to DIFFERENT lanes, so the second is not held waiting for the first) plus an age bonus against starvation. A schedule is data (B-sched-model, done); WHO starts it is an adapter. Port: register(job), unregister, list, status (registered, last fired, next due), heartbeat. data.body: The audit lists about 35 leaf commands with a non-'covered by' exemption and 126 CLI-only flags. data.body: Implements the design of RM-client-exec-research (done, research only). Any step the server cannot or should not run (test and ci commands, git operations, reviewers launched on the client, hooks and companion installs, review detach) returns in the same result an envelope: agent_action: [{id, kind: shell | mcp | ask_user, command (argv), cwd, why, expect (exit 0, files), timeout_s, then: {tool, args} to report the result}]. The reporting call (ddflow_gate record, merge, complete) takes the exit code, an output digest and an output tail, stores them with provenance agent_reported, and the server checks what it can (digest present, exit code consistent, the head sha the run claims equals the item's tree). A gate that needs a trusted result (policy knob) stays partial until a server-verified or CI run exists. Works for every surface: CLI prints the same envelope as text. This is ALWAYS available, never an unavailable dead end. Adversarial tests: a falsified report is recorded as agent_reported and cannot satisfy a policy that demands verification.
