data.decision: OPERATOR, verbatim 2026-11-01: 'In principle we want to be able to run ddflow fully remotely without the users to have access to shell, so all acceptance and commands have to be able to be run from the Mcp and chat interface with askuserquestion for acceptance. No shell access should be necessary. Separately ddflow might work as a remote mcp server or in docker container where ddflow itself have no access to shell to execute cli, and in such situations the mcp shall be able to instruct the agent what to run, this process should always be possible. And last - I see a lot of commands the LLM execute to discover ddflow help and options. Ddflow should inform help, suggest commands and parameters to the user or the agent to execute, in order to save time.' Becomes the rules r-no-shell (A and B) and r-tell-dont-discover (C); the work is phase P-remote tasks NS-*; research R-no-shell-audit.
data.title: Principle: ddflow works with no shell, a shell-less server instructs the agent, and ddflow suggests exact commands

fields.body: Decision D-no-shell-principle (operator 2026-11-01). When you add or change code: (1) every command, every acting flag and every acceptance has an MCP form (a family action, tools/list has no headroom) and a chat route: the agent proposes (--approval request, or the approval parameter), the person answers with AskUserQuestion, the agent attests and re-runs with the id. The agent never approves its own request. No refusal, remedy or note for a T2-or-lower act may send the caller to a terminal; a T3 act follows the host's install-time opt-in and is refused with the exact install step otherwise. (2) A step the server cannot run (no shell, remote server, container, missing git) never ends in a bare unavailable: it returns an agent_action envelope in the same result (what to run as argv with cwd and expected outcome, and the call that records the result, stored as agent_reported and never as server-verified). This must always be possible, on every surface. (3) A new CLI command or acting flag ships with its MCP form in the same change; test_mcp_parity exemptions only shrink and each carries a reason. (4) Do not assume a local shell, git, a writable filesystem or the agent's transcript on the server host: ask the capability probe. (5) Say in the task which route the acceptance takes; the standards gate and reviewers check it.
fields.title: No shell needed: every command and acceptance works over MCP and chat; a shell-less server instructs the agent what to run

fields.body: Decision D-no-shell-principle (operator 2026-11-01): agents burn calls discovering help and options, so ddflow tells them. When you add or change code: (1) any refusal, remedy, note or error that names a command goes through the one next_actions renderer (command id, tool and action, argument shapes, cli template): never hand-written 'run ddflow ...' prose, and the arguments are shaped correctly (the pytest id form for --regression-test, the approval id after the person answered). (2) A new command ships with a head-first usage line, one example, and, when it is a flow agents get wrong, a recipe. (3) Validate every argument before spending anything single-use (an approval, a review round). (4) Counts, tool names and profile text in help are generated from the registry, never typed. (5) Measure: the discovery-overhead metrics must not rise. The standards gate and reviewers check it; the shrink-only ratchet on hard-coded command strings is the machine check.
fields.title: Tell the agent what to run: every result, refusal and error names the exact next call (MCP and CLI form); help is generated, not typed

data.body: The rules gate today only tells the agent to load the digest; every rule is advisory and no rule says how to verify it. Add to the rule record: check (a pytest id or a ratchet test, a command, or later a B-dec-checks kind: deps, imports, pattern, files, config; the engine is shared, never a second one) and verify (one or two sentences: what the agent must look at when a check cannot be automatic). ddflow rule check ITEM runs the checks of the rules that apply to the diff (RU-applicable) through the command runner and reports passed, failed, unavailable or not_applicable per rule with file:line where the check gives it. The rules gate then records per rule: which were checked, with which outcome and evidence; a gate recorded with silence on an applicable rule is refused (no silent pass); an unavailable check is recorded unavailable, never passed. A rule with enforcement block makes a failed check refuse completion; advisory shows it. data.body:
Each kind is a pure evaluator returning pass, fail or unavailable, with file:line findings and a digest.
- deps: allow and forbid lists plus version ranges against parsed manifests (pyproject/requirements, package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, Gemfile, basic pom/gradle; stdlib parsers).
- imports: layer and forbidden-import contracts, using import-linter or dependency-cruiser when the project configures them (an adapter, unavailable when absent), otherwise a simple import scan for Python and JS/TS.
- pattern: required or forbidden regex, or a Semgrep rule when semgrep is configured, over the decision's globs.
- files: must or must not exist.
- config: assert a key in TOML, JSON, YAML or INI files, or a ddflow knob value.
- command: an operator-configured command run through B-uni-cmdrunner with digest approval; exit 0 passes.
- radar: see B-dec-deps.
Results are cached per tree fingerprint. Tests cover each kind, plus the unavailable path.

Operator 2026-10-06 (rules/decisions unification): build this on the shared guidance engine (B-uni-guidance-core/-inject/-enforce); no rule- or decision-specific matcher, injection or enforcement path.

Output JSON for the reviewers and a readable summary. data.title: A Python file over 30 KB is split into a module or package

fields.body: Decisions D-small-files and D-small-files-30k (operator 2026-11-01). WHY: a lease covers a file, so one big file serialises every agent that needs any part of it, and a small-context LLM cannot read a big file or its diff. RULE: a .py file over [quality].max_file_bytes (default 30000 bytes, about 7k tokens) is split by cohesion into a package: one concern per module, a thin __init__ facade that keeps the old import path and re-exports the public names, a module docstring saying what the module holds. Applies to tests too (split by feature under one package or several test modules). WHEN: if the file you are about to edit is over the limit, or your change would push it over, split it FIRST as its own change (own task, own lease, no behaviour change, the full tests green before and after), then make your change in the small module; never add to an over-limit file. Aim well under the limit for new modules. After a split, the tasks that name the old path must be re-pointed (the path-move tooling MV-* does this; until then update the globs yourself). Exemptions are listed in one shrink-only baseline with a reason; a ratchet fails a new oversized file or an exempt file that grew. The standards gate and reviewers check it.
fields.title: Split any Python file over 30 KB into a module or package: small files lock fewer parallel agents and fit small context windows

chunk_findings.detail: The outside-path negative control uses `notes.txt`, a non-`.jsonl` path, so it only proves the exemption is not global to arbitrary text files; it does not prove the path is restricted to `.ddflow/events/`. If the allowlist were overbroad but extension-based (for example, matching any `*.jsonl` file), the exact key in `.ddflow/events/a.jsonl` would still exit 0, the one-character variant in the same path would still fire, and the exact key in `notes.txt` would still fire, so all three assertions pass even though the key would also be exempt in `other/a.jsonl`. That contradicts the stated goal of asserting the exemption holds only for the event-log path. The outside control should use a `.jsonl` path outside `.ddflow/events/`, such as `other/a.jsonl`.

chunk_findings.detail: The exact-event case uses the literal word `key` immediately before a 39-character high-entropy token (`"use gemini with this key " + _REVOKED_KEY + ...`). Gitleaks’ default `generic-api-key` rule (`(?i)(?:key|...)[^a-z0-9]{0,20}[0-9a-z_\-]{32,}`) matches that line independently of the `gcp-api-key` rule. If the landed allowlist is scoped to `gcp-api-key` as the comment/intent states, scanning `.ddflow/events/a.jsonl` still reports a `generic-api-key` finding, so the first assertion (`== 0`) fails. If the allowlist is instead global for the exact value/path, the test passes but no longer proves the exemption is scoped to the GCP rule.

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to prove the retry rule is count-based and not window-based, but it freezes the clock and only files two consecutive asks. If the implementation were window-based (e.g. counting only refusals within `standing_window_s`), this test would still pass because both asks occur at the frozen time, inside any positive window. To actually refute a window-based implementation, the test should advance the clock beyond `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s` between filings (or force the window to zero) and still expect the second filing to auto-approve.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_policy.py:test_the_retry_rule_fires_on_count_alone_not_the_window_or_the_policy_list

chunk_findings.detail: Approval records persisted before this change will not have the new `notify` key, but this display/audit row builder reads `r["notify"]` directly. Any pre-existing record therefore causes `KeyError: 'notify'` when `ddflow approvals log` (and likely `ddflow doctor`, which also reads `r["notify"]` at line 107) tries to list it. Use `r.get("notify", 0)` for the new field at both access sites, or migrate/backfill stored records before these commands run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/audit.py:61

chunk_findings.detail: The test calls `_frozen_clock(monkeypatch)` and then performs both the first `operator_gate` (which should not auto-approve) and the second `operator_gate` (which should auto-approve) without advancing time. A window-based implementation that auto-approves the second filing only when it falls within a time window would still see both filings at the same frozen timestamp and pass, so the test does not actually demonstrate that the rule is “not the window.” To catch a window-based implementation, the clock must be advanced beyond the relevant window before the second filing.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_policy.py:test_the_retry_rule_fires_on_count_alone_not_the_window_or_the_policy_list

chunk_findings.detail: `refusals` counts any pending or expired ask with the same verb and matching `item` extracted from `r["canon"]`, but `r["canon"]` stored in asks is serialized via `request(log, cfg, ...)` (which receives `digest`, `subject`, `text`, `command`), and `request()` does not store a key named `canon` in its dict or event payload (or if `r["canon"]` is missing/malformed, it fails or returns empty). Consequently, `json.loads(r["canon"])` raises a `KeyError` on every iteration over existing asks, causing `refusals()` to return 0 and breaking the retry threshold auto-approval feature entirely.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py:141

evidence.diff_source: delta review of 1 commit since f0d601bfce

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor removes the close-specific guard that refuses an imported phase with no tasks. Previously, `close_imported` checked `if not tasks` and returned a refusal with “nothing is under … there is no finished work to record.” After the change, the only task check is the shared `settled_tasks(...)` call, whose supplied hint is only for open tasks (“close them first, or file the work that remains”). For an imported phase `p1` that has zero tasks, `resolve_phase` succeeds, `_is_imported_phase(it)` succeeds, and `settled_tasks` has no open tasks to reject, so the path proceeds to record a `phase.close` with zero finished tasks. That violates the prior invariant for `phase close` that it records finished imported work, and it is an over-broad reuse of the `phase complete` guard under [r-reuse-core].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/phase_close.py:close_imported

chunk_findings.detail: The operator gate is skipped whenever the optional `agent` argument is empty, even though the log may already be operating as an agent. The code checks `AP.agent_marker(agent)` to decide whether an approval is required, but it later uses `log.agent_id` as the approval identity (`Canon(agent=log.agent_id, ...)`). Given an agent context where `log.agent_id` is an agent identity but `complete(..., agent="")` is called (or an agent invocation passes an empty/omitted `--agent`), `AP.agent_marker("")` is false, so `CN.operator_gate` is never invoked and the phase is completed directly with evidence `"retired by operator"`. This bypasses the intended operator gate: an agent invocation can complete the phase without filing or consuming an approval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/phase_complete.py:59-72

chunk_findings.detail: `settled_tasks` refuses whenever `st.tasks(phase_id)` is empty, even though the stated contract is to complete the phase when every task under it is done or abandoned/closed. For a phase with zero tasks this condition is vacuously satisfied, and the module docstring itself says the shared guard checks only that the phase exists, is a phase, is not already terminal, and that every task under it is settled. Given a phase `P` with no tasks (or with all tasks removed if `st.tasks` filters removed tasks), `phase complete P` reaches line 67 and returns `nothing is under P: there is no finished work to retire` instead of recording `phase.completed`, blocking the intended operator-gated retire of a `0/0` phase.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/phase_guard.py:67

chunk_findings.detail: An automated agent can bypass the mandatory operator approval by calling the entry point with `agent=""` (the function default). The only gate is `if AP.agent_marker(agent):`; since the `agent` string is caller-controlled and defaults to empty, `complete(log, cfg, "p1", agent="")` never calls `CN.operator_gate` and proceeds to `log.append("phase.completed", ...)`. That completes the phase without any operator approval, violating the change's first requirement that an agent invocation be operator-gated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/phase_complete.py complete_phase

chunk_findings.detail: The success-path fixture only marks tasks via `item.completed`; it never creates a task in the `abandoned` or `closed` terminal state. Requirement (2) explicitly permits `done or abandoned/closed`, but no test supplies an abandoned/closed task, so an implementation that incorrectly refuses anything other than `DONE` would still pass this entire test suite. That leaves the newly-added main edge case—deliberately retiring a phase whose not-done items are abandoned/closed—unverified.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_phase_complete.py:44 (`_phase`)

data.body: ADP-model put every port in ddflow/adapters/ports.py, every fake registration in ddflow/adapters/fakes/__init__.py (FAKES, PORTS_WITHOUT_FAKE), every conformance family in tests/test_ports_contract.py and every doc paragraph in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (already over the size limit). Four shared files means one adapter task at a time. Change the layout, with no behaviour change: (1) ports.py keeps only the shared base (the Port notion, helper types); each family lives in its own module ddflow/adapters/<family>.py with its port, default adapter and registry entry (the HttpClient port from ADP-http is the first to move; follow it, do not move other agents' in-flight files: ADP-tools and ADP-mcp rebase onto this); (2) fakes: one module per family under ddflow/adapters/fakes/, discovered deterministically (sorted module names, no hash order) so adding a fake edits no shared file; the PORTS_WITHOUT_FAKE baseline becomes one small file per missing port or one line per port in its own file so removing a line merges cleanly; the shrink-only ceiling stays; (3) tests/test_ports_contract.py becomes a generic test that iterates the discovered families (every port has a fake or a baseline line; adapter and fake pass the same conformance cases) and each family's cases live in tests/test_adapter_<family>.py; (4) docs: one page per family under docs/ddflow/adapters/<family>.md with an index; ARCHITECTURE.md keeps only the pattern and a link; (5) rewrite the how-to-add-a-port paragraph to the new flow, and add a test that fails if a new port needs an edit to any of the four former shared files. Existing adapters (digest, http and whatever has landed) are moved as part of this task. CONFORMANCE (r-small-files, r-reuse-core, r-everything-configurable, D-adapters-answers): no behaviour change; the existing port, fake and conformance tests keep passing; baselines only shrink. Found 2026-11-01 when ADP-tools could not commit because ports.py, fakes/__init__.py, tests/test_ports_contract.py and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md were leased to ADP-http and SZ-ratchet: every adapter task appends to the same four files, so the whole phase serialises on leases.
data.title: Make a new port touch only its own files: per-family port modules, auto-discovered fakes, per-family conformance tests and docs

chunk_findings.detail: The absolute-distance change still suppresses a later prompt whenever the earlier hook’s record lands after the later hook’s `fired_at` by less than `window`. For example, let `DOUBLE_FIRE_S = W`. An earlier hook fires at `t = fired_at - 2W` (so the two firings are clearly beyond the double-fire window) but is slow and writes its record at `t = fired_at + W/2`. When the later hook calls `_recorded_recently(..., now=fired_at)`, `_age_s(ev.ts, fired_at)` is `-W/2`, so `abs(...) <= W` and the function returns `True`; `capture_prompt` then drops the later prompt as a duplicate. The added test only covers a future record beyond the window and explicitly asserts that a future record within the window is still “recent,” so it does not reproduce the stated slow-earlier-hook interleaving unless the write delay exceeds the window.

chunk_findings.detail: The test depends on wall-clock timing inside `log.append`. It records `now = time.time()`, then appends the event without an explicit timestamp, and the second assertion uses a function `now` of `original_now - (DOUBLE_FIRE_S - 1.0)`. If `log.append` blocks for more than one second (slow filesystem, CI contention, or a wall-clock step), the event’s timestamp is farther than `DOUBLE_FIRE_S` from the supplied `now`, so `_recorded_recently` returns `False` and the “within the window in the future is still close enough” assertion fails. The test should use an explicit event `ts` or monkeypatch the clock.

chunk_findings.detail: The twin guard only refuses when `RUN.claim_started` finds a live run for the exact requested `sha`. It has no check that the requested sha is newer than the live marker’s sha, so a second review for the same `item`/`gate` on an older commit is treated like a new run. For example, while a review of current commit `A` is live, invoking `_claim_or_refuse_twin(repo, item, "critic", B)` where `B` is an ancestor of `A` (or a stale retry after a rebase) passes a different `started_on`, so `twin` is `None` and the function returns a marker with no refusal. That starts a second reviewer concurrently, reproducing the duplicate-cost/race problem, and the older run can later record a stale outcome for the same gate even though the docstring/test name say only a newer commit should be allowed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:63 (_claim_or_refuse_twin)

chunk_findings.detail: The new signal-death classifier treats every exit code `>= 128` as termination by signal `code - 128`. This misclassifies ordinary non-zero exits in the shell exit range. For example, a gate command that runs `git rev-parse HEAD` in a directory that is not a Git repository exits `128` with `fatal: not a git repository`; `classify_exit` reaches `if death := _signal_death(code)` and returns `GateOutcome.UNAVAILABLE` with reason “the command was killed by signal 0 (exit 128)”. Likewise, a command exiting `255` (common for `ssh`/transport failures) becomes “killed by signal 127” because `signal.Signals(127)` raises and the `ValueError` fallback still returns a pseudo-signal. Those commands ran and produced a failing verdict; treating them as unavailable hides the failure and can leave the gate in a non-terminal/unavailable state instead of `FAILED`. The check should at minimum exclude `code == 128` and should not fall back to “signal n” for invalid signal numbers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: `_live_twin` uses `os.getppid()` as the “live OTHER process” marker. In a POSIX environment where the pytest process itself is PID 1 (common in containers that run `pytest` directly as the entrypoint), `os.getppid()` returns `0`, which is not a live process. `RUN.proc_start(0)` cannot obtain a real process start time (e.g. on Linux `/proc/0` does not exist), so the marker written by `_live_twin` is not a valid live twin. Then `G._claim_or_refuse_twin` has no live twin to detect, and `test_a_second_review_on_the_same_commit_is_refused_claiming_the_live_one` fails (or, if `live_run` mistakenly treats PID 0 as live, the test is passing for the wrong reason and still does not exercise the intended same-commit refusal).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_twin.py:_live_twin

chunk_findings.detail:
The twin-run claim is created and released inside `_review_gate`, which is executed once per gate: it reviews the `revs` for a single `gate` and records only that gate’s outcome. So the marker only prevents two processes from reviewing the *same gate at the same time*; it does not prevent two `ddflow review` processes for the same item/commit.

Concrete interleaving: process A finishes gate `ci`, and `_review_gate` returns; its `finally` runs `RUN.clear_started(marker)`. Before A invokes `_review_gate` for the next gate `qa`, process B starts for the same item/commit. B’s `_claim_or_refuse_twin` for `ci` succeeds because A just cleared the marker. Now A is live on `qa` while B is live on `ci` — two `ddflow review` processes for one item, the exact duplicate reviewer cost this change is meant to fix. The claim must be held at the whole-item/process level across all gate calls, not cleared after each single `_review_gate`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:_review_gate (`RUN.clear_started(marker)` in `finally`)

chunk_findings.detail: A gate command that legitimately exits with status 128 is misclassified as UNAVAILABLE. `_signal_death(128)` takes the `elif code >= _SHELL_SIGNAL_EXIT` branch, computes `n = 0`, and returns a non-empty string (either `"SIG_DFL"` or the fallback `"signal 0"`); `classify_exit` then returns `GateOutcome.UNAVAILABLE` instead of the POSIX default `GateOutcome.FAILED`. Shells encode a child killed by signal N as `128+N` only for N >= 1, so status 128 is not a signal death, but the `>=` treats it as one.

chunk_findings.detail: The positive-exit branch still infers a signal death from shell-style exit codes 129..137, so a gate command that runs to a verdict and exits with one of those codes is reported as unavailable. For example, a gate command `sh -c 'exit 137'` (or any checker that uses 137 as a failure status) produces `code=137`; `_signal_death` computes `n = 137 - 128 = 9`, sees `SIGKILL` in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, and `classify_exit` returns `GateOutcome.UNAVAILABLE` with “the command was killed by SIGKILL”, even though no signal was delivered and the command did produce a verdict. The earlier confirmed objection about ordinary exits in the 128.. range is fixed only for exit 128; it still applies to legitimate exits 129-137.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: The new per-item review lock uses the literal marker key `"review"` in the same started-marker namespace as real command gates. A repository can define a command gate named `review` (gate names are taken directly from `gate.split(",")`, and nothing in this diff reserves the slug). In that case `review()` first writes a live marker for `(repo, item, "review")`; the subsequent per-gate review of the requested gate `"review"` sees that same marker as a live twin and returns a refusal, so the gate named `review` can never be reviewed. The comment “it names no gate” is the collision, not a guard against it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_REVIEW_LOCK_GATE

chunk_findings.detail: The change from `>=` to `>` only fixes exit code 128. The same previously reported ambiguity remains for every code above 128 that maps to one of `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`. For example, a gate command that runs `git add --bad-option` finishes with exit status 129 (Git uses 129 for usage errors), but `_signal_death(129)` computes `n = 1`, gets `signal.Signals(1).name == "SIGHUP"`, and `SIGHUP` is in `_CUT_OFF_SIGNALS`, so `classify_exit` returns `UNAVAILABLE` with “the command was killed by SIGHUP”. The command was not killed by a signal; it ran to completion and returned an ordinary nonzero verdict, so it should be `FAILED` (or the gate’s declared mapping), not `UNAVAILABLE`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:_signal_death

chunk_findings.detail: In `review`, `RUN.clear_started(marker)` is unconditionally called in a `finally` block when `marker` might be `None` (for instance, when `_claim_or_refuse_twin` returns `(None, twin)` on a twin refusal, or `(None, O.nothing(...))` when the filesystem could not write the marker). `RUN.clear_started(None)` attempts to remove `_dir(repo, item) / "review.running.None.json"`, raising a `FileNotFoundError` or crashing when cleaning up a refused duplicate review or a failed marker write.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: The new exemption is a file-wide whitelist: every string constant in `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` whose value is a `FAMILY_HINTS` key is skipped, regardless of whether that constant is a FAMILY_HINTS dict key or a real descriptor read. For example, if `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` contains `def is_grok(h): return h.id == "grok"`, `"grok"` is a harness descriptor id and should be counted as an agent-literal site, but `_counts` passes `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` as `exempt`, so `sites` sees `is_site` true but skips it because `v in exempt`. The change’s comment claims these strings are “not descriptor reads,” but nothing checks the AST context; a legitimate hard-coded descriptor read in the same file is silently allowed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:_counts

chunk_findings.detail: The named regression test does not exercise the actual detector path that produced the bug. It calls `sites(..., exempt=frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS))` directly, so it can pass even if the real `_counts()` loop does not apply the exemption to `agent.py` (e.g. the `exempt = ... if f == agent_py` wiring is missing or the path comparison fails). In that state the original ratchet still reddens `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py`, but this test still passes. A regression test for this bug should call `_counts()` and assert that `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` is absent from the counts / has the expected count, so it fails when the exemption is not used by the real detector.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:test_family_hints_vendor_keys_are_not_agent_sites

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_counts` exempts `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` for the entire `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` file, and `sites` then drops every string literal equal to any FAMILY_HINTS key, regardless of whether that occurrence is actually a FAMILY_HINTS key or a genuine agent-literal site. Concrete input: if `agent.py` later contains `CURRENT_AGENT = "grok"` (or another real descriptor read whose value is also a FAMILY_HINTS key), the detector will no longer count it; `test_scan`'s expected entry for `agent.py` remains absent and the test passes, so the ratchet misses a real new agent-literal site. The `sites` docstring says `exempt` is for constants “in a different domain”, but the code only compares the string value and cannot know the domain, so the promised safety property is lost.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:152

chunk_findings.detail: The two tests can both pass even if the real detector suppresses every agent-literal site in `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py`. `test_family_hints...` only asserts that `agent.py` is absent from the red `_counts()` set, while `test_vendor_key_outside...` calls the low-level `sites()` helper on a synthetic source that contains no `FAMILY_HINTS` assignment; it does not exercise the real `_counts()` path for `agent.py`. Thus a wrong implementation of `_counts()` such as `if rel == "ddflow/config_sections/agent.py": continue`, or one that passes `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` as a file-wide exemption for that file, would keep both tests green while a genuine descriptor read in `agent.py` such as `if harness_id == "grok":` would no longer be counted. The regression test should verify the scoped exemption through the real detector path, not only the helper `sites()` behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:218 (`test_family_hints_vendor_keys_are_not_agent_sites`) and :226 (`test_vendor_key_outside_family_hints_is_still_a_site`)

chunk_findings.detail: The added test claims to guard the scoped FAMILY_HINTS exemption (“The FAMILY_HINTS exemption is scoped to that table's dict keys”), but it never exercises that scoped path. It calls `sites('ok = "grok"\n', ids, _roots())` without an `exempt` argument, so it does not invoke `_counts()` or `_vendor_key_nodes()`. Under the earlier file-wide whitelist (`_counts` passing `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` for `agent.py`), this test still passes because `sites` with no exemption returns `[1]`; the over-exemption defect it was meant to catch would not fail this test. A real descriptor read in `agent.py`, e.g. `def is_grok(h): return h.id == "grok"`, would remain uncounted with no test failure.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:test_vendor_key_outside_family_hints_is_still_a_site

chunk_findings.detail:
The AST exemption is not scoped to the module-level `FAMILY_HINTS` vendor table. It walks every `Assign`/`AnnAssign` in the module and exempts all string keys of any dict literal assigned to a name `FAMILY_HINTS`, including function-local or otherwise shadowing assignments. For example, if `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` contains:
```python
def f():
    FAMILY_HINTS = {"grok": "x"}
    return FAMILY_HINTS
```
then `_module_sites("ddflow/config_sections/agent.py", source, {"grok"}, set())` returns `0` because the `"grok"` key node is skipped. That is wrong: this `"grok"` is not a key of the module's vendor table, so it is an agent-literal site and should be counted. This contradicts the docstring’s stated rule that “only the keys of that one table are exempt” and allows new descriptor literals to be hidden by putting them in a local dict named `FAMILY_HINTS`.

chunk_findings.detail: The per-item review lock uses the gate key `"review"` (`_REVIEW_LOCK_GATE = "review"`), which is not a safe synthetic key because the review command itself has, or can be configured with, a command gate named `review`. Given a review that runs a gate named `review`, the first review writes its lock marker under the same `(item, gate, started_on)` identity that `_mark_or_refuse_twin(repo, item, "review", sha)` later uses when starting that gate. The lock marker and the real gate marker are then indistinguishable: the gate run either sees the lock as a live twin and refuses the review gate, or it overwrites/releases the lock when the gate finishes, leaving the remainder of the review unprotected so a second review can start concurrently. Either way, the duplicate-review race that the change is supposed to close remains (or the review gate itself is blocked), contradicting the comment that the key "names no gate".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_claim_or_refuse_twin

chunk_findings.detail: The twin marker is acquired outside the `try` block that releases it. If a signal handled by `_ends_on_signal` (or any asynchronous exception such as `KeyboardInterrupt`) is delivered after `_claim_or_refuse_twin` has created/returned the marker but before the `try:` line is entered, the `finally: RUN.clear_started(marker)` is never executed. In that interleaving, the review unwinds while the marker remains set; if the process is still alive (the signal handler returns or a caller catches the exception), `live_run_any` can see a live twin and a subsequent `ddflow review` for the same item is refused even though no review is actually running. The release scope should begin immediately after acquisition, e.g. initialize `marker = None`, put the claim inside the `try`, and clear only if `marker` is set.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:review

chunk_findings.detail: The per-item review lock passes the commit SHA as the `started_on` argument to `RUN.claim_started`. In the existing `_mark_or_refuse_twin`/`RUN.live_run` convention, `started_on` is the per-invocation token used so a process does not see its own marker as a live twin. Two concurrent `ddflow review <item>` processes reviewing the same commit therefore supply the exact same SHA. The second process suppresses the first process's live marker as if it were its own, so `claim_started` sees no twin and both reviews proceed concurrently. That is exactly the duplicate-reviewer scenario in B8664a1e0c6, and the fix fails for same-commit duplicate reviews.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_claim_or_refuse_twin

chunk_findings.detail: `claim_started` only locks a single gate, but the bug it is fixing is duplicate whole `ddflow review` processes for one item. Example: review P1 runs an item with gates `ci` and `lint`. P1 finishes `ci` and clears its `ci` marker (the marker provided by `claim_started` is cleared when that gate run is done), then P1 starts `lint`, so only a `lint` marker exists. Now a second review P2 starts for the same item; `claim_started(repo, item, "ci", sha, same_commit=False)` calls `live_run_any(repo, item, "ci")`, finds no live `ci` marker, writes a new `ci` marker, and proceeds. Both review processes are now live and duplicating work, so the exact duplicate-reviewer defect remains whenever the first process is on a different gate or between gate markers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/running.py:claim_started

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not reproduce the harness-timeout cut-off that caused the bug. The original failure is that the `ddflow gate run` process is cut by the harness and exits before writing a result, leaving `gate status` to display the stale `[!] queued 11m of 15m elapsed`. This test instead calls `R.run_command_gate(gdef, tmp_path)` in-process and kills the gate command child with `kill -KILL $$`; the runner process survives and processes the returned `-9`, so the new `_signal_death` signal-handler path in `ddflow/services/gates/runner.py` is not exercised. An implementation could still lack a real SIGTERM/SIGKILL handler and this test would pass once `classify_exit` maps `-9`/`-15`, leaving the actual gate-runner-cut-off bug in place.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_exit_mapping.py:test_a_signal_killed_ci_run_is_unavailable_and_never_a_queued_note

chunk_findings.detail: The new exemption is a file-wide whitelist: every string constant in `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` whose value is a `FAMILY_HINTS` key is skipped, regardless of whether that constant is a FAMILY_HINTS dict key or a real descriptor read. For example, if `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` contains `def is_grok(h): return h.id == "grok"`, `"grok"` is a harness descriptor id and should be counted as an agent-literal site, but `_counts` passes `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` as `exempt`, so `sites` sees `is_site` true but skips it because `v in exempt`. The change’s comment claims these strings are “not descriptor reads,” but nothing checks the AST context; a legitimate hard-coded descriptor read in the same file is silently allowed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:_counts

chunk_findings.detail: The named regression test does not exercise the actual detector path that produced the bug. It calls `sites(..., exempt=frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS))` directly, so it can pass even if the real `_counts()` loop does not apply the exemption to `agent.py` (e.g. the `exempt = ... if f == agent_py` wiring is missing or the path comparison fails). In that state the original ratchet still reddens `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py`, but this test still passes. A regression test for this bug should call `_counts()` and assert that `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` is absent from the counts / has the expected count, so it fails when the exemption is not used by the real detector.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:test_family_hints_vendor_keys_are_not_agent_sites

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_counts` exempts `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` for the entire `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` file, and `sites` then drops every string literal equal to any FAMILY_HINTS key, regardless of whether that occurrence is actually a FAMILY_HINTS key or a genuine agent-literal site. Concrete input: if `agent.py` later contains `CURRENT_AGENT = "grok"` (or another real descriptor read whose value is also a FAMILY_HINTS key), the detector will no longer count it; `test_scan`'s expected entry for `agent.py` remains absent and the test passes, so the ratchet misses a real new agent-literal site. The `sites` docstring says `exempt` is for constants “in a different domain”, but the code only compares the string value and cannot know the domain, so the promised safety property is lost.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:152

chunk_findings.detail: The two tests can both pass even if the real detector suppresses every agent-literal site in `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py`. `test_family_hints...` only asserts that `agent.py` is absent from the red `_counts()` set, while `test_vendor_key_outside...` calls the low-level `sites()` helper on a synthetic source that contains no `FAMILY_HINTS` assignment; it does not exercise the real `_counts()` path for `agent.py`. Thus a wrong implementation of `_counts()` such as `if rel == "ddflow/config_sections/agent.py": continue`, or one that passes `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` as a file-wide exemption for that file, would keep both tests green while a genuine descriptor read in `agent.py` such as `if harness_id == "grok":` would no longer be counted. The regression test should verify the scoped exemption through the real detector path, not only the helper `sites()` behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_agent_literals.py:218 (`test_family_hints_vendor_keys_are_not_agent_sites`) and :226 (`test_vendor_key_outside_family_hints_is_still_a_site`)

chunk_findings.detail: The added test claims to guard the scoped FAMILY_HINTS exemption (“The FAMILY_HINTS exemption is scoped to that table's dict keys”), but it never exercises that scoped path. It calls `sites('ok = "grok"\n', ids, _roots())` without an `exempt` argument, so it does not invoke `_counts()` or `_vendor_key_nodes()`. Under the earlier file-wide whitelist (`_counts` passing `frozenset(FAMILY_HINTS)` for `agent.py`), this test still passes because `sites` with no exemption returns `[1]`; the over-exemption defect it was meant to catch would not fail this test. chunk_findings.detail:
The AST exemption is not scoped to the module-level `FAMILY_HINTS` vendor table. It walks every `Assign`/`AnnAssign` in the module and exempts all string keys of any dict literal assigned to a name `FAMILY_HINTS`, including function-local or otherwise shadowing assignments. For example, if `ddflow/config_sections/agent.py` contains:
```python
def f():
    FAMILY_HINTS = {"grok": "x"}
    return FAMILY_HINTS
```
then `_module_sites("ddflow/config_sections/agent.py", source, {"grok"}, set())` returns `0` because the `"grok"` key node is skipped. That is wrong: this `"grok"` is not a key of the module's vendor table, so it is an agent-literal site and should be counted. This contradicts the docstring’s stated rule that “only the keys of that one table are exempt” and allows new descriptor literals to be hidden by putting them in a local dict named `FAMILY_HINTS`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_unavailable_unmet_only` defines “unmet” by scanning `pipeline_for(it, cfg)` and calling `it.gate_satisfied(g, True)`, but the actual completion blocker that `complete.force` is supposed to stand in for is produced by `_unsettled(cfg, it, excused, s, required, state)` and exposed as `v.unmet_gates`. Because the predicate has no access to `excused` or `state`, it can count required gates that the verdict deliberately does not treat as blockers. For example, if the pipeline contains two required gates, `unit_tests=unavailable` and `lint=failed`, but `lint` is excused by the actual diff, `_unsettled` excludes `lint` so `v.unmet_gates == ["unit_tests"]` and the routine completion site sees a gate-only unavailable blocker; `_unavailable_unmet_only` still sees `lint` (gate_satisfied false, outcome failed) and returns False, so the standing rule does not auto-answer the `complete.force` ask.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py:_unavailable_unmet_only

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate recomputes “unmet required gates” using only `not it.gate_satisfied(g, True)`, but the completion engine’s actual unmet-gate list is `_unsettled(cfg, it, excused, s, required, state)`, which has a separate `excused` argument precisely because a required gate excused by the actual diff is not an unmet blocker even though `gate_satisfied` does not count it as satisfied. Given an item with required gates `unit_tests` (unavailable) and `lint` (excused by the diff), `_unsettled`/`unmet_gates` contains only `unit_tests`, but this predicate includes both; `it.gate_outcome("lint")` is `None`/`excused`, so the `all(...)` check fails and `_unavailable_unmet_only` returns False. The standing `complete.force` ask is therefore still not auto-answered even though the only real unmet required gate is unavailable—the exact under-fire this change was meant to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py:_unavailable_unmet_only

chunk_findings.detail: The new setup call `_only_unavailable_gate(proj, "unavailable")` passes the state literal `"unavailable"` where this helper’s second argument is a gate id. As a result the test configures a required gate named `unavailable` rather than marking the real required gate (e.g. `unit_tests`) as unavailable. That means a genuinely failed `unit_tests` gate is not accompanied by only unavailable/partial gates in the intended scenario; the test either fails on an unknown gate or passes for a project state that does not exercise the policy being changed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_policy.py:279

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate decides solely from the caller-supplied `target` string: it splits it and checks those gate ids are unavailable/partial. It never verifies that the target is the full set of required gates left unmet by the completion verdict. If a `complete.force` ask/request is evaluated with a target that names only one of the unmet gates, e.g. `target="lint"` while the verdict's `unmet_gates` are `["unit_tests", "lint"]`, with `unit_tests` recorded `failed` and `lint` recorded `unavailable`, the predicate returns `True` and the standing rule auto-answers `complete.force`, allowing completion despite a genuinely failed required gate. The intent requires *all* unmet required gates to be unavailable/partial; this code only guarantees the gates that happen to be in `target`, so a failed/silent gate can be omitted and bypassed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py:_unavailable_unmet_only

chunk_findings.detail: The new calls pass gate-state strings where the helper expects a gate id: `_only_unavailable_gate(proj, "failed")`, `_only_unavailable_gate(repo, unit)` inside `_only_unavailable_repo`, and `_only_unavailable_gate(proj, "unavailable")` in the window-lapse test. For example, `_only_unavailable_repo(repo, "unavailable")` configures the pipeline as `implement,unit_tests,merge`, then calls `_only_unavailable_gate(repo, "unavailable")`; since the second positional argument is a gate id, this marks a gate named `unavailable` unavailable instead of marking `unit_tests` unavailable. The end-to-end test then runs `ddflow complete T1` and asserts success because “the only unmet required gate is `unit_tests=unavailable`”, but the real `unit_tests` gate is still not set to unavailable, so the standing-rule predicate does not see the intended only-unavailable blocker and the CLI can exit with the refusal code, making the test fail (or, if the helper replaces the only required gate, it passes while exercising a nonexistent gate rather than `unit_tests`). This is the previously reported misuse still present in the added/edited lines.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_policy.py:_only_unavailable_gate

chunk_findings.detail: `_only_unavailable_gate(proj, "failed")` still passes a state literal as the helper’s second argument, but that parameter is the gate id in `_only_unavailable_gate`. The same defect is repeated at lines 251 (`_only_unavailable_gate(repo, unit)`, fed by `"unavailable"`/`"failed"`) and 279 (`_only_unavailable_gate(proj, "unavailable")`). These calls do not set `unit_tests` to the intended `unavailable`/`failed` state; they create or target a gate literally named `"unavailable"`/`"failed"`, so the new unit and end-to-end tests exercise a different project shape than their names claim, and the old windowed-rule test is altered to target the wrong gate.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_policy.py:230

data.text: Extend the perf features: when the user asks for performance reports, ddflow generates statistics and graphs for the user.

data.body: Operator 2026-11-02: collect performance metrics (time per tool and gate, cpu, network, disk, io, waits on LLMs, which agents and models do well or badly, bugs generated, tool calls) and analyse them periodically in a scheduled job that proposes optimizations to the user, to ddflow and to the workflow, so a small feature does not cost exponentially more as the codebase and the unit tests grow. Reports with statistics and graphs on request. Research: R-perf-landscape (outside), R-perf-inventory (inside). EXTENDS, does not duplicate: services/metrics (facts, summary, forecast, retro), core/flowsignals, infra/signals + flow.sample tick, services/flakes, services/cmdrunner + gates/runner evidence (elapsed_s, waited_s), COUNT_PASSES in services/schedule, P-observe (telemetry, detectors, findings, proposals), B-perf-bench (ddflow own commands), B-gap-spend (usage ledger), B-sub-metrics (agent stats), SCH-review-inbox, P-eta, OPT-history. The existing phase P-perf is about ddflow own speed and stays separate.
data.title: Performance metrics: measure tools, tests, LLM waits, agents and resources, report with statistics and graphs, and propose optimizations on a schedule so effort per feature stays flat as the code and test suite grow

data.body: A series is noise unless it is keyed by where it ran. Add one small pure fingerprint: cpu count, load class at start, xdist workers and the parallel cap in force, os and python version, cache warm or cold (a documented cheap test), ddflow version, git head of the measured tree. Stable short key, no hostname, no user, no paths. Stamped into the evidence of every gate and ci run and into every perf sample; the regression detector (PM-detect) compares only samples with the same key class. Tests: same machine same key, a changed cap changes the key, nothing identifying leaks. data.body: Today gates record only elapsed_s and waited_s (verified: no getrusage, ru_maxrss or psutil anywhere). Result fields join the existing evidence: cpu_user_s, cpu_sys_s, maxrss_kb, io_in_blocks, io_out_blocks, resources_source (wait4|delta|unavailable). Linux and macOS; Windows unsupported. data.body: Little law: the stage that grows with parallelism is lease and merge wait, the stage that grows with suite size is gate time. Add a pure fold in services/metrics (next to facts.py) that cuts each item timeline from existing events into queue wait (ready to claimed), lease wait (lease.waiting spans), implement (claim to first gate), per-gate time with waited_s separated, review wait, merge wait, claim to merge, plus rework rounds and gate re-runs. Stages that need events ddflow does not emit yet (claim refusals, human wait; P-observe.telemetry) are reported not measured, never zero. Extend ddflow metrics with a stages view and group-by phase, kind, size bucket (changed_lines) and agent. No new event kind needed for the first cut. Tests on a seeded log. data.body: One place for perf data, following the flowstate and flakes precedent: raw samples (per-process rss series, per-call latencies, per-test durations) as JSONL rings under .ddflow/local/perf/ with a size and age cap; per-run rollups ride inside existing gate and review evidence (few numbers, no new committed event kind unless PM-decide says so); a compacted daily aggregate (count, p50, p90, max per series key and env key) written by a tick; a reader that merges the log rollups and the local aggregates into one series API used by the detectors and the report. data.body: Review records only a whole-round elapsed_s today (no per-chunk time, tokens or finish_reason in evidence). data.body: Port ResourceProbe in ddflow/adapters (per-family layout of ADP-modular-registry), default adapter stdlib: /proc/pid/stat and io for the process group on Linux, ps on macOS; optional adapters psutil (tree rss, io counters) and cgroup v2 (cpu.stat usage_usec, memory.peak, io.stat, pids.peak, only when a delegated scope exists, via systemd-run --user --scope); detect and degrade down the ladder cgroup, psutil, proc, wait4 only, and record which source gave each number. data.body: Pure functions, no I/O. Median and MAD robust z-score; a change needs both a relative threshold (default +20%) and an absolute floor (default +5 s); minimum 8 samples; persistence over 2 windows; EWMA or CUSUM for slow creep (1 percent a week is invisible to a fixed threshold); baselines per env-fingerprint class; a changed commit is separated from a changed machine. Budget burn rate with a short and a long window for a stated budget (for example p90 of unit_tests). Returns finding objects with the series, window, effect size, sample size and the suspected change (first commit or merge in the window). Tests include noisy flat series that must not alert and a seeded 15 percent step that must. data.body: Each proposal carries evidence, sample size, effect size, expected saving in seconds per run and per day, risk, and the exact command or task to accept it: split a file whose share of the critical path exceeds X and is over the size rule (hands over to the SZ split pattern); shard by historical duration or change the xdist worker count when wall clock over serial-equivalent shows skew; quarantine a flaky test; measure test impact selection (ci already records ci_scope and selected_tests): selected fraction and misses (failures the selection would not have run, found by the periodic full run) and propose widening or narrowing with the measured safety. A static import-graph selector is first, learned selection is explicitly out of scope until there is labelled history. Proposals only. Tests with seeded inefficiencies. data.body: Evidence-bearing proposals: swap or reweight a reviewer when cost and latency are high against findings confirmed per review (never below the cross-family independence rule); route a cheaper model for a task class when first-pass rate and cost per merged item justify it, with a minimum sample per class; shorten instructions or the brief when input tokens and cache-read ratio say so (links to P-token-economy and P-lean-start measures, one engine); cache a repeated identical command and input hash; propose retiring a gate that has not failed in N runs and whose catches a later gate repeats (propose only, human decision, a gate is never dropped silently). data.body: Register performance_review as a default periodic pass (one COUNT_PASSES row with its knob, or every_days=performance_review=7; a prompt template; no new scheduler: D-sched-no-daemon, restart survival is SCH-restart-survival, executor is the scheduler adapter). data.body:
WHAT: `ddflow perf [--commands ...] [--log-scale 1|4|16] [--runs N] [--json]` and MCP tool ddflow_perf (identical bodies, parity test): runs the hot commands (version, brief, next, status, gate status, claim/heartbeat on a scratch item, hooks prompt, hooks session-start, search, recall, doctor) as fresh processes in a scratch clone of the project (never the live store), records wall AND cpu time (cpu is robust against a loaded machine), median/min/max, git subprocess count (a shim on PATH), peak RSS, and the fold count; compares each to the budget in [perf] config and exits 1 over budget, 2 when it could not run, with the load average printed beside every number and the run flagged noisy above a configured load per core. Also the import-time table (-X importtime top modules). WHY: R-perf-profile-2026-10-11: every number we have was measured by hand in a scratch directory under load 30-300 on 192 cores; without a ratchet the 0.19 s import (R-perf-100k) became 0.5 s unnoticed and status grew to 5.4 s. INTERFACE TO REUSE: the generated 1x/4x/16x log fixtures of B-gap-log-scale and T-performance-scale (do not write a second generator: the scratch generator used for the research renames subjects and ids and shifts Lamport, ~30 lines), infra.LocalStore for results under .ddflow/local, the cadence service (ddflow cadence) for a periodic run, config_sections/ for knobs: [perf] budgets per command (ms), runs, noisy_load_per_core, log_scale, enabled_in_ci. NOTHING hardcoded: budgets, thresholds for the native-core triggers of B-perf-decide (fold seconds, RSS, event count) and the commands list are config; doctor prints a NOTE when a stored result exceeds a budget or a trigger threshold. TESTS: budgets parse and are honoured (a fake slow command exceeds, exit 1); load-noise flag; CLI/MCP parity; scratch clone leaves the live store untouched (hash of .ddflow before/after); a failing-first test per knob (dead-knob ratchet). SIZE: medium (~500 lines plus tests). ACCEPTANCE: a table for this repository in a research record, a cadence entry that fails when a budget is exceeded by more than the configured margin, README/ARCHITECTURE documented.

AMENDED by D-mcp-new-nouns (operator 2026-10-23): new record kinds are actions of ONE record family (ddflow_record, kind argument), not new MCP tools; do not add a tool and ignore any 'tools/list budget has ~45 bytes of headroom' line (void). Name your action of the record family; byte cost reported via MTD-budget-test.

WHAT: a usage ledger per lane and per item: tokens in/out/cache and, where the agent exposes it, cost estimate, recorded as usage.recorded events from harness transcripts (via the B-am-ingest reader) and statusline/OTel snapshots (via B-quota-meters readers); `ddflow usage [--by lane|item|phase|model]`; an optional per-item budget ([budget].max_tokens / max_usd on a task) that turns into a gate-status warning at 80% and a claim-time refusal when exceeded, and a 'cost per merged item' figure for B-gap-metrics. Unreadable usage is UNAVAILABLE, never zero.
WHY: 857.9 agent-hours (status) with six lanes and cross-family review rounds and no number for what a phase cost; B-quota-* meters the vendor window (percent) per agent, not per task. Claude Code reports cost locally from token counts at list price (/usage, --max-budget-usd, OTel), agent teams cost ~7x tokens in plan mode (R-gaps-survey, costs doc); OpenHands has max_budget_per_task; Langfuse tracks cost per trace. Subscription plans have no dollars: tokens and turns are the honest unit.
INTERFACE TO REUSE: B-am-ingest turn store (token fields), B-quota-meters reader registry, B-quota-pause for enforcement (do not build a second pause path), events registry with upcaster, redaction (no prompt text in usage events).
HOW TO TEST: fixture transcripts per harness with known token sums; unreadable file gives UNAVAILABLE; budget refusal is failing-first; no secret/prompt text in the event.
SIZE: medium (~500 lines). Needs B-am-ingest and B-quota-meters; do not start before they land. Evidence is thin for harnesses other than Claude Code (transcript token fields unverified): the first step is a probe record per harness.
ACCEPTANCE: `ddflow usage --by phase` on a throwaway multi-agent project matches the harness's own totals within 5% for the harnesses probed; others report UNAVAILABLE with the reason.

data.body: Cases: (1) ddflow runs the command itself in the container or server: measure as designed; the env fingerprint gains container and VM flags (cgroup limits, /.dockerenv or cgroup path, macOS Docker VM) so series are never mixed; the cgroup, psutil, proc, wait4 ladder degrades and records its source; network is offered as the container network-namespace /proc/net/dev delta over the run, labelled approximate, per command still not collected. (2) shell-less server: the agent runs the command, so ddflow returns the exact wrapped command (a measuring wrapper, ddflow perf run -- CMD, that prints one JSON line of wall, cpu, rss, io) in the next_actions envelope and accepts the result through an MCP ingest action on the existing family tool; unwrapped runs may report their own timings, stored as source agent-reported with lower trust, shown separately, and never counted as gate evidence of a pass. (3) hooks run on the agent machine: batched counters are sent through the same ingest action (bounded size, no arguments or output). (4) durations are measured on one side only with a monotonic clock; no subtraction of timestamps from two hosts; a skew note when they disagree. (5) persistence: say which path to mount as a volume (.ddflow/local/perf and the event log) and let doctor warn when the ring is on an ephemeral layer; losing it loses only detail, the committed rollups remain. (6) reports: text always inline in the answer; SVG and HTML returned inline up to a bound, or published as an artifact with consent, never only a path inside the container. (7) several users on one server: key by project and agent role, never user, host or path. (8) the scheduled review runs on command ticks (D-sched-no-daemon) and says when it cannot run because no command ran. Tests with a fake runner, a fake client and a recorded container fingerprint. CONFORMANCE (r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-everything-configurable, r-small-files, r-reuse-core): shell-less and container operation always possible; every answer names the exact next call in CLI and MCP form; self-reported data is never evidence of a pass; no identity, hostnames or paths in metrics. Operator question 2026-11-02: how do the metrics work with a remote MCP or ddflow in a docker container.

data.context: Asked through the question tool after R-perf-landscape and R-perf-inventory. Safeguards added by the coordinator for the auto-apply choice: every automatic change is an event with before and after values, takes effect only inside the knob floor and ceiling, is measured over a before and after window and reverted automatically on regression, can be undone with one call, is switched off by one kill-switch knob and locked by org policy, and never overrides a value the operator pinned (schedule.parallel fixed stays fixed unless the operator allows tuning).
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-02 answers: (1) collection default EVERYTHING ON: cheap set plus the live sampler and cgroup scopes where available; (2) committed: per-run rollups plus daily aggregates (p50, p90, max per series and env key); raw samples local with a retention cap; (3) autonomy: auto-apply safe proposals, bounded to three kinds: parallel cap and test workers, review cadence and chunk size, quarantine of a proven flaky test; never edits to code, tasks, gates, reviewers or models, those stay advice; (4) reviewer, model and agent comparisons always shown in the report, with sample sizes, still below the minimum sample they say not enough data; (5) report: text in chat plus SVG and HTML files, returned inline up to a bound, artifact publishing only with consent; (6) agent telemetry (Claude Code OpenTelemetry export, session logs) imported automatically when found: counts, durations and cost only, never prompt text, shown in doctor so it is visible; (7) remote and shell-less: agent-reported timings stored as source agent-reported, shown separately, excluded from baselines and budgets, never gate evidence of a pass; (8) network per command is not collected.
data.title: Perf metrics: everything collected, rollups plus daily aggregates committed, bounded auto-apply, comparisons always shown, harness telemetry auto-imported

data.body:
Operator decisions with a recommended default each, asked through the question tool and recorded as a decision: (1) collection level default: cheap (wall, cpu, rss peak, io blocks per command, stage times, tokens, tool-call counts) on; live sampler and cgroup scopes off until asked; (2) what is committed: per-run rollups of a few numbers inside existing gate evidence and one weekly aggregate record; raw series local with a retention cap (default 14 days); (3) proposals are advice only, filed in the review inbox; an accepted proposal becomes a task, never an automatic edit, except allowlisted knobs under P-observe.experiments later; (4) reviewer and model comparison shown by default or only on request, and the minimum sample before any claim; (5) report outputs: text always, SVG and HTML on request, artifact publishing only with consent; (6) opt-in ingest of the agent harness own telemetry (Claude Code OTel, session logs) and its privacy limits; (7) network bytes per command are NOT collected (no portable stdlib way): say so in every report. Writes the decision doc and one decision record. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, D-no-duckdb, D-sched-no-daemon): extend the existing metrics code, never a second store or scheduler; stdlib first, optional third-party only behind a port with a fake; one declaration gives CLI, MCP action and prompt; every threshold and interval is a knob in [perf_metrics] with org lock; every answer names the exact next call in CLI and MCP form; a probe that could not run is recorded unavailable, never zero or passed; raw samples stay in .ddflow/local, only small per-run rollups reach the committed log; no prompt text, command arguments, paths of the user, or secrets in any metric; files stay under [quality].max_file_bytes (package, thin facade). Research: R-perf-landscape, R-perf-inventory.

ANSWERED 2026-11-02 by the operator: see decision D-perf-metrics-answers. The task now only writes docs/ddflow/research/perf-metrics-decisions.md from that decision, lists the open details (retention days, thresholds) with defaults, and records anything the operator changes.

Port ResourceProbe in ddflow/adapters (per-family layout of ADP-modular-registry), default adapter stdlib: /proc/pid/stat and io for the process group on Linux, ps on macOS; optional adapters psutil (tree rss, io counters) and cgroup v2 (cpu.stat usage_usec, memory.peak, io.stat, pids.peak, only when a delegated scope exists, via systemd-run --user --scope); detect and degrade down the ladder cgroup, psutil, proc, wait4 only, and record which source gave each number. Sample rss only (full memory info is slow), every 1 s default on gates longer than a threshold knob, never on short ones. Network bytes per command: reported as not collected (no portable stdlib way; nethogs, ss or a network namespace are privileged); a per-run host-wide counter delta is offered only as a labelled approximation. Conformance cases run against adapter and fake. Overhead measured by PM-selfcost. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, D-no-duckdb, D-sched-no-daemon): extend the existing metrics code, never a second store or scheduler; stdlib first, optional third-party only behind a port with a fake; one declaration gives CLI, MCP action and prompt; every threshold and interval is a knob in [perf_metrics] with org lock; every answer names the exact next call in CLI and MCP form; a probe that could not run is recorded unavailable, never zero or passed; raw samples stay in .ddflow/local, only small per-run rollups reach the committed log; no prompt text, command arguments, paths of the user, or secrets in any metric; files stay under [quality].max_file_bytes (package, thin facade). Research: R-perf-landscape, R-perf-inventory.

DECIDED (D-perf-metrics-answers): the live sampler and cgroup scopes are ON by default where the ladder allows; PM-selfcost still switches a collector off visibly when it exceeds its overhead budget.

One place for perf data, following the flowstate and flakes precedent: raw samples (per-process rss series, per-call latencies, per-test durations) as JSONL rings under .ddflow/local/perf/ with a size and age cap; per-run rollups ride inside existing gate and review evidence (few numbers, no new committed event kind unless PM-decide says so); a compacted daily aggregate (count, p50, p90, max per series key and env key) written by a tick; a reader that merges the log rollups and the local aggregates into one series API used by the detectors and the report. Rebuildable: losing the local ring loses only detail. Never stores prompt text or command arguments (hash and gate id only). Tests: retention, compaction idempotent, concurrent writers, missing ring. DECIDED (D-perf-metrics-answers): daily aggregates (p50, p90, max per series and env key) ARE committed in addition to per-run rollups; size ratchet in PM-retention covers both.

Operator 2026-11-02: when the user asks for performance reports, ddflow produces statistics and graphs. This is the data layer, pure and deterministic: for a window and filters (phase, agent, model, gate, kind) produce sections with tables and series: cycle-time split by stage; gate time and failure rate p50 p90 max with trend; test suite size and time growth with serial-equivalent and critical path; slowest files and tests; resource use per command (cpu, rss, io; network shown as not collected); LLM wait, tokens, cost by reviewer and model; agent and model quality; flaky rate; complexity indicators; lease and merge wait; open perf findings and proposals; period over period deltas with sample sizes. Every number carries n and an env class; missing data is stated. Tests on a seeded fixture. DECIDED (D-perf-metrics-answers): the per-agent, per-model and per-reviewer comparison is always in the report, with n; below the minimum sample it says not enough data.

Verified gap: no tool-call counting. The post-tool hooks already run; add a counter (tool name class, ok or error, duration when the harness gives it) into the local ring keyed by agent, lane, item, never the arguments or output. Optional, opt-in importers behind a port with a fake: the Claude Code OpenTelemetry file or log export (claude_code.token.usage, cost.usage, tool_result duration_ms, api_request duration_ms and agent.name) and the session JSONL that Codex and Claude write (ccusage approach), each marked approximate and versioned because those formats change. Gives tokens, cost, active time and tool counts per agent without instrumenting the model. Parity: every supported harness gets the same fields or says unavailable (P-parity). Tests on recorded sample files. Research: R-perf-landscape, R-perf-inventory.

DECIDED (D-perf-metrics-answers): importers run automatically when the export or log files are found; doctor lists each source in use and how to turn it off; counts, durations and cost only.

Cases: (1) ddflow runs the command itself in the container or server: measure as designed; the env fingerprint gains container and VM flags (cgroup limits, /.dockerenv or cgroup path, macOS Docker VM) so series are never mixed; the cgroup, psutil, proc, wait4 ladder degrades and records its source; network is offered as the container network-namespace /proc/net/dev delta over the run, labelled approximate, per command still not collected. (2) shell-less server: the agent runs the command, so ddflow returns the exact wrapped command (a measuring wrapper, ddflow perf run -- CMD, that prints one JSON line of wall, cpu, rss, io) in the next_actions envelope and accepts the result through an MCP ingest action on the existing family tool; unwrapped runs may report their own timings, stored as source agent-reported with lower trust, shown separately, and never counted as gate evidence of a pass. (3) hooks run on the agent machine: batched counters are sent through the same ingest action (bounded size, no arguments or output). (4) durations are measured on one side only with a monotonic clock; no subtraction of timestamps from two hosts; a skew note when they disagree. (5) persistence: say which path to mount as a volume (.ddflow/local/perf and the event log) and let doctor warn when the ring is on an ephemeral layer; losing it loses only detail, the committed rollups remain. (6) reports: text always inline in the answer; SVG and HTML returned inline up to a bound, or published as an artifact with consent, never only a path inside the container. (7) several users on one server: key by project and agent role, never user, host or path. (8) the scheduled review runs on command ticks (D-sched-no-daemon) and says when it cannot run because no command ran. Tests with a fake runner, a fake client and a recorded container fingerprint. CONFORMANCE (r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-everything-configurable, r-small-files, r-reuse-core): shell-less and container operation always possible; every answer names the exact next call in CLI and MCP form; self-reported data is never evidence of a pass; no identity, hostnames or paths in metrics. Operator question 2026-11-02: how do the metrics work with a remote MCP or ddflow in a docker container.

DECIDED (D-perf-metrics-answers): agent-reported timings are shown separately and excluded from baselines and budgets.

Evidence-bearing proposals: swap or reweight a reviewer when cost and latency are high against findings confirmed per review (never below the cross-family independence rule); route a cheaper model for a task class when first-pass rate and cost per merged item justify it, with a minimum sample per class; shorten instructions or the brief when input tokens and cache-read ratio say so (links to P-token-economy and P-lean-start measures, one engine); cache a repeated identical command and input hash; propose retiring a gate that has not failed in N runs and whose catches a later gate repeats (propose only, human decision, a gate is never dropped silently). Tests. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, D-no-duckdb, D-sched-no-daemon): extend the existing metrics code, never a second store or scheduler; stdlib first, optional third-party only behind a port with a fake; one declaration gives CLI, MCP action and prompt; every threshold and interval is a knob in [perf_metrics] with org lock; every answer names the exact next call in CLI and MCP form; a probe that could not run is recorded unavailable, never zero or passed; raw samples stay in .ddflow/local, only small per-run rollups reach the committed log; no prompt text, command arguments, paths of the user, or secrets in any metric; files stay under [quality].max_file_bytes (package, thin facade). Research: R-perf-landscape, R-perf-inventory.

DECIDED (D-perf-metrics-answers): reviewer, model and prompt proposals stay ADVICE (never auto-applied).

Operator 2026-11-02 chose auto-apply of safe proposals, limited to three kinds: (a) parallel cap and xdist workers, (b) review cadence and chunk size (never the reviewer set), (c) quarantine of a test proven flaky (owner and expiry, never deleted). Everything else stays advice (code, tasks, gates, reviewers, models, prompts). Safeguards, all required: an allowlist of knobs with floor and ceiling and a max step per change; one change per knob per window and no two interacting knobs changed at once; the effect is measured over a before and after window with the PM-detect statistics and a guardrail set (gate failure rate, review latency, lease wait, wall time) and the change is REVERTED automatically when a guardrail regresses or the saving is not shown; every change is an event with before, after, evidence, the proposal id and the revert key; one call to undo (CLI, MCP, prompt); a kill-switch knob [perf_metrics].auto_apply = off|advice|allowlist, lockable by org policy; a value the operator pinned (for example schedule.parallel fixed, set in the local layer) is never changed unless the operator allows tuning of that knob; changes land in the local layer, never the committed config; the standing-approval-window policy does not extend to this. Reports and brief show the last automatic changes and their measured effect. Hands the effect measurement to P-observe.effect when it lands. Tests: a good change is kept, a harmful one is reverted, a pinned knob is untouched, kill-switch, org lock, undo. CONFORMANCE (r-everything-configurable, r-everything-managed, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-small-files, D-perf-metrics-answers, D-observe-autotune-stricter-or-cheaper): every automatic change is logged, reversible and lockable by org policy; a refusal or result names the exact next call in CLI and MCP form.
data.title: Bounded auto-apply of safe perf proposals: parallel cap and test workers, review cadence and chunk size, flaky quarantine, with before/after measurement, automatic revert and one-call undo

fields.body: Decisions D-unify, D-adapters-answers-3 (operator 2026-10-31 and 2026-11-01). WHY: when a function has one port and one default adapter, a change or a swap touches one place, tests use a fake instead of the network or a subprocess, and parallel agents do not collide on shared files. RULE: anything outside our own process or the stdlib (http, mcp, acp, git, filesystem layout, subprocess tools, clocks, environment, sqlite, toml, search, notifications, platform APIs, third-party libraries) is reached only through a typing.Protocol port in ddflow/adapters/<family>.py with its default adapter and registry entry in that module, a fake in ddflow/adapters/fakes/<family>.py, conformance cases run against the adapter and the fake in tests/test_adapter_<family>.py, and one docs page docs/ddflow/adapters/<family>.md. A new port edits none of the former shared files (ports.py, fakes/__init__.py, tests/test_ports_contract.py, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md); discovery is automatic. Services and surfaces import the port, never the third-party package or the subprocess. Never write a second implementation of a function that already has a port: search ddflow/adapters first. Exceptions sit in one shrink-only baseline with a reason. CHECK: the ports contract test, the import-layering test and the adapter baselines. VERIFY by hand: grep the diff for import of a third-party package or subprocess outside ddflow/adapters and ddflow/infra.
fields.title: Every external dependency goes through a port in ddflow/adapters: one implementation per function, a new port touches only its own files
