chunk_findings.detail: After the split, `complete()` lives in `finish.py`, so its references to `_load_fresh`, `fold`, `_dispose`, `_complete_umbrellas_above`, etc. are looked up in `finish.py`’s globals, not in the package facade. Re-exporting those names from `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/__init__.py` makes them importable, but it does not make old monkeypatch paths effective: a test doing `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete, "_load_fresh", fake)` (or patching `fold`, or patching `complete` to intercept umbrella recursion) now changes only the facade attribute, while `finish.complete` still calls the original object in `finish.py`. In the old single module, patching `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.fold` with a raising function would make `complete()` raise; after the split the same patch is silently ignored.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/finish.py:complete

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes a line from `tests/file_size_baseline.txt`, but the stated size/layout guard baseline is `tests/guard_baselines/file_size_baseline.txt` (the same guard-baseline tree as the renamed complexity baseline). That leaves the baseline entry for the deleted `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py` in the guard baseline, so `tests/test_lifecycle_layout.py` still sees a stale baseline entry for a file that no longer exists and the old file is not de-baselined as intended.
chunk_findings.title: tests/file_size_baseline.txt

chunk_findings.detail: The facade makes the old names importable, but it does not preserve the old monkeypatching semantics of a single module. In the old `complete.py`, a test that replaced `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._close_bugs` (or `_dispose`, etc.) changed the global used by all calls inside that module. After this split, the package attribute is only a lazy re-export; the docstring itself says tests that replace a name must patch the defining submodule. Thus `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._close_bugs", fake)` before calling `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.complete(...)` will bind `fake` only on the package, while the `complete` function in `finish.py` resolves `_close_bugs` from its own submodule namespace, so the real implementation still runs. This breaks the stated no-behaviour-change / monkeypatched-name guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/__init__.py (`_reexport.reexport`)

chunk_findings.detail: `abandon` imports `_dispose` directly into its own module namespace (`from .dispose import _dispose`) and then calls that module-global. Monkeypatching the old/facade helper name, e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._dispose", lambda *a: {"worktree": "fake"})` (or even `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.dispose._dispose` after import), therefore does **not** change the helper used by `abandon`: it still calls the original `_dispose` bound in `abandoning.py`. A test that patches the old complete-module name to avoid real worktree/branch cleanup will still execute the real disposal side effects and return the real disposal dict, violating the split’s stated goal of preserving monkeypatched names.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/abandoning.py:17 (`abandon` / `_dispose`)

chunk_findings.detail: The split changes monkeypatch semantics for the old facade. `_auto_complete_unavailable` calls `_only_unavailable` and `_approved_force` as globals in `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.approval`, and `_override_by_approval` calls `_approved_force` there. In the deleted single module, those calls resolved through `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete`, so tests or callers that monkeypatched `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._approved_force` (or `_only_unavailable`) changed the behaviour of the helpers. After this split, assigning `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._approved_force = lambda *a, **k: (True, {"approval": "fake"}, "")` only changes the facade attribute; a call to `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._auto_complete_unavailable(..., approval="", agent=<agent-marker>)` with a verdict such as `v.unmet_gates=["gate"]`, `v.coverage_gaps=["gate"]`, `v.blockers=["required gates"]`, `v.may_complete=False` still uses the original `_approved_force` in `approval.py` and can return the real refusal instead of the fake stamp. That violates the stated no-behaviour-change / monkeypatched-name compatibility.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/approval.py:_auto_complete_unavailable

chunk_findings.detail: The malformed-regression-test pre-check validates the `regression_test` argument, but the close that follows spends the `tests` argument: `_close_bugs` calls `bug_fixed(..., regression_test=tests, ...)`. Nothing in the helper ties `regression_test` to `tests`, so a malformed value in `tests` can bypass the validate-before-spend check. For example, with `tests=["tests/foo.py"]`, `regression_test="tests/test_x.py::test_ok"`, `lint_exempt=""`, `closing=True`, and `pending=["B1"]`, `_close_arg_refusal` returns `None` because `regression_test` is a valid node id, then `_close_bugs` passes the file path to `bug_fixed`, which refuses only after the operator’s single override has been spent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/closing.py:_close_arg_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: The split changes the module where `complete`'s callable globals live. `finish.py` binds every helper and even the top-level `complete` into its own module namespace at import time (`from ..._base import _load_fresh`, `from .checks import ...`, and the recursive call `done = complete(...)` at line 259). Existing monkeypatches that target the old public path `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._load_fresh` (or `...complete.complete`) now only change the facade package attribute; `finish.complete` still calls the original objects. For example, `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete, "_load_fresh", fake)` before calling `complete(repo, item)` makes `fake` visible via the package `dir()` but line 81 still calls the real `_load_fresh`, so the test hits the real repository/log instead of the fake. Likewise, a patch of `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete.complete` no longer intercepts the umbrella recursion at line 259. This is a behavior change from the old single module and defeats the facade's monkeypatched-name contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/finish.py:20-29, 259

chunk_findings.detail: `queue_ops` captures `_dispose` as a module-level name with `from .dispose import _dispose`. In the old single-module layout, `remove` resolved `_dispose` through `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete` at call time, so tests or callers that monkeypatched `ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._dispose` changed `remove`’s behaviour. After this split, patching the facade attribute only changes the package namespace; `queue_ops.remove` still calls the function object bound in `queue_ops`. For example, `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._dispose", fake)` followed by `remove(repo, "x")` still executes the real `_dispose`, so any test that suppresses/records disposal through the old monkeypatch target fails or production patching silently does nothing. This is a behaviour change relative to the stated “monkeypatched name” compatibility goal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete/queue_ops.py:15

chunk_findings.detail: The SZ-ratchet baseline line for the deleted `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py` is removed from the wrong path. The change’s stated baseline location is `tests/guard_baselines/file_size_baseline.txt` (and the sibling guard baselines live under `tests/guard_baselines/…`), but this diff only edits `tests/file_size_baseline.txt`; the manifest contains no edit to the guard-baseline copy. If the SZ-ratchet reads the guard-baseline copy, it still contains `ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py | 30393 | …`, so after the source file is deleted the ratchet still sees a stale baselined path and the split does not actually clear the SZ-ratchet failure.
chunk_findings.title: tests/file_size_baseline.txt

chunk_findings.detail: The test only proves that the facade attribute and the defining submodule attribute are the same object; it does not preserve the old monkeypatching contract. After the split, a helper such as `_failed_review` is defined in `checks.py` and used by the implementation in `finish.py`. If an existing test does `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.lifecycle.complete._failed_review", lambda *a: False)`, the new test still passes because the unpatched objects are identical, but the patch changes only the package attribute and not the global actually referenced by `finish.complete`. Thus old-path monkeypatches silently stop affecting behavior, contradicting the stated “monkeypatched name”/no-behaviour-change intent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lifecycle_complete_split.py:test_each_name_is_the_object_its_submodule_defines_and_has_one_home

chunk_findings.detail: The new `platform.system` exemption is based only on the receiver’s syntactic name, not on what `platform` is bound to. Given a scanned source file containing `import os as platform` and `platform.system("pkill -f foo")`, the AST scanner sees `f.value.id == "platform"` and sets `name = "platform.system"`, so the call is no longer treated as the `os.system` process launcher the kill-path test is supposed to flag. The following alias lookup cannot recover the original `system`/`os.system` name, so `test_no_kill_paths` passes even though an unreviewed shell-launching kill path was added.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_kill_paths.py:77-82

chunk_findings.detail: The new module map stores the full dotted import name and then tests exact equality to `"os"`. In Python, `import os.path` binds the name `os` to the top-level `os` module, so `os.system(...)` is still a real process launcher, but `mods` becomes `{"os": "os.path"}` and the Call handler classifies `os.system` as `platform.system`, not a killer. Example scanned source: `import os.path` followed by `os.system("kill ...")` passes the no-kill-paths guard unflagged. If the file also has `import os` before `import os.path`, the latter overwrites `mods["os"]` and hides all `os.system` calls in that file, defeating the guard.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_kill_paths.py:mods

chunk_findings.detail: The module resolution is applied only to attribute calls `X.system`; imported safe `platform.system` remains flagged. The new code uses the name `system` to flag `os.system`, so `system` is treated as a killer name; consequently `aliases` maps `from platform import system as uname` to `system`, and `uname()` is yielded as `system` and flagged even though it is the OS-name read. Example: `from platform import system as uname; uname()` should not be a kill path, but the scanner still treats it as one.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_kill_paths.py:aliases

chunk_findings.detail: The package import block in `__init__.py` (the one containing `STILL_QUEUED`, `bug_fixed`, and `could_not_run_text`) is importing `regression_arg_refusal` from `ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_close`, but `bug_close.py` after this change imports only `_regression_status` and `could_not_run_text` from `verify_status` and never defines or re-exports `regression_arg_refusal`. Any `import ddflow.api.knowledge` will therefore raise `ImportError: cannot import name 'regression_arg_refusal' from 'ddflow.api.knowledge.bug_close'`, breaking the knowledge package import and every caller/tests that loads it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/__init__.py:30

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `mods` map stores the full dotted import name for `ast.Import`, so `import os.path` binds the local name `os` to the value `"os.path"`. Later, when scanning `os.system(...)`, the condition `mods.get("os", "os") == "os"` is false, so the call is classified as `platform.system` instead of the process launcher `system`. Given a scanned file containing:

```python
import os.path
os.system("pkill worker")
```

the no-kill-path test wrongly passes and misses a real kill path.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_kill_paths.py:mods

chunk_findings.detail:
`from platform import system` is not resolved through `mods` (which only processes `ast.Import`, not `ast.ImportFrom`), so a later bare `system()` call yields the name `"system"`. Because this branch treats `"system"` as the `os.system` process launcher, a read-only platform call is reported as a kill path. A scanned file containing:

```python
from platform import system
print(system())
```

would fail the no-kill-path check even though it launches no process.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_no_kill_paths.py:walk system branch

data.body: Implements D-baseline-red-auto-accept. (1) Run the unit_tests gate even when ci is partial (today it refuses to start, found 2026-11-02), and record per-test failing ids. (2) Baseline cache: one full-suite result per base sha (shared by every item, expires when the base moves; local, under .ddflow/local) so measuring costs a comparison, not a run; if the cache is missing, run it once on a scratch checkout of the base, queued under the suite lock. (3) Accept when failing ids are a subset of the baseline failing ids AND none is in a file the item changed or imports (import graph); record baseline.red evidence and the acceptance with the ids; the gate stays partial and shows accepted-baseline-red; complete prints the warning. (4) Notify: inbox message to the coordinator and a brief line, naming the ids and the bug. (5) Bug: file or link by test-id dedup; the bug is tagged baseline-red and counted. (6) Knobs [gates].baseline_red_auto (on|off, default on, strictest off = person only), baseline_cache_ttl_s, baseline_red_rate_warn. (7) Agent briefs and the next_actions text say: do NOT request an approval for a baseline-red partial; run the gate and complete normally (an explicit --approval request is reserved for a person and bypasses the rule). Tests: subset accepted, one new failure blocks, failure in a changed file blocks, missing cache runs the base once, unavailable probe never accepts, notice and bug filed once. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-adapters, D-baseline-red-auto-accept, D-accept-baseline-red-partial): extend gate_accept and the baseline measurement that exist; no second comparer; a probe that could not run is unavailable, never accepted; org policy can lock the knob to person-only.
data.title: Automatic baseline-red acceptance: measure failing tests against a cached run of the base, accept, notify the coordinator and file or link the bug

data.alternatives: Only inside the standing window; keep person-only
data.context: Observed 2026-11-02: nearly every completion in this session needed a forced approval only because ci or unit_tests was partial from failures that also fail on main (the B-ci-main-* bugs), and agents recorded those partials by hand so ddflow never measured them. Related: accept_baseline_red standing rule, complete_unavailable.
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-02: a partial ci or unit_tests gate is accepted AUTOMATICALLY (no person, no window needed) when ddflow measured that every failing test also fails on the base branch and none of the failing tests is in a file the item changed or imports (evidence baseline.red written by the gate run). The gate stays partial in the record and is shown as accepted-baseline-red, never as passed; complete warns it settled on that acceptance. A failed gate, a new failing test, an unavailable tool, a silent gate and any partial whose failures are not all baseline-red stay blocking and still need a person. Every automatic acceptance (1) notifies the coordinator through the inbox, brief and approvals log, naming the failing test ids; (2) files a bug for the baseline-red test ids unless an open bug or fix task already names them (dedup by test id), or links the existing one; (3) is counted, and above a knob rate a doctor note says main is red and what to fix. Org policy can lock it off (strictest: person only). This supersedes the person-only rule of D-accept-baseline-red-partial; the measured-baseline requirement of that decision stands.
data.title: A partial required gate is accepted automatically when ddflow measured every failure as baseline-red; the coordinator is notified and the bug is filed or linked

chunk_findings.detail: The description and rule 1 advertise plural item-id scopes (“item ids”, “batch of task ids”), but the agent’s stated launch path is the `/ddflow-wave` command, whose argument contract in this change is a single scope token. If an operator follows this description and runs `/ddflow-wave 101 102`, only `101` reaches the orchestrator as the scope and `102` is silently excluded (or rejected), so the agent does not drive the advertised multi-item scope to empty.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:2

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten command prompt tells the orchestrator to fan the `ddflow next --json` ready set directly to `task` subagents, with no claim/lease step. Given two `/ddflow-wave` background subtasks whose scopes overlap (for example `/ddflow-wave phase-1` and `/ddflow-wave bugs` when phase-1 contains bugs), or a driver and another agent, both can read the same unclaimed ready item from `ddflow next --json` and fan it out to subagents, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges. The earlier delta fix that requires “claim each ready item, then fan” does not change this emitted command body, which is the prompt loaded when the Kilo background subtask runs.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/command/ddflow-wave.md:12

chunk_findings.detail: The emitted agent spec still advertises plural/batch item scopes (“item ids” in the description and “a batch of task ids” in rule 1), while the only operator entry point, `ddflow/templates/commands/kilo/ddflow-wave.md`, declares a single argument and interpolates only `$1`. If an operator follows the agent description and invokes `/ddflow-wave 101 102`, the command passes only `101`; `102` is silently omitted even though the agent spec says it will drive a batch of ids to empty. The earlier fix made the command description singular but did not remove the plural/batch claim from the agent spec, so the harness data still advertises unsupported behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:2

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence rule claims that keying the wave position by `<scope>` means “two concurrent `/ddflow-wave` runs never share a slot,” but two runs with the same scope use the identical key, e.g. `orchestrator_wave:bugs`. If an operator starts `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice concurrently, both orchestrators persist to the same memory slot; the second wave can overwrite the first wave’s last read/claimed/merged state, causing the first wave to resume without knowledge of its claimed items or required heartbeats. Scoping by `<scope>` only separates different scopes; the emitted spec’s absolute “never share a slot” guarantee is false for same-scope concurrent runs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:33

chunk_findings.detail: The new fan-out wording tells the background wave driver to read `ddflow next --json` and fan the ready set to opencode sub-agents “one item each,” but it no longer says to claim each item before spawning the sub-agent. If two opencode wave drivers, or a driver and another agent, run `ddflow next --json` concurrently and both see item `101` ready, both can fan `101` to a sub-agent before either claims it, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges. The old delta explicitly said “claim one item”; the Kilo delta was fixed to “claim each ready item, then fan,” so this emitted opencode spec is missing the required claim step.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:6

chunk_findings.detail: The opencode delta says “Stop only where an operator answer is required (an approval, a policy decision).” Given a scope that becomes empty after the last merge or park — no ready items and no held/blocked items — no operator answer is required, but the wave is complete and should stop. Under the literal rule, the agent has no completion stop and is told to stop only on an operator answer, so it can keep waiting/re-reading an empty scope forever or stop in violation of the rule. The intended fixed wave rule allows stopping on an empty scope in addition to question/operator gates.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:13

chunk_findings.detail: The delta says the orchestrator must “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate, or when the scope is empty,” but then says that where the runtime has no `task`-subagent run (Roo), the agent should “do ONE item directly — claim, gate, merge — then print `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` as the handoff.” On Roo with two independent ready items and no question/operator gate, this directs the agent to stop after the first item even though the scope is not empty, contradicting the preceding stop-only rule and prematurely abandoning the wave.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:21

chunk_findings.detail: Given a scope that becomes empty after the last ready item is merged or parked, `ddflow next` reports nothing ready. The emitted delta says “Stop only where an operator answer is required (an approval, a policy decision).” That omits the required empty-scope completion stop, so an opencode agent following this delta is instructed not to stop when the wave is actually complete and will keep the background wave loop alive/re-reading instead of reporting completion.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: The new opencode iteration text says “one read of `ddflow next --json`, the ready set fanned out to sub-agents … one item each,” but it no longer says to claim each ready item before dispatching. If two opencode background sub-agents, or a background sub-agent and another agent, read the same `ddflow next --json` ready set and follow this wording literally, both can select the same unclaimed ready item and fan it out, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:9

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is scoped only by the scope string, not by a run/invocation id, so two concurrent invocations of the same scope still share one memory slot. The text explicitly says “two concurrent `/ddflow-wave` runs never share a slot,” but `/ddflow-wave phase-1` launched twice does share `orchestrator_wave:phase-1`. Concrete interleaving: run A reads wave 10, run B reads wave 12 and saves the key; a lagging run A then saves wave 11 and overwrites B’s newer position. If B restarts/compacts next, it resumes at wave 11, *before* its actual position, redoing work despite the “never before it” promise. The key should include a run id or same-scope concurrent launches must be prevented.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md rule 4 (`orchestrator_wave:<scope>`)

chunk_findings.detail: The emitted agent metadata still advertises “item ids” (description) and “a batch of task ids” (rule 1), while the `/ddflow-wave` command interface only forwards the single positional `$1` (the command description/hint was corrected to singular in this same change). Given `/ddflow-wave item-1 item-2`, the orchestrator receives only `item-1`, and `item-2` is silently ignored, so the agent file describes a scope the command cannot actually pass to it.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:2 and rule 1

chunk_findings.detail: The Kilo orchestration data record says `dispatch = "task (one ready item each, model chosen by tier)"`. The prior confirmed issue (#7) requires the Kilo orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanout; this record says to fan ready items unclaimed. Since this change’s purpose is to emit the orchestration DATA per harness, a generator or consumer using this field will emit the unclaimed-ready wording. With two `ddflow-wave` orchestrators whose scopes overlap, both can read the same ready item from `ddflow next --json` and fan it to task subagents without claiming it, causing duplicate implementation/conflicting merges. The field should say `task (one claimed item each, model chosen by tier)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/kilo.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The command description now says the orchestrator should “stop only on a question” and the body’s only stopping condition is “a `question` only at operator gates”; the old explicit completion line `goal_report when ddflow next ends 2 with nothing ready` was deleted and not replaced with the corrected empty-scope completion. The fixed orchestrator rule in this same change stops when the scope is truly empty (no ready and no held/blocked) or on a question gate. Running `/ddflow-wave phase-1` on a phase that empties gives the subagent conflicting termination instructions: the command prompt says the only stop is a question, while the agent rule says empty scope is completion, so the subagent may keep re-reading an empty scope or ask a spurious question instead of terminating. The command should include the empty-scope stop condition.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/command/ddflow-wave.md

chunk_findings.detail: The new closed vocabulary for `orchestration.loop` includes `"none"`, even though `Orchestration` already has a separate `none: bool` disable flag and the constant's own comment says every value is a BACKGROUND primitive. Given input descriptor `[orchestration] loop = "none"`, both `_section_values` and `validate_sections` accept it because the string is in the set, producing `Orchestration(loop="none")`. That names no background wave loop, so the emitted harness spec loses the orchestration loop entirely while the record claims one is configured.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:ORCHESTRATION_LOOPS

chunk_findings.detail: The loop discriminator is not required. The new check is only `if orch and orch.loop:`, and the section loader above only requires at least one non-`none` key, not specifically `loop`. Given input `[orchestration] dispatch = "Agent"` (or `wait`/`persist`/`stop` only), validation succeeds and yields `Orchestration(loop="")`. Since `loop` is the field that selects the background primitive the rest of the section depends on, this accepted descriptor produces an orchestration record with no loop to emit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:validate_sections

chunk_findings.detail: The emitted command description says the wave runs "stop only on a question", but the orchestrator agent this command launches is required to stop for exactly two reasons: the scope is empty or a question gate requires a person (`ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md` rule 5). Given `/ddflow-wave` on an already-empty scope, the subagent stops with no question, so the command's advertised termination contract is false and misleads an operator about whether the background wave finished normally; the body's own "drive exactly that scope to empty" confirms empty-scope completion is expected, making the description internally inconsistent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/commands/kilo/ddflow-wave.md:3

chunk_findings.detail: The new fanout wording (“the ready set fanned out to sub-agents … one item each”) drops the previous claim step (“claim one item — and hand the work to a sub-agent”) and never instructs the orchestrator to `ddflow claim` each ready item before dispatching it. If two orchestration processes read the same `ddflow next --json` ready set before either sub-agent claims an item, the same unclaimed item can be dispatched to two opencode config/zen agents, causing duplicate implementations and conflicting merges. The equivalent Kilo delta was corrected to “claim each ready item, then fan”; opencode needs the same step.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/opencode.md item 1

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop condition says “Stop only where an operator answer is required (an approval, a policy decision)” but omits the required stop on an empty scope. After the final ready item merges and `ddflow next --json` returns no ready and no held/blocked items, no operator answer is required; an agent following this text literally keeps re-reading `next` instead of reporting completion and stopping. This is the empty-scope stop condition the corrected Kilo orchestrator and kilo-cline delta already include, so these emitted deltas should state it as well.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/opencode.md item 1; ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md item 2

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence rule still keys wave state only by the scope token (`orchestrator_wave:<scope>`), not by an invocation/run id, so two concurrent `/ddflow-wave` runs for the same scope overwrite each other's memory. For example, if an operator starts `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice, run B saves claimed/merged state for a later wave, then a lagging run A saves an older wave into the same slot; when B resumes after a compaction or restart, it loads A's stale position and may re-claim or skip items even though the spec says restart resumes AT the wave. The wording change to “runs for different scopes never share a slot” only removes the false claim; it does not make same-scope concurrent runs safe.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The new opencode orchestration record says `dispatch = "opencode config/zen agent (one item each)"`, which omits the claim-before-fan step. This is the same defect that was confirmed and fixed for Kilo in this change (`kilo.toml` now says “one claimed item each”). If two opencode wave drivers with overlapping scopes, e.g. `/ddflow-wave bugs` and `/ddflow-wave phase-1` where `phase-1` contains `bugs`, both read the same ready item from `ddflow next --json` and follow this data record, they can both dispatch the unclaimed item to sub-agents, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The new vscode orchestration record says `dispatch = "another window / terminal agent (one item each)"`, again omitting that the item must be claimed before fan-out. Given two vscode wave drivers whose scopes overlap, both can read the same ready item and, following this record, fan the unclaimed item to another window/terminal agent; the claimed-item invariant required by the corrected command and deltas is not present in the emitted orchestration data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The wave-completion test is defined only as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left”; it never says to keep the wave alive while items claimed by this orchestrator are still being implemented by background `task` children. Given `/ddflow-wave bugs` on a scope with exactly one ready item `101`, rule 2 tells the agent to claim `101` and launch a background task (lines 16-19). If the agent then re-reads `ddflow next --json` to decide whether to wait or finish, the rule’s DONE test can be satisfied because the only item is no longer ready and the text does not require outstanding claimed/in-progress items to be counted as `held`/`blocked`; line 23 then instructs “the scope is DONE — complete it” even though the task child has not merged or parked. This can stop the wave before the fanned-out work is complete, contrary to the intent’s re-read-after-merge/park and wait rules.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:22

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop tells the surface to read `ddflow next --json`, fan the ready set, and re-read `next` after each merge or park, but it never states the required empty-scope completion stop. The earlier fix added that stop to the opencode delta, but not here. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope whose last ready item has merged and whose `ddflow next --json` result has no ready and no held/blocked items, an agent following this text has no explicit rule to report completion and stop; it only has “re-read `next` after each merge or park” and “then end” for a request, so it can keep re-reading/waiting on an empty scope or stop arbitrarily.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:10

chunk_findings.detail: The fan-out wording says “the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item” without first claiming each ready item. Given two VS Code background surfaces whose scopes overlap, for example a second window running `/ddflow-wave phase-1` and a terminal agent running `/ddflow-wave bugs` where `bugs` is part of `phase-1`, both can read the same unclaimed ready item from `ddflow next --json` and, following this wording literally, fan it to separate agents before either claim removes it from the ready set. This reintroduces the duplicate-dispatch/conflicting-merge failure that the opencode delta and the earlier confirmed findings address by requiring “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:11

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code wave text tells the background orchestrator to read `ddflow next --json` and fan the ready set to one window/terminal agent per ready item, but unlike the opencode delta in the same change it never says to claim each ready item before fan-out. Given two VS Code background wave drivers with overlapping scopes (for example one on `phase-1` and one on `bugs` when `bugs` is inside `phase-1`), both can read the same unclaimed ready item, see it as ready, and fan it to separate window/terminal agents. The later statement that each agent “claims its own item” is after dispatch and does not prevent the orchestrator from spawning duplicate processes for the same unclaimed item, so the wave can duplicate implementation or create conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:12

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. The edit softens the claim to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect remains: launching `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice concurrently causes both runs to persist to the same memory slot. Concrete interleaving: run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving; run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; run A then saves wave 11, overwriting B’s newer position. If B later compacts/restarts it resumes from wave 11 instead of 12, causing items to be re-processed or skipped. The fix does not answer this because it only stops asserting same-scope safety; it does not separate same-scope runs or prevent two waves on the same scope.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:33 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The OpenCode orchestration data record says dispatch is `opencode config/zen agent (one item each)` but omits the claim-before-dispatch step that the opencode driver delta in this change now requires. A generator consuming this record (the change's stated purpose is to emit orchestration DATA per harness) will emit “one item each” without claiming; two concurrent opencode waves on overlapping scopes can both fan the same ready `ddflow next` item before either claims it, causing duplicate implementation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The VSCode orchestration data record has the same omission: `dispatch = "another window / terminal agent (one item each)"` lacks the claim step. The emitted vscode delta now tells the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanout, so a consumer using this data field emits unclaimed per-item dispatch; concurrent second-window waves can dispatch the same ready item twice and produce conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The new source-of-truth record still documents the pre-fix loop semantics that the rest of this change corrects: `dispatch` says the primitive is “one item per ready id” (unclaimed), and the class docstring plus `stop` field comment say the loop stops “ONLY on a question or operator gate” / “the question/ask/approval operator gates”, omitting the required empty-scope completion. Since this record is the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a generator that transcribes these field semantics will emit orchestrators that fan ready items without first claiming them and that never stop after the last ready item merges/park and `ddflow next --json` returns no ready/held/blocked items. The record should encode “one claimed item each” and include the empty-scope stop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:Orchestration

chunk_findings.detail: The previous fix softened the wording to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect still holds: the persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`. Two concurrent invocations of the same scope, e.g. `/ddflow-wave phase-1` launched twice, both write `orchestrator_wave:phase-1`. A lagging run A that read wave 10 can later save that old wave over run B’s newer wave 12; a compaction/restart then resumes from a stale or overwritten wave position. The softening removes the false claim but does not add a run/invocation id or same-scope disambiguation, so the same data-loss interleaving remains.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-33

chunk_findings.detail: The loop says to re-read `ddflow next` after each merge/park, but the empty-scope completion test only checks that exit 2 has no ready and no held/blocked items. If one wave has two ready items, 101 and 102: the orchestrator claims both and launches background task children; task 101 merges first, triggering a re-read while task 102 is still implementing its item. At that point `ddflow next` returns nothing ready and no held/blocked (102 is neither ready nor in the stated held/blocked categories), so the orchestrator declares the scope DONE and stops while 102 is still in flight; item 102 is stranded. The completion test must wait until all task children from the current wave have merged/parked, or `ddflow next` must include in-progress claimed items in its empty-scope determination.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/commands/kilo/ddflow-wave.md:12, ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:21-23

chunk_findings.detail: The Roo one-shot fallback instructs “claim, gate, merge” but omits the `park` alternative that the same paragraph gives for the background loop: “after the merges land (or park, in the PR flow)”. On a Roo runtime processing a PR-flow item whose long gate (ci/review) is pending, the instruction as written directs the agent to merge the item after the gate instead of parking it, which would merge an item before its gate completes. The fallback must say “claim, gate, then merge or park” (or otherwise branch on whether the item is blocked/parked).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:21

chunk_findings.detail: The new fan-out wording says “one read of `ddflow next --json`, the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item,” but unlike the opencode and Kilo deltas it does not instruct the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanning it. Given two background vscode orchestrators with overlapping scopes (for example a second VS Code window and a terminal agent both running the wave loop), both can read the same ready set before either claims an item; both then fan the same unclaimed item to separate windows, and item 3 only says each subagent claims its own item, so duplicate work/lease contention occurs where the other deltas would have claimed first.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: This background loop now re-reads `ddflow next` after each merge or park but omits the required stop condition when the scope becomes empty. On a scope whose last ready item merges, `ddflow next --json` returns no ready items and no held/blocked items; the surface is told only to re-read `next` after each merge/park, so it can keep polling an empty scope forever instead of reporting completion. The opencode delta in the same change explicitly adds “or when the scope is empty”; vscode needs the same completion stop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code delta says the iteration runs in the background with the operator as the exception and describes a wave loop that re-reads `next` after each merge or park, but then the same item instructs “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” On a scope with two ready items and no question, an agent following this text ends the background request after the first merge and prints a handoff; the second ready item is not driven until someone starts a new request. The delta therefore still stops at end-of-request rather than only on a question/operator gate or an empty scope, contradicting the heading and the orchestration stop contract this change is supposed to emit.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The updated kilo-cline delta states that where the runtime has no task-subagent run (Roo), the agent should "do ONE item directly — claim, gate, merge — then print `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` as the handoff." However, the rule [r-adapters] requires that every external dependency goes through a port in `ddflow/adapters`, and this hardcoded string-matching instruction bypasses the adapter abstraction by instructing the agent to directly output raw command strings instead of invoking an adapter-managed handoff function or port.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:23

chunk_findings.detail: The text instructs the VS Code driver to print `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` (with an underscore), but the canonical command name used throughout ddflow and in the neighboring deltas (e.g. opencode.md, kilo-cline.md) is `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` (with a space). An agent executing this delta literally will output `ddflow_next`, which is not a valid command and breaks the handoff.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: `gate` can return an ok approval stamp for an agent whose bound key set is empty (for example, an approval request made with `--history-only` naming a ref that matches no current finding, or when there are currently no matching findings). It returns `("", {"keys": []})`. `accepting` passes that empty key set as `approved`, and `accept` uses `if approved:` to decide whether the caller is a person; an empty set/list therefore takes the person branch and accepts whatever is open (subject only to `only`). Thus the approval stamp does not encode “agent approved zero findings” versus “person at terminal”, so the person-only guarantee is not actually carried through the stamp: a zero-key agent approval is indistinguishable from a direct person accept, and an extra finding appearing after the approval can be accepted on the agent’s side.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/repairs/accepted.py:gate/accept

chunk_findings.detail: The new refusal handling is only on the non-JSON path. The JSON branch runs first and emits only the whitelisted body fields `problems`, `notes`, `events`, `items`, `wait_cycles`, and `auto_order`; the new `out.reason` printing for `REFUSED` is below it and is skipped. For example, running `ddflow doctor --json --accept-history` without `--history-reason` (or with `--approval request` where the useful reason/approval id is in `out.reason`) exits with the refusal code but the JSON body contains no reason, unlike the human path. This breaks the agent approval route because the agent cannot read why the command was refused or recover the approval id from JSON output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/reporting.py:doctor JSON/REFUSED branch

chunk_findings.detail: The second “new” Lamport regression is not actually a new decrease. After the first appended event, the adjacent clock sequence in the shard ends `..., L, 1` and the test accepts that `L -> 1` decrease. The next event is built from the original last row but is appended after the `lamport=1` event, with `lamport=2`; the adjacent sequence becomes `..., L, 1, 2`. Since `2 > 1`, there is no new adjacent clock decrease—the original bug’s “105645 then 105644” is also an adjacent decrease. A doctor that accepts only the recorded decrease should still exit 0, but the test asserts `code == 1` and one new “Lamport clock decreases” message. To create a genuinely new decrease, the new event’s clock must be lower than the immediately preceding appended event (for example, make `ev` have `lamport=2` and `ev2` have `lamport=1`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_accepted_history.py:103-107

chunk_findings.detail: After the first regression `ev` with `lamport=1` is accepted, the test appends `ev2` with `lamport=2`. Since `2` is greater than the currently last accepted event's Lamport value (`1`), this is not a “new Lamport clock decrease.” The assertion `code == 1 and text.count("Lamport clock decreases") == 1 and "PROBLEM" in text` therefore does not demonstrate that acceptance is specific; it either fails on a valid non-decreasing append, or passes for an unrelated event-validity problem created by cloning stale `rows[-1]`, not for a new clock regression.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_accepted_history.py:test_an_accepted_clock_regression_stays_specific

data.alternatives: Fallback only when every other-family reviewer was recorded unavailable; keep strict
data.context: Reviewers were frequently unavailable (HTTP 429, timeouts) in this session, forcing gate skips and overrides. CLAUDE.md and the enforced-rules list name cross-family review; this decision relaxes it explicitly.
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-02: the requirement that at least one reviewer come from a different model family than the author becomes a SOFT requirement. Preference ladder: (1) a reviewer of a different family; (2) when none is available, a different MODEL of the same family also satisfies the gate, recorded as tier model (same-family fallback); (3) the author own model never counts as a reviewer; with neither, the gate stays blocked or unavailable and is never passed unaided. Every review carries its independence tier (family | model | none); complete and gate status show a warning for tier model; metrics count the fallback rate. Knob [agent].reviewer_independence = family | model | off, default model, strictest family, org-lockable; the boolean reviewer_family_must_differ maps onto it (true means family). An unrecognised model still establishes nothing (not counted as different). The picker prefers a different family and falls back only when no other-family reviewer is configured or reachable.
data.title: Reviewer independence is a preference: a different family first, a different model of the same family as a recorded fallback

data.body: Implements D-reviewer-independence-soft. (1) Knob [agent].reviewer_independence = family|model|off (default model; strictest family; org-lockable); reviewer_family_must_differ maps onto it and keeps working. (2) The independence check returns a tier: family, model or none, per review and for the gate (the best tier among its passing reviewers); the author own model never counts; unrecognised models establish nothing. (3) Evidence: the tier is stored in the review outcome; complete and gate status print a warning for tier model naming the exact way to get a family review (which reviewers are configured, ddflow review --reviewer ...). (4) The reviewer picker prefers a different family and falls back only when none is configured or reachable. (5) Metrics: fallback rate per reviewer, visible in ddflow metrics and the perf report. (6) Update CLAUDE.md, the managed instructions and docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md so the rule text matches (the enforced-rule line about different family becomes a preference with a recorded fallback). Tests: family satisfies; only same-family different model passes as tier model with the warning; same model never passes; unknown model establishes nothing; strictest family via org lock refuses the fallback; legacy boolean maps. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, D-reviewer-independence-soft): extend the existing independence check in services/reviewer_trust and the families map; no second implementation; an unrecognised model establishes nothing; the author own model never reviews; a review that could not run is unavailable, never passed.

data.text:
Why reviewer independence is soft: users on a single subscription have models from one family only
Operator clarification after the soft-independence decision. The hard floor stays: the author own model never reviews its own work.
OPERATOR 2026-11-02: the reason for D-reviewer-independence-soft is NOT to weaken review. It is to let users who work with ONE subscription, where the available models are all (or mostly) from the same family, use ddflow with full review gates. A same-family, different-model review is therefore a normal supported state, not a degraded one: it is recorded (tier model) and shown neutrally, without nagging. Ddflow compensates for the shared blind spots inside the family instead of only reporting them: prefer the model farthest from the author (another size or generation); fresh context and no author reasoning handed to the reviewer; gate-specific reviewer roles and prompts; findings grounded in probes or tests; and measure whether same-family reviews find as much as cross-family ones (confirmed findings per review by tier) so the operator decides from evidence.

data.body:
Implements D-reviewer-independence-soft. (1) Knob [agent].reviewer_independence = family|model|off (default model; strictest family; org-lockable); reviewer_family_must_differ maps onto it and keeps working. (2) The independence check returns a tier: family, model or none, per review and for the gate (the best tier among its passing reviewers); the author own model never counts; unrecognised models establish nothing. (3) Evidence: the tier is stored in the review outcome; complete and gate status print a warning for tier model naming the exact way to get a family review (which reviewers are configured, ddflow review --reviewer ...). (4) The reviewer picker prefers a different family and falls back only when none is configured or reachable. (5) Metrics: fallback rate per reviewer, visible in ddflow metrics and the perf report. (6) Update CLAUDE.md, the managed instructions and docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md so the rule text matches (the enforced-rule line about different family becomes a preference with a recorded fallback). Tests: family satisfies; only same-family different model passes as tier model with the warning; same model never passes; unknown model establishes nothing; strictest family via org lock refuses the fallback; legacy boolean maps. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, D-reviewer-independence-soft): extend the existing independence check in services/reviewer_trust and the families map; no second implementation; an unrecognised model establishes nothing; the author own model never reviews; a review that could not run is unavailable, never passed.

SCOPE (operator 2026-11-02): applies to EVERY reviewer-backed gate: rubber_duck, critic, standards and bug_hunt and dedupe when a roborev or other reviewer serves them, the review inbox and any reviewer-backed check; one shared independence check, never a per-gate copy. The shipped default of [agent].reviewer_independence is model for ALL projects ddflow manages (set in code, so existing projects get it with an upgrade note in ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/ saying how to pin family); this project sets it explicitly after the knob lands (the coordinator does that from the primary checkout, do NOT edit .ddflow/config.toml in the worktree: the primary copy has uncommitted operator changes).

OPERATOR CLARIFICATION 2026-11-02 (D-reviewer-independence-soft-why): the purpose is to let single-subscription users, whose models are all from one family, operate with full gates. So: (a) a tier-model review is a NORMAL supported state: print it neutrally once at complete and gate status (which models reviewed, tier), no urgency wording, no repeated nagging; the way to get a cross-family review is a hint, not a warning; (b) compensate inside the family: the picker prefers the model farthest from the author (different size or generation, then different tier), reviewers get a fresh context and never the author reasoning or transcript, reviewer prompts stay gate-specific, findings must be grounded in a probe or test where one exists; (c) setup and ddflow reviewers detect what the account can actually reach and propose a reviewer set of DIFFERENT models of the one family (and say so plainly); (d) metrics: confirmed findings per review and fallback rate BY TIER, so the operator can see from evidence whether same-family reviews find as much; (e) the hard floor stays: the author own model never counts; with only one model reachable at all, the gate is recorded unavailable, never passed.

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence rule still keys wave state only by the scope token (`orchestrator_wave:<scope>`), not by an invocation/run id, so two concurrent `/ddflow-wave` runs for the same scope overwrite each other's memory. For example, if an operator starts `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice, run B saves claimed/merged state for a later wave, then a lagging run A saves an older wave into the same slot; when B resumes after a compaction or restart, it loads A's stale position and may re-claim or skip items even though the spec says restart resumes AT the wave. The wording change to “runs for different scopes never share a slot” only removes the false claim; it does not make same-scope concurrent runs safe.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The new opencode orchestration record says `dispatch = "opencode config/zen agent (one item each)"`, which omits the claim-before-fan step. This is the same defect that was confirmed and fixed for Kilo in this change (`kilo.toml` now says “one claimed item each”). If two opencode wave drivers with overlapping scopes, e.g. `/ddflow-wave bugs` and `/ddflow-wave phase-1` where `phase-1` contains `bugs`, both read the same ready item from `ddflow next --json` and follow this data record, they can both dispatch the unclaimed item to sub-agents, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The new vscode orchestration record says `dispatch = "another window / terminal agent (one item each)"`, again omitting that the item must be claimed before fan-out. Given two vscode wave drivers whose scopes overlap, both can read the same ready item and, following this record, fan the unclaimed item to another window/terminal agent; the claimed-item invariant required by the corrected command and deltas is not present in the emitted orchestration data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The wave-completion test is defined only as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left”; it never says to keep the wave alive while items claimed by this orchestrator are still being implemented by background `task` children. Given `/ddflow-wave bugs` on a scope with exactly one ready item `101`, rule 2 tells the agent to claim `101` and launch a background task (lines 16-19). If the agent then re-reads `ddflow next --json` to decide whether to wait or finish, the rule’s DONE test can be satisfied because the only item is no longer ready and the text does not require outstanding claimed/in-progress items to be counted as `held`/`blocked`; line 23 then instructs “the scope is DONE — complete it” even though the task child has not merged or parked. This can stop the wave before the fanned-out work is complete, contrary to the intent’s re-read-after-merge/park and wait rules.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:22

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop tells the surface to read `ddflow next --json`, fan the ready set, and re-read `next` after each merge or park, but it never states the required empty-scope completion stop. The earlier fix added that stop to the opencode delta, but not here. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope whose last ready item has merged and whose `ddflow next --json` result has no ready and no held/blocked items, an agent following this text has no explicit rule to report completion and stop; it only has “re-read `next` after each merge or park” and “then end” for a request, so it can keep re-reading/waiting on an empty scope or stop arbitrarily.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:10

chunk_findings.detail: The fan-out wording says “the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item” without first claiming each ready item. Given two VS Code background surfaces whose scopes overlap, for example a second window running `/ddflow-wave phase-1` and a terminal agent running `/ddflow-wave bugs` where `bugs` is part of `phase-1`, both can read the same unclaimed ready item from `ddflow next --json` and, following this wording literally, fan it to separate agents before either claim removes it from the ready set. This reintroduces the duplicate-dispatch/conflicting-merge failure that the opencode delta and the earlier confirmed findings address by requiring “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:11

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code wave text tells the background orchestrator to read `ddflow next --json` and fan the ready set to one window/terminal agent per ready item, but unlike the opencode delta in the same change it never says to claim each ready item before fan-out. Given two VS Code background wave drivers with overlapping scopes (for example one on `phase-1` and one on `bugs` when `bugs` is inside `phase-1`), both can read the same unclaimed ready item, see it as ready, and fan it to separate window/terminal agents. The later statement that each agent “claims its own item” is after dispatch and does not prevent the orchestrator from spawning duplicate processes for the same unclaimed item, so the wave can duplicate implementation or create conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:12

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. The edit softens the claim to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect remains: launching `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice concurrently causes both runs to persist to the same memory slot. Concrete interleaving: run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving; run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; run A then saves wave 11, overwriting B’s newer position. If B later compacts/restarts it resumes from wave 11 instead of 12, causing items to be re-processed or skipped. The fix does not answer this because it only stops asserting same-scope safety; it does not separate same-scope runs or prevent two waves on the same scope.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:33 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The OpenCode orchestration data record says dispatch is `opencode config/zen agent (one item each)` but omits the claim-before-dispatch step that the opencode driver delta in this change now requires. A generator consuming this record (the change's stated purpose is to emit orchestration DATA per harness) will emit “one item each” without claiming; two concurrent opencode waves on overlapping scopes can both fan the same ready `ddflow next` item before either claims it, causing duplicate implementation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The VSCode orchestration data record has the same omission: `dispatch = "another window / terminal agent (one item each)"` lacks the claim step. The emitted vscode delta now tells the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanout, so a consumer using this data field emits unclaimed per-item dispatch; concurrent second-window waves can dispatch the same ready item twice and produce conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The new source-of-truth record still documents the pre-fix loop semantics that the rest of this change corrects: `dispatch` says the primitive is “one item per ready id” (unclaimed), and the class docstring plus `stop` field comment say the loop stops “ONLY on a question or operator gate” / “the question/ask/approval operator gates”, omitting the required empty-scope completion. Since this record is the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a generator that transcribes these field semantics will emit orchestrators that fan ready items without first claiming them and that never stop after the last ready item merges/park and `ddflow next --json` returns no ready/held/blocked items. The record should encode “one claimed item each” and include the empty-scope stop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:Orchestration

chunk_findings.detail: The previous fix softened the wording to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect still holds: the persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`. Two concurrent invocations of the same scope, e.g. `/ddflow-wave phase-1` launched twice, both write `orchestrator_wave:phase-1`. A lagging run A that read wave 10 can later save that old wave over run B’s newer wave 12; a compaction/restart then resumes from a stale or overwritten wave position. The softening removes the false claim but does not add a run/invocation id or same-scope disambiguation, so the same data-loss interleaving remains.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-33

chunk_findings.detail: The loop says to re-read `ddflow next` after each merge/park, but the empty-scope completion test only checks that exit 2 has no ready and no held/blocked items. If one wave has two ready items, 101 and 102: the orchestrator claims both and launches background task children; task 101 merges first, triggering a re-read while task 102 is still implementing its item. At that point `ddflow next` returns nothing ready and no held/blocked (102 is neither ready nor in the stated held/blocked categories), so the orchestrator declares the scope DONE and stops while 102 is still in flight; item 102 is stranded. The completion test must wait until all task children from the current wave have merged/parked, or `ddflow next` must include in-progress claimed items in its empty-scope determination.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/commands/kilo/ddflow-wave.md:12, ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:21-23

chunk_findings.detail: The Roo one-shot fallback instructs “claim, gate, merge” but omits the `park` alternative that the same paragraph gives for the background loop: “after the merges land (or park, in the PR flow)”. On a Roo runtime processing a PR-flow item whose long gate (ci/review) is pending, the instruction as written directs the agent to merge the item after the gate instead of parking it, which would merge an item before its gate completes. The fallback must say “claim, gate, then merge or park” (or otherwise branch on whether the item is blocked/parked).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:21

chunk_findings.detail: The new fan-out wording says “one read of `ddflow next --json`, the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item,” but unlike the opencode and Kilo deltas it does not instruct the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanning it. Given two background vscode orchestrators with overlapping scopes (for example a second VS Code window and a terminal agent both running the wave loop), both can read the same ready set before either claims an item; both then fan the same unclaimed item to separate windows, and item 3 only says each subagent claims its own item, so duplicate work/lease contention occurs where the other deltas would have claimed first.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: This background loop now re-reads `ddflow next` after each merge or park but omits the required stop condition when the scope becomes empty. On a scope whose last ready item merges, `ddflow next --json` returns no ready items and no held/blocked items; the surface is told only to re-read `next` after each merge/park, so it can keep polling an empty scope forever instead of reporting completion. The opencode delta in the same change explicitly adds “or when the scope is empty”; vscode needs the same completion stop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code delta says the iteration runs in the background with the operator as the exception and describes a wave loop that re-reads `next` after each merge or park, but then the same item instructs “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” On a scope with two ready items and no question, an agent following this text ends the background request after the first merge and prints a handoff; the second ready item is not driven until someone starts a new request. The delta therefore still stops at end-of-request rather than only on a question/operator gate or an empty scope, contradicting the heading and the orchestration stop contract this change is supposed to emit.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The updated kilo-cline delta states that where the runtime has no task-subagent run (Roo), the agent should "do ONE item directly — claim, gate, merge — then print `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` as the handoff." However, the rule [r-adapters] requires that every external dependency goes through a port in `ddflow/adapters`, and this hardcoded string-matching instruction bypasses the adapter abstraction by instructing the agent to directly output raw command strings instead of invoking an adapter-managed handoff function or port.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:23

chunk_findings.detail: The text instructs the VS Code driver to print `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` (with an underscore), but the canonical command name used throughout ddflow and in the neighboring deltas (e.g. opencode.md, kilo-cline.md) is `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` (with a space). An agent executing this delta literally will output `ddflow_next`, which is not a valid command and breaks the handoff.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: The updated source-of-truth loop spec defines an empty scope as “no ready, held or in-flight items”, but the Kilo instance emitted in this same change defines DONE as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left” and no claimed item in flight. The docstring omits blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) and no ready, held, or in-flight items, this record says the scope is empty and the loop should stop, while the emitted Kilo rule says it is a WAIT. Since this record is meant to be the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a driver delta generated from it can stop with blocked work still pending.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:Orchestration

chunk_findings.detail: The new claim-before-fan wording tells the VS Code background orchestrator to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items” to another window/terminal agent, but the same delta later says that for parallelism “each claims its own item and gets its own worktree” (line 23). Given one ready item, say `101`, an orchestrator following line 13 claims `101` and then opens a terminal/window agent for `101`; the terminal agent, following the same delta, attempts to claim `101` itself. If claims are exclusive, that claim fails and the item is left claimed by the orchestrator but not worked, stalling the wave. The emitted instruction does not say that dispatched agents must skip claiming or that the orchestrator’s claim transfers to the dispatched process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:13

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop rule says the background wave stops only when the scope is empty (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight) or on an “operator answer,” but it omits the required stop on an unanswered `question` or operator gate. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope with one ready item that, when claimed/fanned, raises a `question` (or is parked at an operator gate), the scope is not empty and no operator answer has arrived yet, so the literal rule tells the driver not to stop; it will keep waiting/re-reading or continuing instead of stopping and surfacing the question/gate. This contradicts the intended loop (“stop ONLY on a question or operator gate”) and the kilo-cline delta in the same diff, which says “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate.”
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence slot is still keyed only by `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, and the added text “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” is only an instruction, not an enforcement mechanism: no run/invocation id, lock, or active-run marker is specified for a second orchestrator to check. If an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice from two terminals, run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 over it. A later compaction/restart resumes from the stale wave. The prior fix does not answer this interleaving because both runs are already concurrent and neither has a way to detect the other before writing the same key.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-35 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. The new sentence “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” does not tell the agent how to detect an existing same-scope run or refuse to start, and there is no lock on the memory slot. The prior interleaving still occurs as soon as that instruction is violated: run A reads wave 10 and stalls, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 and overwrites B; a later compaction or restart resumes from the stale position and can re-claim or skip items. The fix is a normative prohibition, not a guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32

chunk_findings.detail: The source-of-truth `Orchestration` docstring defines empty scope as “(no ready, held or in-flight items)”, but the emitted Kilo template’s DONE test requires no ready, no held **or blocked** items, and no claimed item still in flight. `blocked` is a separate category in the template’s own wording (“`held`/`blocked` items come later”), so the harness-agnostic data omits it. A generator transcribing this docstring will emit a stop rule that treats a blocked item—e.g. an item waiting on a lease/dependency that will later become ready—as not preventing completion, so the driver stops while the scope is not empty and skips that item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:89

chunk_findings.detail: The new text tells the background surface to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items to one window/terminal agent each”, but the Subagents section below still says parallelism is separate processes and “each claims its own item and gets its own worktree.” Given one ready item, the background surface claims it and then hands an already-claimed item to a second window/terminal agent; that agent cannot claim its own item and gets no worktree. The two instructions contradict for the same VS Code driver.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14-15

chunk_findings.detail: The paragraph says “Stop only on the empty scope … or an operator answer. Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” For a scope with two ready items, after the first merge the empty-scope stop condition is false (the second item is still ready/in flight), so the “then end” instruction causes a premature handoff instead of re-reading `ddflow next` after each merge until the scope is actually empty. The rewrite did not remove this conflict.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16-18

chunk_findings.detail: The stop condition says “Stop only on the empty scope … or an operator answer,” but the correct loop stop is on a `question` or operator gate, not on the answer. Given a ready item that raises an operator gate/question and then waits, an agent following this line sees no operator answer yet and therefore does not treat the pending gate as the stop; it may keep re-reading/polling instead of waiting for the operator. The neighboring kilo-cline delta uses the correct “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate” wording.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The handoff instruction still writes `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` with underscores, while the current kilo-cline delta says `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` and the actual commands use a space. An agent executing the VS Code delta literally prints invalid command names, breaking the handoff.
