chunk_findings.detail: The person-only check trusts the caller-supplied `agent` marker: `who = agent_marker(agent); if not who: return "", {}`. An agent that invokes the doctor command with an empty/absent agent marker (for example `DDFLOW_AGENT=` or `--agent ''`, depending on the surface) gets `agent_marker("")` empty, so `gate` returns `("", {})`. `accepting` then passes `approved=frozenset()` and `accept` appends `repair.applied` records for every currently open content mismatch or clock regression, attributed to the OS user. That bypasses the required person approval/chat route and contradicts the stated intent that the accept is person-only.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/repairs/accepted.py:gate

chunk_findings.detail: `accept` uses truthiness of `approved` to distinguish a direct person call from an agent call bounded by an approval: `if approved: todo = [i for i in todo if i.key in approved]`. An empty approval set is therefore treated as “person accepts all.” `gate` can legitimately return an agent stamp with `keys=[]` when `_fresh(log)` has no matching findings (for example, `--history-only` names an already accepted/nonexistent ref, or there are no findings at approval time). If another process appends a new content mismatch or clock regression after `gate` has read the log but before `accept` opens its transaction, `accept` sees the new finding while `approved` is still empty and accepts it even though the person approved no such finding. This breaks the invariant that the approval binds the exact findings accepted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/repairs/accepted.py:accept

chunk_findings.detail: The new `accept_history` parameter is declared as an ordinary surface parameter: it is not `cli_only=True` (unlike `accept_lost_events`) and it carries no `t="T2"`/person-only marker. The stated intent explicitly requires the acceptance to be person-only and to be declared T2 so the chat route works (NS-person-acts). As declared, `ddflow doctor --accept-history --history-reason ...` is exposed through the normal agent-accessible doctor command, with the person-only requirement only in help text; an agent can therefore use the normal command path to record an accepted-history entry without a person's approval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/setup.py:accept_history

chunk_findings.detail: The new `accept_history` and `history` parameters were inserted before the existing `start_texts` parameter. Any caller using the previously valid positional form `doctor(repo, log, cfg, agent, parser, tools, accept_lost_events, start_texts)` now silently binds `start_texts` to `accept_history`. For example, `doctor(repo, log, cfg, agent, None, None, False, ["start text"])` makes `accept_history` a truthy list, causing the function to enter the `if accept_history:` branch with the default empty `history` tuple and run `RP.accepted.gate(...)` / `RP.accepted.accepting(...)`, potentially recording a bogus acceptance or refusing a normal doctor run. New parameters should be appended after `start_texts` or made keyword-only.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:doctor signature

chunk_findings.detail: `regressions()` destructures only one `(n, before, after)` tuple per shard from `log.clock_regressions().items()`. A dict keyed by shard cannot hold more than one regression for the same shard, so a log where the same cloned agent id regresses at two different events yields only the one tuple the existing method exposes. For example, if shard `a` regresses at event 10 and again at event 20, `regressions()` produces a key only for whichever single tuple `clock_regressions()` retained; the other event is absent from `_fresh()`. `accept` therefore records only that one key, and the second Lamport regression remains a PROBLEM after `--accept-history`, so doctor can still exit 1.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/repairs/accepted.py:regressions

chunk_findings.detail: When `doctor` is invoked with `--json` and the new accepted-history validation refuses (for example `doctor --json --accept-history` without the required `--history-reason`), the `if c.json:` branch returns `out.exit` before the new `if out.exit == REFUSED:` branch is reached. The JSON body emitted is `out.body(("problems", "notes", "events", "items", "wait_cycles", "auto_order"))`, which does not include `out.reason`, so a JSON caller gets a non-zero exit with no refusal explanation, while the non-JSON path prints `out.reason` to stderr. This makes the new refusal mode unrecoverable for JSON consumers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/reporting.py: if out.exit == REFUSED

chunk_findings.detail: `accepting` invokes `accept(...)` without passing the `approved` parameter (line 159), whereas `gate(...)` computes and returns an `approved` set (via `stamp.setdefault("keys", keys)`) that is necessary to enforce that an agent can only accept approved findings. When `accepting` is called downstream by agent or MCP workflows that rely on approval gating, `approved` defaults to an empty frozenset, bypassing the approval security check and allowing unapproved findings to be permanently accepted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/repairs/accepted.py:159

chunk_findings.detail: `api.doctor(scrubbed, agent="bot", accept_history=True, history=ask)` passes an argument `history=ask` to `api.doctor`, but `ddflow/api/reporting/health.py` (referenced in the manifest) accepts no such parameter `history`, raising a `TypeError: doctor() got an unexpected keyword argument 'history'` when this test runs.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_accepted_history.py:173

chunk_findings.detail: This diff deletes the only assertion in the clock-regression acceptance test that proves an acceptance is specific to one recorded decrease. The removed lines appended a second, distinct clock decrease and asserted that doctor still exits 1 and reports `PROBLEM`; the replacement is only a comment. As a result, if the accepted-history key for Lamport regressions is too broad (for example, it accepts future decreases on the same shard or accepts any `Lamport clock decreases` finding once one has been accepted), this test still passes because no second decrease is ever added.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_accepted_history.py:100

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test no longer exercises that an accepted clock regression is scoped to the exact accepted key. The removed lines appended a new distinct decrease after the first acceptance and asserted `code == 1` with `"PROBLEM"`; they are replaced only by a comment claiming that behavior. If the acceptance logic later over-matches clock regressions (for example suppressing any subsequent Lamport decrease after one history acceptance), this test would still pass because that scenario is no longer executed. Since accepted-history records permanently suppress findings, the missing scoping assertion leaves a real regression unguarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_doctor_accepted_history.py:100

evidence.diff_source: delta review of 1 commit since f01ab63811

evidence.budget_forced: all 38 findings triaged (34 fixed in-branch, 4 refuted); final confirmation round

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence rule still keys wave state only by the scope token (`orchestrator_wave:<scope>`), not by an invocation/run id, so two concurrent `/ddflow-wave` runs for the same scope overwrite each other's memory. For example, if an operator starts `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice, run B saves claimed/merged state for a later wave, then a lagging run A saves an older wave into the same slot; when B resumes after a compaction or restart, it loads A's stale position and may re-claim or skip items even though the spec says restart resumes AT the wave. The wording change to “runs for different scopes never share a slot” only removes the false claim; it does not make same-scope concurrent runs safe.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The new opencode orchestration record says `dispatch = "opencode config/zen agent (one item each)"`, which omits the claim-before-fan step. This is the same defect that was confirmed and fixed for Kilo in this change (`kilo.toml` now says “one claimed item each”). If two opencode wave drivers with overlapping scopes, e.g. `/ddflow-wave bugs` and `/ddflow-wave phase-1` where `phase-1` contains `bugs`, both read the same ready item from `ddflow next --json` and follow this data record, they can both dispatch the unclaimed item to sub-agents, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The new vscode orchestration record says `dispatch = "another window / terminal agent (one item each)"`, again omitting that the item must be claimed before fan-out. Given two vscode wave drivers whose scopes overlap, both can read the same ready item and, following this record, fan the unclaimed item to another window/terminal agent; the claimed-item invariant required by the corrected command and deltas is not present in the emitted orchestration data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The wave-completion test is defined only as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left”; it never says to keep the wave alive while items claimed by this orchestrator are still being implemented by background `task` children. Given `/ddflow-wave bugs` on a scope with exactly one ready item `101`, rule 2 tells the agent to claim `101` and launch a background task (lines 16-19). If the agent then re-reads `ddflow next --json` to decide whether to wait or finish, the rule’s DONE test can be satisfied because the only item is no longer ready and the text does not require outstanding claimed/in-progress items to be counted as `held`/`blocked`; line 23 then instructs “the scope is DONE — complete it” even though the task child has not merged or parked. This can stop the wave before the fanned-out work is complete, contrary to the intent’s re-read-after-merge/park and wait rules.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:22

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop tells the surface to read `ddflow next --json`, fan the ready set, and re-read `next` after each merge or park, but it never states the required empty-scope completion stop. The earlier fix added that stop to the opencode delta, but not here. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope whose last ready item has merged and whose `ddflow next --json` result has no ready and no held/blocked items, an agent following this text has no explicit rule to report completion and stop; it only has “re-read `next` after each merge or park” and “then end” for a request, so it can keep re-reading/waiting on an empty scope or stop arbitrarily.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:10

chunk_findings.detail: The fan-out wording says “the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item” without first claiming each ready item. Given two VS Code background surfaces whose scopes overlap, for example a second window running `/ddflow-wave phase-1` and a terminal agent running `/ddflow-wave bugs` where `bugs` is part of `phase-1`, both can read the same unclaimed ready item from `ddflow next --json` and, following this wording literally, fan it to separate agents before either claim removes it from the ready set. This reintroduces the duplicate-dispatch/conflicting-merge failure that the opencode delta and the earlier confirmed findings address by requiring “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:11

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code wave text tells the background orchestrator to read `ddflow next --json` and fan the ready set to one window/terminal agent per ready item, but unlike the opencode delta in the same change it never says to claim each ready item before fan-out. Given two VS Code background wave drivers with overlapping scopes (for example one on `phase-1` and one on `bugs` when `bugs` is inside `phase-1`), both can read the same unclaimed ready item, see it as ready, and fan it to separate window/terminal agents. The later statement that each agent “claims its own item” is after dispatch and does not prevent the orchestrator from spawning duplicate processes for the same unclaimed item, so the wave can duplicate implementation or create conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:12

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. The edit softens the claim to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect remains: launching `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice concurrently causes both runs to persist to the same memory slot. Concrete interleaving: run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving; run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; run A then saves wave 11, overwriting B’s newer position. If B later compacts/restarts it resumes from wave 11 instead of 12, causing items to be re-processed or skipped. The fix does not answer this because it only stops asserting same-scope safety; it does not separate same-scope runs or prevent two waves on the same scope.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:33 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The OpenCode orchestration data record says dispatch is `opencode config/zen agent (one item each)` but omits the claim-before-dispatch step that the opencode driver delta in this change now requires. A generator consuming this record (the change's stated purpose is to emit orchestration DATA per harness) will emit “one item each” without claiming; two concurrent opencode waves on overlapping scopes can both fan the same ready `ddflow next` item before either claims it, causing duplicate implementation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/opencode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The VSCode orchestration data record has the same omission: `dispatch = "another window / terminal agent (one item each)"` lacks the claim step. The emitted vscode delta now tells the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanout, so a consumer using this data field emits unclaimed per-item dispatch; concurrent second-window waves can dispatch the same ready item twice and produce conflicting merges.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml:[orchestration].dispatch

chunk_findings.detail: The new source-of-truth record still documents the pre-fix loop semantics that the rest of this change corrects: `dispatch` says the primitive is “one item per ready id” (unclaimed), and the class docstring plus `stop` field comment say the loop stops “ONLY on a question or operator gate” / “the question/ask/approval operator gates”, omitting the required empty-scope completion. Since this record is the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a generator that transcribes these field semantics will emit orchestrators that fan ready items without first claiming them and that never stop after the last ready item merges/park and `ddflow next --json` returns no ready/held/blocked items. The record should encode “one claimed item each” and include the empty-scope stop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:Orchestration

chunk_findings.detail: The previous fix softened the wording to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect still holds: the persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`. Two concurrent invocations of the same scope, e.g. `/ddflow-wave phase-1` launched twice, both write `orchestrator_wave:phase-1`. A lagging run A that read wave 10 can later save that old wave over run B’s newer wave 12; a compaction/restart then resumes from a stale or overwritten wave position. The softening removes the false claim but does not add a run/invocation id or same-scope disambiguation, so the same data-loss interleaving remains.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-33

chunk_findings.detail: The loop says to re-read `ddflow next` after each merge/park, but the empty-scope completion test only checks that exit 2 has no ready and no held/blocked items. If one wave has two ready items, 101 and 102: the orchestrator claims both and launches background task children; task 101 merges first, triggering a re-read while task 102 is still implementing its item. At that point `ddflow next` returns nothing ready and no held/blocked (102 is neither ready nor in the stated held/blocked categories), so the orchestrator declares the scope DONE and stops while 102 is still in flight; item 102 is stranded. The completion test must wait until all task children from the current wave have merged/parked, or `ddflow next` must include in-progress claimed items in its empty-scope determination.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/commands/kilo/ddflow-wave.md:12, ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:21-23

chunk_findings.detail: The Roo one-shot fallback instructs “claim, gate, merge” but omits the `park` alternative that the same paragraph gives for the background loop: “after the merges land (or park, in the PR flow)”. On a Roo runtime processing a PR-flow item whose long gate (ci/review) is pending, the instruction as written directs the agent to merge the item after the gate instead of parking it, which would merge an item before its gate completes. The fallback must say “claim, gate, then merge or park” (or otherwise branch on whether the item is blocked/parked).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:21

chunk_findings.detail: The new fan-out wording says “one read of `ddflow next --json`, the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item,” but unlike the opencode and Kilo deltas it does not instruct the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanning it. Given two background vscode orchestrators with overlapping scopes (for example a second VS Code window and a terminal agent both running the wave loop), both can read the same ready set before either claims an item; both then fan the same unclaimed item to separate windows, and item 3 only says each subagent claims its own item, so duplicate work/lease contention occurs where the other deltas would have claimed first.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: This background loop now re-reads `ddflow next` after each merge or park but omits the required stop condition when the scope becomes empty. On a scope whose last ready item merges, `ddflow next --json` returns no ready items and no held/blocked items; the surface is told only to re-read `next` after each merge/park, so it can keep polling an empty scope forever instead of reporting completion. The opencode delta in the same change explicitly adds “or when the scope is empty”; vscode needs the same completion stop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code delta says the iteration runs in the background with the operator as the exception and describes a wave loop that re-reads `next` after each merge or park, but then the same item instructs “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” On a scope with two ready items and no question, an agent following this text ends the background request after the first merge and prints a handoff; the second ready item is not driven until someone starts a new request. The delta therefore still stops at end-of-request rather than only on a question/operator gate or an empty scope, contradicting the heading and the orchestration stop contract this change is supposed to emit.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The updated kilo-cline delta states that where the runtime has no task-subagent run (Roo), the agent should "do ONE item directly — claim, gate, merge — then print `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` as the handoff." However, the rule [r-adapters] requires that every external dependency goes through a port in `ddflow/adapters`, and this hardcoded string-matching instruction bypasses the adapter abstraction by instructing the agent to directly output raw command strings instead of invoking an adapter-managed handoff function or port.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:23

chunk_findings.detail: The text instructs the VS Code driver to print `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` (with an underscore), but the canonical command name used throughout ddflow and in the neighboring deltas (e.g. opencode.md, kilo-cline.md) is `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` (with a space). An agent executing this delta literally will output `ddflow_next`, which is not a valid command and breaks the handoff.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14

chunk_findings.detail: The updated source-of-truth loop spec defines an empty scope as “no ready, held or in-flight items”, but the Kilo instance emitted in this same change defines DONE as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left” and no claimed item in flight. The docstring omits blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) and no ready, held, or in-flight items, this record says the scope is empty and the loop should stop, while the emitted Kilo rule says it is a WAIT. Since this record is meant to be the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a driver delta generated from it can stop with blocked work still pending.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:Orchestration

chunk_findings.detail: The new claim-before-fan wording tells the VS Code background orchestrator to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items” to another window/terminal agent, but the same delta later says that for parallelism “each claims its own item and gets its own worktree” (line 23). Given one ready item, say `101`, an orchestrator following line 13 claims `101` and then opens a terminal/window agent for `101`; the terminal agent, following the same delta, attempts to claim `101` itself. If claims are exclusive, that claim fails and the item is left claimed by the orchestrator but not worked, stalling the wave. The emitted instruction does not say that dispatched agents must skip claiming or that the orchestrator’s claim transfers to the dispatched process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:13

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop rule says the background wave stops only when the scope is empty (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight) or on an “operator answer,” but it omits the required stop on an unanswered `question` or operator gate. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope with one ready item that, when claimed/fanned, raises a `question` (or is parked at an operator gate), the scope is not empty and no operator answer has arrived yet, so the literal rule tells the driver not to stop; it will keep waiting/re-reading or continuing instead of stopping and surfacing the question/gate. This contradicts the intended loop (“stop ONLY on a question or operator gate”) and the kilo-cline delta in the same diff, which says “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate.”
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence slot is still keyed only by `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, and the added text “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” is only an instruction, not an enforcement mechanism: no run/invocation id, lock, or active-run marker is specified for a second orchestrator to check. If an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice from two terminals, run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 over it. A later compaction/restart resumes from the stale wave. The prior fix does not answer this interleaving because both runs are already concurrent and neither has a way to detect the other before writing the same key.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-35 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. The new sentence “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” does not tell the agent how to detect an existing same-scope run or refuse to start, and there is no lock on the memory slot. The prior interleaving still occurs as soon as that instruction is violated: run A reads wave 10 and stalls, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 and overwrites B; a later compaction or restart resumes from the stale position and can re-claim or skip items. The fix is a normative prohibition, not a guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32

chunk_findings.detail: The source-of-truth `Orchestration` docstring defines empty scope as “(no ready, held or in-flight items)”, but the emitted Kilo template’s DONE test requires no ready, no held **or blocked** items, and no claimed item still in flight. `blocked` is a separate category in the template’s own wording (“`held`/`blocked` items come later”), so the harness-agnostic data omits it. A generator transcribing this docstring will emit a stop rule that treats a blocked item—e.g. an item waiting on a lease/dependency that will later become ready—as not preventing completion, so the driver stops while the scope is not empty and skips that item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:89

chunk_findings.detail: The new text tells the background surface to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items to one window/terminal agent each”, but the Subagents section below still says parallelism is separate processes and “each claims its own item and gets its own worktree.” Given one ready item, the background surface claims it and then hands an already-claimed item to a second window/terminal agent; that agent cannot claim its own item and gets no worktree. The two instructions contradict for the same VS Code driver.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:14-15

chunk_findings.detail: The paragraph says “Stop only on the empty scope … or an operator answer. Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” For a scope with two ready items, after the first merge the empty-scope stop condition is false (the second item is still ready/in flight), so the “then end” instruction causes a premature handoff instead of re-reading `ddflow next` after each merge until the scope is actually empty. The rewrite did not remove this conflict.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16-18

chunk_findings.detail: The stop condition says “Stop only on the empty scope … or an operator answer,” but the correct loop stop is on a `question` or operator gate, not on the answer. Given a ready item that raises an operator gate/question and then waits, an agent following this line sees no operator answer yet and therefore does not treat the pending gate as the stop; it may keep re-reading/polling instead of waiting for the operator. The neighboring kilo-cline delta uses the correct “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate” wording.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The handoff instruction still writes `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` with underscores, while the current kilo-cline delta says `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` and the actual commands use a space. An agent executing the VS Code delta literally prints invalid command names, breaking the handoff.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentence claims the claim lease enforces "one run per scope, so the slot is never written by two runs", but a claim lease guards *claims*, not writes to the memory slot `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, which is still keyed only by the scope token. Demonstrating input: `/ddflow-wave bugs` is started twice; run A claims item 101, launches its task child, and stalls before persisting; run B then reads `ddflow next`, finds item 102 still unleased, claims it (the lease never fires, because A and B claimed disjoint items), and persists the newer wave position into `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; when A's child merges 101, A persists its older wave position over B's. A later compaction or restart of run B loads A's stale position and loses track of 102's in-flight/merged status. The lease therefore does not make the "never written by two runs" claim true, and the earlier confirmed defect (persistence keyed only by scope, with no run/invocation id or slot lock) still stands at this new wording; the change also gives no instruction telling a second run to stop when its claims fail, while rule 5 says stop happens only on DONE or a question, so the losing run keeps driving and keeps writing the shared slot.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36-37 (and the identical text at ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:35-36)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop still gives the orchestrating request a direct claim step: “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge”. That contradicts the immediately preceding sentence, which says the fan-out dispatches each ready item to a window/terminal agent that “claims its OWN item”. Given one ready item `101`, a background VS Code surface following this paragraph fans `101` to a terminal agent (which will claim `101`) and then follows the “claim” instruction itself; ddflow’s exclusive lease then refuses one of the two claims, so either the child cannot start or the background contends, and the wave can stall or skip that item. The delta should say the dispatched processes claim/gate/merge while the background only waits and re-reads. The same text is in `docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The added “enforcement” does not make the persistence slot single-writer. ddflow’s claim lease is item-scoped — the text itself says “those items already leased” — not a run/scope mutex. Given a scope with two ready items 101 and 102, run A can claim 101 and pause before saving, while run B (`/ddflow-wave bugs`) starts, claims 102, and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; then A saves its older read over B’s slot. A later compaction/restart resumes from whichever write landed last, not necessarily the newest wave. This is the previous persistence-overwrite defect still present; the claim-lease fix does not answer it because it only stops duplicate per-item claims, not concurrent same-scope runs writing the same memory key.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36 (rule 4) and ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The empty-scope stop test is `empty scope (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight)`, but the new dispatch model tells the background surface to fan each ready item WITHOUT claiming it (lines 13-14) and then re-read only `ddflow next --json`. `ddflow next` does not list an item that has been claimed and is still being implemented; the matching Kilo loop in this same change requires a separate “no item you claimed is still in flight” test for exactly that reason. Because the vscode surface did not claim the items and is given no instruction to wait for or track the spawned window/terminal agents, it cannot evaluate “none in flight.” Concrete input: ready items 101 and 102 are fanned to two agents; 102 merges first. The surface re-reads `ddflow next --json` and sees no ready and no held/blocked (101 is claimed/unreported). It can declare the scope empty and stop/hand off while 101 is still being implemented, so the loop stops before all in-flight work has finished.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16 (same text in docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md)

chunk_findings.detail: The handoff instruction still says to output `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence`, with underscores. The actual commands used throughout ddflow and earlier in this same delta are `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` (space-separated). An agent following this literally outputs `ddflow_next`, which is not a valid command, so the handoff is broken.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:19 (same text in docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md)

chunk_findings.detail: The new ownership rule persists “your own agent/session id” and tells the agent to stop if, on resume, the stored id is not the current one, but it never clears the slot on a normal stop or checks whether the stored owner is still alive. This makes a completed or crashed run permanently own the scope. For example, run A starts `/ddflow-wave bugs`, saves session id `s1`, then crashes; a later Kilo session starts as `s2`, loads `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, sees `s1 != s2`, and follows rule 4 by stopping instead of resuming or starting, even though no run owns the scope. The same text is shipped in `.kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md`, so the emitted agent inherits the failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:33

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope stop defines completion as `ddflow next` reporting “no ready and no held/blocked” and then asserts “an in-flight item is held by its lease.” That assertion is not how the corrected wave loop semantics work: a claimed/in-flight item is not reported as `held`/`blocked` by `ddflow next`, which is why the Kilo wave rule requires a separate “no item you claimed is still in flight” check. Given a scope with one ready item `101`, the background request fans `101` to a terminal/window agent, that agent claims it and is still implementing it. A re-read of `ddflow next --json` now returns no ready and no held/blocked items, so this text tells the VS Code driver that the scope is empty and the request may stop and print the handoff while `101` is still in flight, prematurely ending the wave and leaving no driver waiting for the merge/park.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The new ownership token is checked only “On resume, if the stored id is not yours,” not when a fresh `/ddflow-wave` run starts. A brand-new run never reads the existing `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` before claiming or saving, so two concurrent same-scope runs can still overwrite each other’s wave position. Concrete interleaving: an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` from two terminals. Run A saves wave 10 with id A; run B starts fresh, sees no resume condition, claims items, and saves wave 12 with id B, overwriting A. Run A then saves wave 11 over B. A later compaction or restart resumes from whichever write landed last, potentially re-claiming or skipping items. The stated “one `/ddflow-wave` run per scope at a time” is therefore still not enforced for concurrent fresh starts.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32-36 (rule 4; same text in ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-35)

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope condition asserts that “an in-flight item is held by its lease,” so it defines empty solely as `ddflow next` reporting no ready and no held/blocked. But this VS Code driver has the background surface fan each ready item to a child process that claims its own item, and the surface keeps no separate record of which children are still implementing. `ddflow next` after a claim does not show the claimed, still-in-flight item as held/blocked — the Kilo loop in this same change had to add an explicit “no item you claimed is still in flight” check for exactly that reason. Concrete failure: with one ready item `101`, the surface fans `101` to a terminal agent, which claims it and starts the gates/merge; the surface re-reads `ddflow next`, sees no ready and no held/blocked, and, following this line, treats the scope as empty and stops/hands off before `101` completes. The stop condition must test for no fanned/claimed item still in flight, not infer that state from `ddflow next`’s held/blocked categories.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten stop condition defines completion as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited … and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” but it no longer requires that there be no held or blocked items. Given a VS Code background wave on a scope with ready item `101` and blocked item `102` (for example, `102` waiting on an unmet dependency), the driver fans `101`; after `101` merges and its child exits, `ddflow next --json` reports no ready items. Following line 17 literally, the driver treats that as the empty scope and stops, even though `102` remains blocked and the scope is not DONE. The corrected wave loop requires no ready, held, blocked, or in-flight items before stopping, so this delta can abandon remaining work.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code wave stop condition defines completion as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited (merged or parked) and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” dropping the previous “no held/blocked” part of the empty-scope test. Since `ddflow next` only reports ready work, a scope with no ready or in-flight items but one blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) satisfies this literal rule, so a background VS Code driver can stop and treat the scope as complete while blocked work remains; the corrected wave DONE test used elsewhere in this change requires no held or blocked items left.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten vscode empty-scope stop condition now says to stop when all dispatched windows/terminals have exited and `ddflow next` reports “nothing ready,” but it no longer requires `ddflow next` to report no held/blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a held or blocked item (for example an item `ddflow park`ed waiting on a long gate, or blocked on an unmet dependency), `ddflow next --json` reports that item as held/blocked rather than ready, and no dispatched window is running; an agent following this text treats the scope as empty and stops, leaving the held/blocked item unprocessed. The previous wording explicitly included “no ready and no held/blocked”; the new wording drops the held/blocked half of the completion test.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope stop condition is defined as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited (merged or parked) and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” but it omits held/blocked items. Concrete input: a scope has one held or blocked item and no ready items, and all previously dispatched windows/terminals have exited. `ddflow next` reports nothing ready, so an agent following this line stops the wave, leaving that held/blocked item unprocessed. The loop’s empty-scope condition must be no ready and no held/blocked items (plus no in-flight), as the rest of this change requires.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The background orchestrator is first told to “fan each ready item to one window/terminal agent each (the dispatched process claims its OWN item)”, then in the same paragraph is told “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge”. Concrete input: one ready item 101; the orchestrator fans 101 to a child that claims it, then following the later “claim” instruction attempts to claim 101 itself. ddflow’s exclusive lease refuses that duplicate claim, so the wave stalls or errors. The orchestrating request must not claim an item it has already handed to a self-claiming child.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:19

data.context: Operator question 2026-11-02 during a long restart wait. Reuses DX-park-and-resume, the brief RESUME section and recover, the P-soft-upgrade shim, the PreCompact and SessionStart hooks, P-governor pause, heartbeat and inbox notices.
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-02: restarts of ddflow MCP and the Claude agent are frequent, so ddflow supports (1) WIND DOWN: a draining state; next and claim stop offering new work (the answer names the next call); running agents get a wrap-up notice on their next heartbeat (finish gates, merge, release); unfinished work is parked with branch and commit recorded; (2) RESTART READINESS: a status that says ready or not and lists what blocks (running lanes and gates left, pending approvals with the exact re-ask text, worktrees with uncommitted work, lease chains, operator-owned uncommitted files in the primary checkout); (3) WIND UP: runs from the SessionStart hook, clears draining, restores the local-layer overrides the session set, lists parked lanes in resume order derived from needs and lease waits, re-asks pending approvals. The surfaces are ACTIONS on the existing ddflow_session family tool plus matching CLI verbs: NO new MCP tool. The handoff pack is DERIVED from the event log and the worktrees (never hand-written), stored as a record and rendered to a local file; no secrets, endpoints or keys in it. Restarting Claude or the MCP process is not a ddflow command: wind-down ends with the exact thing for the operator to do (the soft-upgrade shim already restarts the worker alone). APPROVALS: an approved but unspent approval may be RE-BOUND to the successor agent for the same item and the same exact command, only with the operator explicit confirmation at wind-down (one question listing each approval); single-use, digest and expiry are unchanged.

chunk_findings.detail: This test is not a real regression guard for `test_every_extra_has_a_contract`: it only checks a locally constructed set against the global `_EXTRA_IMPORTS`, never pyproject or the actual contract test. If `numpy` is later added as a legitimate optional dependency (add `numpy` to `_EXTRA_IMPORTS` and to `forbidden_modules` so the contract test passes), this test fails because `dists - set(_EXTRA_IMPORTS)` no longer contains `numpy`. Conversely, if `test_every_extra_has_a_contract` is reverted to the old hard-coded extra-name check while `_EXTRA_IMPORTS` and `_dist_name` remain, this test still passes, so it does not prevent the original bug from returning.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_architecture_import_contracts.py:test_package_added_under_existing_extra_is_checked

chunk_findings.detail: `_dist_name` omits `@` from the separator regex, but PEP 508 also supports direct-reference requirements such as `name@url`. Given a pyproject optional dependency like `mcp@https://example.com/mcp-1.0.tar.gz`, `_dist_name` returns the whole string (or a wrong prefix if the URL contains `=`, `[`, `;`, etc.), so `dists` mismatches `_EXTRA_IMPORTS` and `test_every_extra_has_a_contract` fails/misclassifies the package even though its distribution name is `mcp`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_architecture_import_contracts.py:_dist_name

chunk_findings.detail: The new “regression” test never invokes `test_every_extra_has_a_contract` or `_contracts()`. It only builds a local `extras` dict and asserts that `"numpy"` is absent from `_EXTRA_IMPORTS`. In an environment where the actual guard is reverted to the old hard-coded `_EXTRA_MODULES` behavior while `_EXTRA_IMPORTS` remains as-is, this test still passes, so it does not actually detect the B-arch-guard-extras-hardcoded regression it claims to cover.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_architecture_import_contracts.py:test_package_added_under_existing_extra_is_checked

chunk_findings.detail: When the parametrization reaches `ddflow_decision_add`, the test sends `relation="merge_into:<old-decision-id>"` and asserts `body["extended"] == old` and `body["relation"] == "extends"`. That is a concrete input that still extends an existing decision in place: an open/unclaimed `D-orphan-recovery` answered with `merge_into:D-orphan-recovery` returns success, records `extended=D-orphan-recovery`, and therefore adds the new globs to the old decision while the new decision text is not filed. This contradicts the change's own statement that decisions are never edited in place and the bug's expected behavior (new linked record, or a refusal that does not edit the target); the fix only changes the `extends` answer, leaving an API/MCP path that mutates the old decision.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_add_dedupe_mcp.py:test_relation_extends_answers_the_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: The updated regression tests do not verify the reported core symptom: that the new decision text is preserved on the newly filed record. For `decision add --id D-new --title SECOND --decision SECOND --globs src/b.py --extends D-old`, the tests assert only the new id, globs, and link (`out.data["id"]`, `st.decisions["D-new"].globs`, `st.links["D-new"].linked("extends")`), and the CLI test only checks that `"D-new"` appears in stdout. A partial fix that creates `D-new` with the correct link/globs but stores `decision=""` or `title=""`—i.e. still drops the new decision text—would pass these tests. Thus the test change does not certify the bug described in the intent and can pass an implementation that still loses the new decision content.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_extend_globs.py:test_decision_extends_files_a_new_linked_record_and_leaves_the_target

chunk_findings.detail: The comment says decisions are “never edited in place,” but it also says “duplicate_of still merges.” For an open/unclaimed decision, `ddflow decision add --duplicate_of <old-id>` will still take the pre-change in-place extension path: the old decision is mutated and no new record is made. That is the same class of mutation as B-decision-extends-mutates-old-record, just under the `duplicate_of` answer, and it contradicts the invariant this change adds.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/_dedupe.py: LINK_ONLY_KINDS / duplicate_of

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring states “``extends X`` is never an extension: it files a new record linked to X,” but the same change still tests non-LINK_ONLY tools with `relation="extends"` and asserts `body["extended"] == old` in `tests/test_add_dedupe_mcp.py`. So for kinds not in `LINK_ONLY_KINDS`, `extends` still causes an in-place extension exactly as before; the documented contract is false, and a caller relying on it will get an old-record mutation instead of a new linked record.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/_dedupe.py: module docstring

chunk_findings.detail: The acceptance condition `keep and keep_partial and keep != list(it.globs)` treats any list difference from the current globs as a gain, so it can accept a proper subset of the currently held globs instead of only a partial widening. For example, if a live item currently holds `["src/a.py", "src/b.py"]` and a request asks for `["src/a.py", "src/c.py"]`, where `"src/c.py"` clashes with another live lease, `_clash_text` can return `keep=["src/a.py"]`. With `keep_partial=True`, `_clash_rule` returns accepted `["src/a.py"]` (because it differs from the two-element current list), so `plan_retarget` reports success and the caller writes the subset, silently dropping the currently leased `"src/b.py"`. The stated fix is for accepting the non-overlapping subset of a *widening*; an accepted subset that does not retain all currently held globs should still be refused.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py:_clash_rule

chunk_findings.detail: The new `if data.get("globs_withheld")` block is indented inside the preceding `if data.get("globs_dropped")` block, so a successful partial widening that withholds globs but drops none gets no withheld message. For example, if M1's current globs are `mine.py`, another live lease holds `pkg/gates/x.py`, and the user runs `update M1 --globs mine.py,docs/r.md,pkg/gates/x.py`, the update can return `ok` with `globs_withheld=["pkg/gates/x.py"]` and `globs_dropped=[]`. Because `data.get("globs_dropped")` is falsey, the withheld branch never runs, so the CLI prints success but omits that `pkg/gates/x.py` was withheld, contrary to the stated intent to name withheld globs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/update_message.py:20

chunk_findings.detail: The final assertion only checks that the whole event log contains *some* event of kind `lease.waiting`; it no longer bounds the check to events emitted by the `update` invocation, and it does not verify that the waiting event is for the withheld `docs/x.md` path or lease. An implementation that prints `withheld docs/x.md`, updates T1 to `src/a.py,src/c.py`, and emits a `lease.waiting` event for an unrelated path (or where any prior helper/fixture event of that kind already exists) would pass this test even though the withheld path was not registered as waiting, which is exactly what the docstring claims to prove. The previous test recorded `n = len(EventLog(...).read_all())` and asserted the exact new event kinds, so this change weakens the regression check.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_update_globs_lease.py:test_widening_partly_into_another_live_lease_keeps_the_subset

chunk_findings.detail: The new partial-accept condition does not actually require the request to be a widening. It accepts whenever `keep` is non-empty, `keep_partial` is true, and `keep != list(it.globs)`, but `keep` is only the non-overlapping part of the requested `globs`. A non-widening replacement that removes a currently held glob and adds an unavailable overlapping glob is therefore accepted and silently drops the held glob. Example: `X.globs == ["a", "b"]`; another lease holds `"c"`; request `globs == ["a", "c"]` with `keep_partial=True`. `_clash_text` returns `keep == ["a"]`. Since `["a"] != ["a", "b"]`, `_clash_rule` returns `["a"], ""`, so `plan_retarget` returns accepted `["a"]`. The all-or-nothing behavior the feature was meant to relax for widenings would have refused and kept `["a", "b"]`; instead `"b"` is lost even though it was never part of the overlap refusal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py:_clash_rule

chunk_findings.detail: The new partial-acceptance guard uses order-sensitive list equality (`keep != list(it.globs)`) to decide whether the request “gains nothing,” so a request whose surviving globs are the same set as the current lease but listed in a different order (or with duplicates) is accepted instead of refused. For example, if the live lease holds globs `["a", "b"]`, another live lease holds `c`, and the agent widens to `["b", "a", "c"]`, `_clash_text` returns `keep=["b", "a"]`; `_clash_rule` returns `(["b", "a"], "")`, so `plan_retarget` treats the partial widening as accepted and the caller writes the lease globs, even though the docstring says a request whose surviving globs are exactly the ones already held gains nothing and must stay a refusal. The check should compare sets (or require a strict superset if this is specifically a widening path) rather than raw lists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py:_clash_rule

chunk_findings.detail: The new withheld hint tells the user to “re-run with them once that holder is done”, but in this command `--globs` replaces the entire list, as the adjacent `globs_dropped` hint states. If an item currently has globs `mine.py` and the user runs an update to `mine.py,pkg/gates/x.py` where `pkg/gates/x.py` is withheld, the update succeeds and leaves `mine.py` accepted. The message then says to re-run with `pkg/gates/x.py`. If the user follows that literally and runs `--globs pkg/gates/x.py`, the command will record only `pkg/gates/x.py` and silently drop the existing `mine.py` glob. The hint should tell the user to re-run with the withheld globs plus the globs they want to keep, not just “with them”.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/update_message.py:20

chunk_findings.detail: The new test no longer isolates the event log to the update under test. It reads the entire event log and only checks that some event with kind `lease.waiting` exists anywhere. If the repository state produced by the fixture or `_two_claims` already contains a `lease.waiting` event (for example from a previously queued claim or another operation), and the partial update withholds `docs/x.md` but fails to append a new `lease.waiting` event, the test still passes. The previous version captured `n = len(EventLog(...).read_all())` before the update and asserted that the post-update delta was exactly `["lease.waiting"]`; removing that delta check makes the test falsely pass when the required wait event was not produced by the update.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_update_globs_lease.py:169

chunk_findings.detail: In the partial-widening success path, `_waiting(log, cfg, it, lease, withheld, queue)` and `L.retarget(log, it.id, lease, accepted, resources)` both receive the same `lease` returned by `plan_retarget`. A partial widening into “another live lease” necessarily involves two distinct leases: the item’s own lease, which should be retargeted to `accepted`, and the other live lease that currently holds the withheld globs, which is the lease whose release should wake this item. The single `lease` cannot serve both roles; if `lease` is the item’s lease, the wait is attached to the wrong lease and the item is never woken when the real holder frees the withheld globs, and if `lease` is the other holder, `L.retarget` mutates the other lease instead of the item’s lease. This makes the changed partial-widening success path incorrect for any partial overlap with a distinct live lease.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:421

chunk_findings.detail: The test expects the update to add the new non-overlapping glob `src/c.py` to `st.items["T1"].globs` and `st.items["T1"].lease.globs` while also recording `lease.waiting` for `docs/x.md` under `T1`. That is a hold-and-wait state: `T1` acquires a new hold on `src/c.py` and waits for `docs/x.md`. The previous version of this test asserted exactly the opposite behavior for a widening into a live lease: the edit/lease change recorded nothing and only a `lease.waiting` event was emitted, explicitly citing `DX-no-hold-and-wait`. The new expectation codifies a deadlock-prone state and contradicts that invariant, so a correct no-hold-and-wait implementation would reject the update rather than pass this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_update_globs_lease.py:test_widening_partly_into_another_live_lease_keeps_the_subset

chunk_findings.detail: The signature and all the early returns shown now return a 3-tuple `(Lease | None, str, list[str] | None)`, but the terminal success return after the `if resources:` block is still the old two-element `return lz, ""`. Example input: a live lease for item `M1` is retargeted to `globs=["new.py"]` with `resources=None` and no live clash or queued ahead; the function falls through and returns two values. Any caller that unpacks the new three-element contract, such as `lease, msg, accepted = plan_retarget(...)`, raises `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 2)` on the normal successful update path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py:plan_retarget

data.budget: about 3 hours, read-only, scratch worktrees in a temp dir
data.claim: PARTLY. ddflow already runs a real fail-before/pass-after check for bug fixes (verify_regression_test); the gaps are (a) 40 percent of bug fixes closed without a machine-run F2P, (b) no F2P/weakening/flake check for ordinary tasks, (c) hand-recorded gates (research, rules, implement, bug_hunt, dedupe) pass on a note, (d) reviewers see only the diff and are not prompted for test quality. A deterministic evidence gate (F2P of new tests on the pre-change tree, weakening detector, skip-is-not-pass, flake rerun, bounded mutation on risk globs) covers most of it; an LLM QA reviewer should be an advisory lens fed those results, never a separate blocking round. DESIGN PART IS THEORETICAL; the measurements are CONFIRMED.
data.falsifier: On the 25-bug F2P sample and 19-merge revert sample, the proposed checks classify fewer than 80 percent the way a manual run did, or the seeded bad-test set (QA-eval) is caught below 90 percent, or per-item cost exceeds 5 percent of current gate wall time.
data.mechanism: Reuse services/gates/mutation.verify_regression_test + regression_run.not_a_pass/not_a_failure on the item's own base with the new test files overlaid; AST diff of tests for weakening; flakes.py for rerun; mutation {file,old,new} registry format for bounded mutants; LLM only proposes mutants or triages anomalies, ddflow runs them.
data.probe: event-log analysis (131306 events, 2026-09-28..2026-11-03, window 2026-10-04..): bug.fixed regression_verified counts; gate.failed rates; ci.result stages; git worktree checkout of landed_before with test files overlaid from landed_after, python -m pytest <node ids>; AST scan of 1126 merges / 8811 new test functions; revert of source files for 19 merges
data.probe_output: 731 bugs fixed in window: 711 declared a regression test; regression_verified verified 427, verified-by-mutation 10, could-not-run 115, not-applicable 67, overridden 41, exempt-lint 20, none 51 (unverified share fell from >50pct Oct4-10 to ~17pct Oct25-Nov3). Own F2P run of 20 unverified fixes: 11 fail before with AssertionError, 2 fail only by ImportError, 6 pass before (all test-file-only fixes), 1 skipped; 5 of 5 control (verified) fail before (1 of 5 also failed after: env noise). New-test AST scan: 8811 new tests in 1126 merges; 0.6pct no assert (static, upper bound), 2.1pct only truthy/is-not-None asserts, 74 merges (6.6pct) net-removed tests, 18 merges lowered assert count, 24 new skip/xfail. Revert-all-source on 19 merges: 18 detect (6 by ImportError only), 1 passes (a pure file split). Gate yield: bug_hunt failed on 0.1pct of completed items, dedupe 0.1pct, standards 0.8pct, unit_tests 7.2pct, ci 40pct, rubber_duck 68pct, critic 68pct. merge-stage ci failed 121/1309 (9.2pct), all lint/format/bandit/gitleaks, 0 test failures. 45 distinct main-red bugs filed in window (14 on 2026-10-18). Hypothesis installed, 4 property suites; no coverage.py, no mutmut, no pytest-cov.
data.question: Does ddflow need a QA agent as a gate that verifies the changes produce trustworthy test evidence and are correct and resilient?

data.alternatives: Advisory LLM lens only (recommended by research, not chosen); neither; fold into P-test-flows
data.context: R-qa-gate measured: 60 percent of fixed bugs carry a machine-run fail-before proof (rising); 98-99 percent of bug_hunt/dedupe/rules/implement passes are note-only; reviewers carry no test-quality instruction; mutation_tests cadence skipped 3 of 5 runs for lack of a tool; reviews already fail 68 percent of items.
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-02/03, after R-qa-gate: (1) EVIDENCE CHECKS on EVERY code task, WARN for the first month: run the new and changed tests on the pre-change tree (fail-before), weakening detector (net-removed tests, lowered asserts, new skip/xfail, loosened tolerance, updated snapshot), flake rerun of the new tests on HEAD; each check flips from warn to block only after a seeded bad-test set shows a false-positive rate the operator accepts. Mutation on changed lines only for risk globs (security, engine, hooks, leases, tier:deep) and on a cadence, with a hard budget; survivors recorded. (2) A SEPARATE BLOCKING QA REVIEWER AGENT (operator choice, against the research recommendation of an advisory lens): a judgement gate qa after the evidence gate. Guardrails the coordinator adds so it cannot add non-converging rounds: it reads the diff, the test evidence and the deterministic results; one full round and at most one delta round; a BLOCKING finding must cite a probe ddflow actually ran (a failing mutant, a test that passes before the fix, an uncovered failure path run); findings without a probe are advisory and never block; it may propose up to 5 mutants that ddflow executes; reviewer independence follows D-reviewer-independence-soft (single-subscription users: the deterministic checks carry the weight). (3) TOOLING: the operator consents to coverage.py (pytest-cov), diff-cover and mutmut as dev dependencies; report-only coverage (no threshold); mutmut limited to risk globs and the cadence because a full run takes tens of minutes. (4) New phase P-qa-evidence; the existing P-test-flows tasks (TF-filters, TF-mutation, TF-readonly, TF-lens, TF-eval) later extend these tasks and are not duplicated.
data.title: A QA evidence gate: deterministic checks on every code task (warn first), plus a separate blocking QA reviewer agent bounded to probe-backed findings

data.body: Operator 2026-11-03 (D-qa-evidence-answers; research R-qa-gate). Extends services/gates/mutation.py, regression_run.py, flakes.py; the P-test-flows tasks later extend these. Warn first, block only after measured false-positive rates.
data.title: QA evidence: trustworthy test evidence for every change: fail-before, weakening, flakes, bounded mutation, and a probe-backed QA reviewer

data.body: Make the 2026-11-03 measurements repeatable in ddflow metrics: share of fixed bugs with a machine-run fail-before outcome (verified, verified-by-mutation, could-not-run, not-applicable, overridden, none) by week; weakening counts per merge; merge-stage ci failures by cause (lint, format, bandit, gitleaks, tests). Falsifier: the view disagrees with R-qa-gate counts by more than 2 percent. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-adapters, D-qa-evidence-answers, D-reviewer-independence-soft, D-baseline-red-auto-accept): extend verify_regression_test, regression_run.py, gate verify mutations, flakes.py, the baseline-red measurement and the review runner; no second runner or comparer; a check that could not run is unavailable, never passed; a skip, xfail or not-collected is never a pass; the pre-change run covers at most about 8 test ids with a short timeout and never occupies the suite lock; warn by default; every message names its next call in CLI and MCP form. Research: R-qa-gate.

data.body: Generalise verify_regression_test (services/gates/mutation.py) and regression_run.py from bug fixes to every task: in a scratch tree of the base with the item's new and changed test files overlaid, run only those test ids (at most about 8, -n0, short timeout, never the suite lock) and record per id: failed-before (assertion or import-error kind), passed-before, skipped, errored. data.title: Pre-change run of the new and changed tests for any code task

data.body: Detect net-removed tests, lowered assert counts in a same-named test, new skip or xfail, loosened numeric tolerances, updated snapshots, deleted test files, assertions replaced by bare truthiness. data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-03, after R-research-mgmt: (1) NO NEW PHASE: the RS-* tasks extend P-research (claims, sources, verification, staleness, gate) and P-research-flows (flows, ledger, run, roles); the science tasks RS-sci-* sit under P-research-flows tagged profile=science so disabling the pack removes them. (2) VERDICTS: keep CONFIRMED, REFUTED, THEORETICAL; add evidence_type (executable | cited | reasoned) and DERIVED marks PROVED, REPLICATED, STALE (STALE computed from review_by); no enum migration. (3) The research gate becomes REQUIRED for kind=research only, after B-rw-gate-link: a pass needs a linked note with a non-empty probe and falsifier; falsifier is mandatory for CONFIRMED and REFUTED notes; other kinds keep the optional gate. (4) SCIENCE PACK is scheduled with the rest (not parked): pre-registration bound to the event-log timestamp, ethics/consent checklist, large data as hash pointers outside git, PHI/genomic redaction before any record, provenance export. (5) Defaults the coordinator applied for unasked points: fetched content is stored as hash plus short quote under a length cap, never whole pages; web access by research agents needs consent per project with a cost cap (RF-native-policy, P-safeguards.envelope). (6) Fetched pages are untrusted data, never instructions. Scope kinds: literature, programming, engineering, scientific, math (proof ladder: proved by kernel check, SMT-decided, CAS-derived, numeric-tested, conjecture), for this project, for another project (XP-target-project), and research as a standalone project.

data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-03, after R-test-mgmt: (1) QA-AS-A-PROJECT is a first-class profile in BOTH variants (a separate QA project with a [target] pointer to another repository, readonly or worktree mode; and a QA profile inside the target repository), starting with the target pointer. TM-target IS the shared target-project mechanism (called XP-target-project by the architecture, research and multi-repo tracks): other tracks depend on TM-target. (2) TWO PHASES: P-test-ops (TM-*, 18 tasks) and P-devsecops-ops (DS-*, 6 tasks). (3) NO NEW TEST-CASE TRACKER: a test case is a test card (TF-card) that points at executable tests or is a manual case with step results and evidence blobs; code stays the source of truth; bug records are the defects (new fields found_in, steps, expected, actual, environment, SUT pin, escaped). (4) DEFECT EXPORT: files first (markdown, CSV, JUnit); pushing to a target's forge only with a per-project consent recorded once. (5) ENVIRONMENTS a tester agent may touch WITHOUT asking: sandbox, ci and STAGING (operator choice, wider than the research default of sandbox and ci); production-like and production need a recorded human grant; egress allowlist and destructive-command denylist per environment; synthetic test data only. (6) Defaults applied for unasked points: a go/no-go is accepted by a person only (agents recommend); TDD is an OPTIONAL kind pipeline per task or project (red step must fail with an assertion, not an import error); Gherkin is an optional EXPORT only, no runner; compliance mappings are SSDF v1.1 and ASVS with the control list supplied as data. (7) TM-derive drafted tests need a probe that fails when the criterion is violated (not a reviewer opinion); QA-* and TF-* tasks are extended, never duplicated.

data.context: R-arch-product (measured: 445 decisions, 0 records of the shipped requirement/fitness/risk/stakeholder/assumption/proposal kinds, 31 percent of tasks cite a D- id, 11 percent an R- id, traceability planned seven times, 11 of 19 architecture follow-ups idle 24 days, 50 percent of decisions with empty consequences).
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-03, after R-arch-product: (1) TWO THIN INTEGRATION PHASES, P-architecture-ops (AR-) and P-product-ops (PO-; PD- is taken by product-docs), carrying needs-edges into P-decisions, P-product-docs, P-iac, P-constellation and rewriting none of them. The shared target-project mechanism is the already filed TM-target (not a separate XP-target-project); its requirements from this track are appended to it. (2) ONE CANONICAL REQUIREMENT KIND with a class (engineering, product, nfr, constraint) and a shared link vocabulary (realises, refines, verifies, governs, derived_from); PO-kinds-reconcile maps the seven overlapping kinds (shipped requirement, RQM, PD-req, SD, US, SPEC, SDD) BEFORE RQM-model, PD-req-kind and SD-model are built. (3) The ARCHITECTURE MODEL is derived: elements and edges are PROPOSALS the operator accepts, never silent writes; fitness checks WARN by default and block per fitness; a check that could not run is unavailable, never passed; checks for other stacks are proposed through the toolkit with consent, never installed. (4) ONE TRACE ENGINE: a citation index then one ddflow trace matrix; the seven per-kind trace tasks (RQM-trace, US-trace, SPEC-trace, PD-trace, SDD-trace, CN-trace, TF-trace) become adapters of it. (5) Defaults applied for unasked points: ddflow records and checks environments and never deploys (IA-release extends the environment kind), auto-promotion stays opt-in; assessments run weekly and at phase close through SCH-project-review once it is released from its hold; PM and architect agents get a docs-and-records lease profile and never edit product code.
data.title: Architecture ops and product ops are thin integration phases: one canonical requirement kind, one trace engine, a derived architecture model as proposals, fitness warn-by-default

data.body:
A [target] section naming another repository (path or forge URL) and a ref; mode readonly (checkout at the pinned sha) or worktree; the target hooks are disabled; every record made in the project carries the SUT pin (TF-pin vocabulary). THIS IS the shared target-project mechanism (XP-target-project) used by QA, research, architecture, product, change and multi-repo work: those tracks depend on this id. (3) The JOINT GATE of a cross-repo change set runs in the TESTS repository as integrator BY DEFAULT, UNLESS the user or company policy defines otherwise: [constellation].integrator (repo name | tests | owner | dedicated:NAME) is a knob, org-lockable. (4) PARTIAL FAILURE: stop the line, mark the set partial, offer forward-fix, revert items (new reviewed items in reverse order) or hold; NEVER auto-revert; resume is idempotent. (5) Defaults applied for unasked points: impact and drift findings warn (D-constellation), the joint gate blocks landing only for members of a declared change set; policy sharing goes through the org layer only (no new constellation layer, D-config-layer-order stays); [schedule] repos migrates into the manifest with an alias; reads are local sibling paths first, mirror and forge reads later; the shared target-project mechanism is TM-target (no XP-target-project).

data.context: R-change-mgmt measured: 346 approvals, 312 answered, ZERO denied; 16.5 percent of 1,565 completions forced (109 with no approval record, all before approval gating); config.set leaves no event (only git); no change classes, risk scores, freeze windows or rollback plans; 66 percent of bugs have no item link (median 18 min to detection for the linked ones). DORA: peer review plus automated pipeline beats external CAB.
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-03, after R-change-mgmt: (1) NEW PHASE P-change-mgmt with prefix CHG- (CM- is taken by commit-message tasks). (2) A CHANGE RECORD is a DERIVED VIEW over existing records (item.completed, ask.*, gates, ci.result, bugs, decisions, ledger), no new tracker; optional item fields risk_class, rollback_plan, window, change_class. (3) ENFORCE FROM DAY ONE (operator choice, against the advisory-first recommendation): [change].mode = enforce | warn | off, default enforce, org-lockable. Coordinator safeguards so enforcement cannot cause false refusals that block work: every refusal names the exact next call and a waiver path with a recorded reason; the emergency class always passes with a mandatory after-the-fact review item; the checks that need unproven data (risk scoring) start as classification labels with an explanation list and gate only through the rules the operator turned on; a check that could not run is unavailable, never passed. (4) THREE CLASSES: standard (pre-approved by a named bounded rule, low risk, evidence present, notice sent: docs-only, upgrade-note regeneration, baseline-red accept, patch dependency bumps), normal (today's pipeline), emergency (expedite with a mandatory after-the-fact review item). (5) FREEZE WINDOWS and change calendar are OPT-IN, OFF by default; an override needs the operator's T2 approval; the emergency class passes with after-review. (6) Defaults applied for unasked points: rollback plan required for high risk only and the revert helper is manually triggered (never automatic); approval evidence is shown with every request and a sampled audit of auto-approved and standard changes runs on a cadence; the standing window keeps its 24 h cap; cross-project change management waits for CN-cr and TM-target and until then records intent as a link only.
data.title: Change management as a derived change view with classes, risk, rollback and a report, ENFORCED from the start, freeze windows opt-in

data.alternatives: On-by-default profiles; always-block or always-warn stage gates; drafts-only feedback; separate project-management phase
data.context: R-lifecycle: about 40 phases already plan every stage, 0 requirement/story/spec records exist, only task to commit and bug to regression test are typed edges today; failures in multi-agent systems cluster at specification, misalignment and verification (MAST taxonomy), so the acceptance test is a seeded-failure run.
data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-03, after R-lifecycle: (1) ONE CAPSTONE PHASE P-lifecycle (prefix LF-, 19 integration tasks): no new record kind, no new tracker, no second suspect-link mechanism; each LF task reuses a topic track's ids. (2) LIFECYCLE PROFILES (agile iterative, V-model regulated, kanban flow, research-only, ops-only, docs-only) ship as PACKS, OFF by default, enabled at onboarding with consent, agile offered first; a profile may tighten but never silently loosen company floors (D-config-layer-order). (3) STAGE-EXIT GATES aggregate the entry and exit checks registered by the owning tracks; a check that is unavailable is recorded unavailable and never passed: BLOCK under the V-model profile, WARN under agile. (4) FEEDBACK LOOP (operator choice, against the drafts-only recommendation): operational signals (incidents, support tickets, usage signals, user feedback) CREATE PROPOSED items AUTOMATICALLY, each with a typed edge back to the signal and to the release that shipped it. Coordinator safeguards: items are PROPOSED only (never accepted, never started) until the operator adopts them; dedupe at add (D-no-duplicates); a per-source cap and backpressure (B-sched-backpressure); imported text is fenced as untrusted data (CN-spec-fence, RS-untrusted); no outward sends (PD-no-send); a flood trips a circuit breaker with a visible note. (5) PERSON-ONLY in every profile: acceptance, go/no-go, risk acceptance and release; agents recommend and may accept only low-risk requirement classes. (6) Defaults applied for unasked points: ONE trace read model: LF-trace-view is the lifecycle health view ON TOP OF the single trace engine PO-trace-matrix (no second engine), PD-trace stays the only suspect-link primitive; TM-target is the only shared target-project mechanism (XP-target-project is not filed); GC-roles is the single role record (LF-roles is a view, design starts after the GC-roles hold lifts); project management view stays inside P-lifecycle as LF-pm-view.

data.decision: OPERATOR 2026-11-03, after R-extension-points / R-extension-contract-design: new features (the phases added this week) must plug into the optimizer, gates, joins, proposals, notices and reports WITHOUT edits to shared files. (1) ONE DATA-ONLY FEATURE MANIFEST per feature, ddflow/features/NAME.toml, discovered by a sorted scan (duplicate id raises), code referenced lazily through the existing Lazy; the per-domain directories (config_sections, templates/events, templates/kinds, declared, harnesses) stay; each manifest carries contract = 1 and an unknown contract is skipped and reported. No plugin framework, no pluggy, no third-party in-process plugins (D-extension-seams). (2) ONE PROPOSAL RECORD with a registry of kinds and appliers (resolve the shipped proposal.toml against B-prop-model into one shape before SCH-review-inbox, PM-review-job, WP-merge-propose and P-observe.proposals start); peer suggestions between lanes stay a separate handoff record reusing the same apply interface. (3) OPTIMIZER INPUT OPENED NOW: a provider registry (kinds signal, constraint, cost-term, resource) with weight knobs, caps, explain text, simulation on/off, error isolation and fallback to v1, a populated ctx and open per-candidate facts; the 30 percent cap and the +10 percent makespan guard stay. (4) GATE PLUGINS with registered check kinds (command, probe, reviewer, rule, human, composite) inferred from old fields so old configs behave the same; JOIN POLICIES as data: default all (byte-identical to today), any_of, quorum, first_failure_stops and by_class are available but TIGHTEN-ONLY (loosening needs an approval); NO weighted join yet; a join changes only through a recorded plan revision; a merged gate keeps its own outcome. (5) Predicate and class registry shared by applies_when, approval rules and ticks; approval sites and rules as manifest rows, tighten-only, new rules ship OFF. (6) PLACEMENT: the 13 EX- tasks extend the existing phase P-extension-seams (no new phase). (7) Order to avoid rework: LK-config-autodiscover and LK-events-autodiscover plus EX-contract first, then the registries, then the phase tasks, each becoming one manifest. (8) YAGNI: the event fold stays closed, no second scheduler or simulator, no weighted join.

data.body:
A command gate evidence after unit_tests: runs QA-f2p-task and QA-weakening, stamps tree_sha, stores per-check results and a verdict; [qa].evidence = off|warn|block (default warn, strictest block, org-lockable); a bare pass is refused (B-evidence-contract); coordinates with DX-gate-auto-record-mechanical (bug_hunt cites the evidence result). Uses the config autodiscover seam if landed. CONFORMANCE (r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-adapters, D-qa-evidence-answers, D-reviewer-independence-soft, D-baseline-red-auto-accept): extend verify_regression_test, regression_run.py, gate verify mutations, flakes.py, the baseline-red measurement and the review runner; no second runner or comparer; a check that could not run is unavailable, never passed; a skip, xfail or not-collected is never a pass; the pre-change run covers at most about 8 test ids with a short timeout and never occupies the suite lock; warn by default; every message names its next call in CLI and MCP form. Research: R-qa-gate.

EXTENSION CONTRACT 2026-11-03 (D-extension-contract-answers): implement this as a feature manifest (ddflow/features/NAME.toml) plus the matching registry (gate plugin, join policy, optimizer provider, proposal kind, notice, predicate, section) instead of a special case or an edit to a shared hub file (defs.py, inbox.py, policy.py, flowsignals.py, health.py, README, config.py, mcp.py). The meta test EX-meta-test must stay green. See R-extension-contract-design.

Operator choice: a QA agent definition (read-only tools like the reviewer) and a judgement gate qa after evidence. It reads the diff, the test evidence and the deterministic results and answers: would these tests catch a regression, do they exercise failure paths and resilience (timeouts, concurrency, partial failure, restart, idempotence), is the evidence trustworthy.
